Uncertainty-Aware Fairness: reviewer notebook¶

This notebook accompanies the paper and presents the C1–C4 methods, experimental settings, results and supporting analyses. Each section connects the research question to its calculation, tables and figures.

Run: use a Python 3 kernel with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib and IPython; choose Restart Kernel and Run All. All numerical inputs and displayed figures are embedded. No account, network connection, patient records or external file paths are required. Saved output is supplied so that the evidence can also be read without execution.

Execution. Running the notebook recalculates C1 probabilities, C2 conditional quantities, an allocation-algorithm example and exact pooled C4 decisions. Other tables are reconstructed from the included aggregate experiment records; model fits and runtime benchmarks are supplied as recorded results.

1. Study questions and pipeline¶

The study audits fixed predictions; it does not train a model to make every group fair. An audit records a difference in errors or selection rates, compares its interval with a declared tolerance, and preserves an inconclusive outcome when the evidence supports neither passing nor failing. This keeps sparse groups visible instead of silently treating missing evidence as a pass.

Question / contribution What is initially known? Calculation Decision informed
RQ1 / C1 Group counts, a shared reference, a fixed audit rule and a count law Exact probabilities of repeated pass, inconclusive and fail; reusable boundary runs Whether a recorded verdict is stable and whether computation can be reused
RQ2 / C2 Repeated supported hospital comparisons and fitted variance components Conditional risk attribution and sufficient count guard Which fitted variation additional within-hospital observations could reduce
RQ3 / C3 Positive-outcome group membership, finite group sizes and pilot prediction linkage Budget allocation, confirmation probabilities and pilot-based forecast bounds Where to verify more records and whether the pilot supports a gain over balancing
RQ4 / C4 Two frozen predictions and their disagreement records Outcome verification and criterion-specific finite-population bounds Whether a proposed policy meets a declared miss/false-alert criterion

C2 is a sensitivity branch, not an input that has been validated to set C3 allocations. C3 verifies prediction linkage within a known positive frame; C4 verifies outcomes within known prediction disagreements. Their review units and assumptions must not be exchanged.

2. Cohorts, models, parameters and data checks¶

Texas-100X predicts length of stay greater than three days. The two ICU cohorts predict hospital mortality after a 24-hour ICU landmark. Hospital-separated or patient-separated development partitions have different roles: training fits parameters, tuning chooses configurations, calibration fixes the operating threshold, and test predictions supply the audit inputs. All clinical analyses are exploratory because these cohorts had already been examined.

The code below checks partition arithmetic and reconstructs the main cohort table. Missing patient identifiers in Texas mean that hospital separation cannot establish patient separation. MIMIC-III has one institution; the repeated 1 in the hospital column does not mean one patient.

2.1 Complete training and audit configuration¶

Training-only preprocessing learns medians, missingness indicators, scaling and category vocabularies. The principal Texas model uses age code, admission type, admission source and admitting diagnosis. eICU uses 90 numeric and two categorical predictors; MIMIC-III uses 42 numeric predictors and constant context. The feature inventory below lists the recorded columns. Source recording times limit ICU inputs to information available by 24 hours; Texas prospective timing is unverified.

Logistic regression: search $C\in\{0.1,1\}$, $L_2$ regularization, LBFGS and at most 1,000 iterations. Selected $C$ values are 1, 0.1 and 0.1 for Texas, eICU and MIMIC.

XGBoost: search depth 3 or 6, maximum 1,000 trees, learning rate 0.05, row and column subsampling 0.8, minimum child weight 10 and $L_2=1$. Histogram fitting stops after 40 rounds without tuning-log-loss improvement. All selected depths are six. Seed-11 tree counts are 1,000, 377 and 142, with thresholds 0.421920, 0.073716 and 0.083448. The stored table gives unrounded thresholds. Seeds 29 and 47 provide conditional training sensitivities, not new cohorts.

Neural comparators: two-layer MLP and two-block residual network search widths 64/128, with dropout 0.1. Two attention blocks use four heads, pre-normalization, GELU and token widths 16/32. Selected MLP widths are 64/128, residual widths 128/128, and attention widths 32/16 for eICU/MIMIC. AdamW uses learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.0001, binary cross-entropy with logits, at most 40 epochs, gradient norm cap one, patience six and minimum log-loss improvement $10^{-5}$. Training batches are 2,048 for MLP/ResNet and 256 for attention; prediction batches are 512.

Configuration selection maximizes tuning average precision. The selected within-configuration checkpoint minimizes tuning log loss. A separate calibration partition selects the highest threshold reaching 80% sensitivity. This is a declared research operating point, not a clinically endorsed threshold.

Audit configuration: family error 0.05, minimum denominator one and principal tolerance 0.10, with 0.05/0.15 sensitivity. Principal unit bootstraps use 9,999 draws, secondary families 1,999 and predictive intervals 500. These are separate from C–C's 1,999 and UM's 19,999 draws in the external-method comparison. Section 3 gives their exact definitions.

Training environment records specify Python 3.12.14, NumPy/pandas 2.3.3, SciPy 1.16.2, scikit-learn 1.7.2, XGBoost 3.0.5, joblib 1.6.0 and PyTorch 2.8.0 with CUDA 12.8 on an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU. Historical timing studies used a different Python/SciPy environment, stated in Section 3. Saved settings establish provenance; this notebook does not retrain those models.

3. C1: exact repeated audit probabilities¶

For an FNR comparison, $n_g$ is the number of positive outcomes and $k_g$ the number missed. The reference count is shared across the comparisons. Conditional on a reference count, independent group masses can be summed over the pass, inconclusive and fail ranges. Summing these conditional probabilities over the reference mass retains their shared dependence.

With interval $[L_g-U_0,U_g-L_0]$ and tolerance $\delta$, pass means the entire interval lies inside $[-\delta,\delta]$; fail means it lies strictly outside; all other cases are inconclusive. Zero positive support stays inconclusive. Any change, mean conclusiveness and all-group conclusiveness are separate probabilities, but can nearly coincide up to a factor when all recorded states are inconclusive and simultaneous resolutions are extremely rare.

The kernel below prepares integer decision ranges, combines consecutive reference counts whose ranges agree, and evaluates probability masses on those runs. Prefix and suffix sums reduce cancellation. Reuse requires the same denominators, tolerance and rule; a changed decision boundary requires rebuilding. The implementation is a readable reviewer kernel, not the memory-engineered benchmark executable.

Synthetic check passed on 3,000 count combinations.
Maximum error across the three summary probabilities: 1.67e-15

3.2 External methods: same samples, explicit targets¶

The Cherian–Candès adapter jointly bootstraps the positive-outcome loss and shared reference. It uses 1,999 draws, group mass floor 0.01 and full shrinkage to the overall-loss scale; minimum-support one and twenty retain other boundary and undefined-bootstrap safeguards. Its asymptotic population-gap target differs from UM's predictive target.

Uncertainty Matters uses a Dirichlet(1,1,1,1) confusion-table prior and 19,999 posterior-predictive draws, sharing the reference across comparisons. Undefined positive denominators remain [-1,1]. Its future-gap evaluation uses 100 independently generated same-size future confusion tables per clinical audit. The population-gap diagnostic applies the unchanged predictive intervals to a different target and is labelled accordingly.

The following reconstruction averages audit-level outcomes, retaining unsupported categories in the resolution denominator. A wrong family assertion means at least one wrong pass or fail. These saved experiments comprise 8,000 synthetic audits and 1,800 clinical replacement audits; they do not validate an arbitrary future hospital population.

4. C2: source variation and conditional evidence limits¶

The historical sex-FNR analysis separates supported-hospital variation from sampling variation. It has 58 supported Texas hospitals and nine eICU hospitals; MIMIC cannot identify between-hospital variation. The count guard assumes one random supported hospital and sampling variance c/n. It is sufficient under fitted Gaussian inputs, not a minimum count or a clinical recruitment guarantee. The following code recomputes the two-source attribution and guard rather than refitting source data.

5. C3: confirmation allocation and forecast evidence¶

5.1 Algorithm 2 in readable form¶

For each group, $N_g$ is the complete positive-frame size, $m_g$ the pilot reviews and $k_g$ the pilot errors. The remaining frame is $N_g-m_g$. A confirmation allocation chooses additional counts from a declared grid while respecting capacity and total budget. The utility $U_g(n_g,n_0)$ is the expected probability of a conclusive full-frame decision, conditional on the pilot model. The reference allocation influences every comparison.

For a fixed reference increment, the recurrence is $$D_g(b)=\max_{e\in E_g,\ e\leq b}\{D_{g-1}(b-e)+U_g(a_g+e,n_0)\}.$$ The algorithm saves the best reachable value and backtracks the allocation. Infeasibility is explicit. Maximizing this predicted average does not prove that every group's true resolution improves. The next cell checks the allocation recurrence against exhaustive enumeration on a small labelled numerical example; the empirical results are then reconstructed from their saved policy records.

5.2 Forecasts, correctness and group losses¶

Nine of 160 forecasts support the 10% total-conclusiveness target, five exclude it and 146 remain unresolved. This is not a count of correct or failed fairness verdicts. Complete totals show that 111 unresolved records attain the target. No gain over matched balancing is certified. Texas's 41.64% versus 30.23% result is an average correct-resolution improvement at equal cost, not a uniformly beneficial group allocation.

Uniform increments coincide with balancing in these 160 records. Greedy chooses immediate gain per review, DP optimizes the full finite grid, and the oracle uses unavailable full totals. Its objective is total conclusiveness, so it is not a correctness upper bound. Finer grids change feasible plans; unmatched completed subsets must not be compared as if they contained the same pilots.

The synthetic factorial uses 640 pilots in 64 fixed cells. Predictive floors and the DP-or-balancing switch reduce group losses at the cost of average gain. The confidence safeguard always retains balancing. All these results are preserved in Table XI and the complete groupwise results catalogue.

6. C4: policy construction, finite-population review and six comparators¶

The 42 single-direction policies are study-generated threshold changes; they are not 42 methods proposed by external publications. Six frozen XGBoost models (two ICU cohorts × seeds 11/29/47) supply six calibration sensitivity targets 60/70/75/85/90/95%, each compared with its original 80% threshold. Existing group/global/budget contrasts complete the 54-policy panel. Forty-two have a single prediction-change direction and qualify for pooling; the 12 mixed-direction cases retain strata. These correlated policies share patients.

The primary criterion requires no net subgroup increase in missed outcomes and positive utility $\Delta TP-w\Delta FP$, with research weight $w=0.10$. Single-direction additions cannot increase misses, so their criterion reduces to the total number of positives among disagreements; removals require zero removed positives. These simplifications do not validate subgroup false-alert caps.

At each policy's matched review count, the six comparators are pooled exact SRS; stratified exact SRS; equal-allocation stratified exact; equal-allocation Gaussian stratified; SRS Gaussian prediction-powered inference; and SRS finite-sample betting prediction-powered inference. SRS methods share reviewed records. Equal allocation changes acquisition while matching the total review count. The next cell reruns hypergeometric inversion for every observed pooled-review count and checks all 42,000 primary decisions.

The six-method primary panel contains only policies that fail the chosen criterion. Correct rejection therefore measures resolved review, not improved treatment. Pooling trades more correct rejections for more incorrect acceptances than betting PPI. At weight 0.05 the 20 addition policies become acceptable, providing a separate acceptance sensitivity; no removal is acceptable. A weight choice changes the target and must not be selected after observing the preferred conclusion.

8. Complete technical-companion evidence catalogue¶

This reference section contains every numbered companion table, every displayed scientific figure, and the main table definitions. Cohorts, prediction settings and audit definitions¶

How were cohorts, predictions and thresholds defined? Section 2 gives the complete model search, selected settings, preprocessing, partitions and calibration rule. These tables retain all predictive metrics, group operating points and sensitivity settings; timing-available ICU features are distinct from the exploratory Texas diagnosis model.

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Cohorts, prediction settings and audit definitions

Clinical tasks and model development

Texas-100X contains 2006 surgical discharges from Texas public-use data.[1, 2] The target was length of stay exceeding three days. The released benchmark excluded unknown-sex records and missing required values. Removing 1,200 suppressed-hospital records and 174 identical rows left 923,754 records from 439 hospitals. The principal predictor used age code, admission type, admission source and admitting diagnosis. Age was recorded at discharge and feature timestamps were unavailable, precluding a verified prospective interpretation.

A three-field model without admitting diagnosis had flagged every patient aged 65 or older. This observation prompted the exploratory diagnosis-model choice. Both models were frozen for evaluation. Charges and discharge status entered only timing diagnostics. Charges were not treated as income or a protected socioeconomic attribute. Cost proxies can misrepresent health needs [3]; this motivates keeping recorded charges distinct from those constructs.

The eICU and MIMIC-III targets were hospital mortality after a 24-hour ICU landmark.[4, 5] First-stay selection preceded filtering for adulthood and survival in ICU and hospital until the landmark. eICU retained the first ICU stay per encounter and removed patients crossing hospital partitions, leaving 111,214 stays from 97,956 patients. MIMIC-III retained one selected stay per patient, giving 32,315 patients and 3,366 deaths. Available observation and recording times had to precede the landmark. MIMIC-III laboratory predictors were excluded because the extracted table lacked storage times for this availability check.

Texas-100X and eICU used disjoint hospital partitions with approximate training, tuning, threshold-selection and test proportions of 55/15/15/15% and shuffle seed 7319. Hospital sizes determined the counts in Table S2. Texas patient separation could not be verified without patient linkage. MIMIC-III used patient partitions, seed 91173 and no outcome stratification.

Training records alone supplied medians, missingness indicators, standardization and categorical vocabularies. Unseen categories received the reserved unknown code. eICU had 90 numeric and two categorical predictors. MIMIC-III had 42 numeric age and vital predictors with constant context. XGBoost depth was selected from $\{3,6\}$ by tuning AUPRC, with six selected throughout. Settings were at most 1,000 trees, learning rate 0.05, row and column subsampling 0.8, minimum child weight 10 and $L_2$ penalty one. Histogram fitting used 40-round early stopping on tuning log loss. Seed 11 used 1,000, 377 and 142 trees in Texas-100X, eICU and MIMIC-III, respectively.

The highest threshold reaching 80% sensitivity in the separate threshold-selection partition was frozen before testing. Seed-11 thresholds were 0.421920, 0.073716 and 0.083448, respectively. This operating point did not optimize demographic fairness. Texas diagnosis-model seeds 29 and 47 reused the depth, training-only preprocessor and partitions, each with its own threshold-selection predictions. Seed-11 predictions were preserved. Test outcomes did not refit the stored predictor, but these repetitions did not undo the exploratory feature choice.

The comparison retains logistic regression and neural models on their documented feature views. Logistic regression selected $C\in\{0.1,1\}$ with a 1,000-iteration limit. The two-layer MLP and two-block residual network selected width 64 or 128 with dropout 0.1. The two-block, four-head attention model selected token width 16 or 32. Neural fitting used AdamW, learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.0001, gradient clipping at one and six-epoch patience on tuning log loss.

Demographic comparisons and repeated audits

Attributes retained source definitions regardless of predictor inclusion. Texas recorded race, separate Hispanic ethnicity, sex and age. Its stored Asian label represented Asian/Pacific Islander. eICU recorded combined ethnicity, gender and age. MIMIC-III supplied ethnicity labels, sex and derived age. Missing and unknown values remained separate from named categories.

The wider evaluation comprised 57 Texas, 66 primary eICU and 153 MIMIC metric comparisons, including intersections. Exact joint calculations used disjoint groups. Principal FNR references were White, Caucasian and WHITE, respectively. Separate Texas ethnicity comparisons used Not Hispanic. Other references were Male, age 40 to 64, and Male aged 40 to 64. All 41 MIMIC ethnicity labels remained, giving 40 contrasts even without positive outcomes.

The principal rule used tolerance 0.10, family error input 0.05 and at least one observation per metric denominator. Sensitivities used tolerances 0.05 and 0.15, denominator gates 10, 20 and 30, and endpoint error input 0.10 with its different budget explicit. Independent binomial masses at observed fractions and beta-binomial predictive masses from independent Jeffreys $\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,1/2)$ priors tested rate-uncertainty sensitivity while preserving the decision map. Neither law represented hospital-population variation or selective missingness.

Clinical resampling instead drew complete Texas hospitals, eICU patient-linked components, or MIMIC patients. In eICU, 80 cross-hospital patients joined 32 test hospitals into 25 components. Each draw recomputed denominators and intervals, assigning absent denominators an inconclusive state. Principal FNR families used 9,999 draws and secondary families 1,999. Probabilities and Monte Carlo uncertainty described the empirical resampling law. An earlier matched independent-count Monte Carlo check used 10,000 draws.

Hyperparameter search and selected configurations

The search space and training settings below were checked against the model-fitting implementation and saved tuning records. Selection maximized tuning-set average precision. Early stopping used tuning log loss. Threshold selection used a separate partition, and no tuning candidate was selected by test fairness or test prediction accuracy. Random seeds were 11, 29 and 47; deterministic logistic-regression outputs are not independent replications.

Neural models minimized binary cross-entropy with logits, using AdamW at learning rate 0.001 and weight decay 0.0001. Training used at most 40 epochs, gradient-norm clipping at one and six-epoch patience; a log-loss improvement had to exceed $10^{-5}$. Prediction batches were 512. The selected checkpoint minimized tuning log loss within its configuration. Model-specific early-stopping epochs and exact unrounded thresholds remain in saved run records. The primary eICU directory is distinct from the common-vital transport models; their selected configurations must not be interchanged.

The cached primary-model identities record Python 3.12.14, NumPy and pandas 2.3.3, SciPy 1.16.2, scikit-learn 1.7.2, XGBoost 3.0.5, joblib 1.6.0 and PyTorch 2.8.0 with CUDA 12.8. The recorded GPU was an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Laptop GPU. These training-environment records are distinct from a guarantee of identical floating-point predictions on another device; Section S3 reports the measured cross-device differences.

The source datasets were Texas 2006 public-use discharges, eICU Collaborative Research Database v2.0 and MIMIC-III v1.4. eICU observations originate in 2014--2015; MIMIC dates are shifted and do not support an ordinary calendar-time validation claim. Version and source checksums are retained in the extraction manifests. The fixed cohort has 923,754 Texas records with 415,728 positive outcomes; the final eICU development cohort has 111,214 stays with 9,881 deaths after cross-partition exclusions; MIMIC has 32,315 patients with 3,366 deaths. These are cohort counts, not three independent prospective validations.

The eICU preparation began with 200,859 stays. First-stay selection per hospital encounter retained 166,355, known adult age retained 165,795, ICU duration beyond 24 hours retained 115,941 and hospital duration beyond that landmark retained 115,877. Known outcome status retained 114,810 stays from 99,382 patients at 207 hospitals, with 10,114 deaths. Removal of 3,596 stays belonging to patients crossing the fixed hospital partitions produced the development cohort in Supplementary Table S2. The extractors preserve separate cohort eligibility and model-information rules so their effects can be reviewed independently.

The primary eICU laboratories were albumin, bilirubin, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate, haemoglobin, lactate, platelets, potassium, sodium and white-cell count. The ten vital channels were heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature and invasive/non-invasive systolic, diastolic and mean blood pressure. Minimum, mean, maximum and last values were extracted within the landmark window. Laboratory draw and revised-entry times had to fall within 1,440 minutes, with entry no earlier than draw. Unit conversion and fixed value bounds preceded aggregation. Untimed height and weight, discharge fields and existing mortality predictions were excluded. The 555 eligible stays missing all extracted clinical measurements were retained with missingness indicators.

MIMIC source checksums were checked against the publisher manifest for PATIENTS, ADMISSIONS, ICUSTAYS, D_ITEMS and CHARTEVENTS. From 61,532 ICU stays, first-encounter and first-patient selection retained 46,476, adult eligibility retained 38,509 and ICU duration beyond 24 hours retained 32,548. Subsequent hospital-duration, admission-order and known-outcome checks yielded 32,315 patients. The cohort retained 394 patients without valid vital aggregates. Shifted source ages above 200 were represented as age 90 with a separate indicator. Each accepted chart record had chart time no later than storage time, both preceding prediction. The latest available revision was selected before invalid values were rejected, and concept-time duplicates were combined before aggregation.

An earlier MIMIC cohort applied ICU-before-hospital discharge ordering and retained only 27,611 patients and 1,247 deaths. The rule was amended before primary MIMIC training because it disproportionately excluded deaths on administrative timing grounds. That historical cohort remains an eligibility diagnostic and was not used by the present models. The current training loader and split hashes identify the safe 32,315-patient revision. Before primary MIMIC model training, revision handling and one age encoding were corrected. Membership, outcomes and vital aggregates were unchanged, and all reported MIMIC models used the corrected data_revision_safe cohort. The new demographic analysis verifies that its inputs match this same cohort.

AUPRC denotes average precision. The always-negative rule predicts a stay of at most three days or survival for every record. Model thresholds were selected on a separate calibration partition to reach at least 80% sensitivity and were frozen before test evaluation. No model was retrained or selected using these comparisons. The 500 paired bootstrap draws resample 66 Texas hospitals, 25 patient-linked eICU hospital components, or 4,848 MIMIC patients, retaining all records within sampled units. Intervals describe this empirical resampling law conditional on the fitted models. They do not establish future-hospital coverage or incorporate training and model-selection uncertainty. All metric intervals and paired model differences are supplied with the reproducibility outputs.

Figure S1 — Protected-group support in the held-out cohorts. The upper panels show records or stays. The lower panels show positive outcomes forming FNR denominators. Source categories are ordered by record count, with all panels using $\log_{10}(n+1)$. Zero marks denote absent categories. Orange marks fewer than 20 positive outcomes, a sensitivity gate rather than a clinical sample-size requirement. Gray denotes missing or unknown categories. MIMIC retains all 41 source labels by rank. Section S2 lists their full names.

Protected-category denominators¶

Which groups and denominators were actually audited? Every source category is retained. Records, positive outcomes and reference groups determine whether each FNR, FPR or selection-rate contrast is defined. Missing identities and zero-support groups remain explicit instead of being discarded.

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Protected-category denominators

The following tables retain the complete held-out single-attribute vocabulary, including absent and unknown labels. Each row gives records and observed positive outcomes, so the reader can identify when FNR support is limited despite a larger group size. An absent category is not a zero-risk population, and records excluded by the original Texas preprocessing cannot be recovered from the released benchmark. That preprocessing retained race and ethnicity fields but excluded records with unknown sex or incomplete required values. Sex-by-age rates, confusion counts and all model/seed comparisons are supplied in the executed notebook and aggregate tables.

Source fields and coding. Texas-100X used SEX_CODE, PAT_AGE, RACE and ETHNICITY. Released sex codes 0/1 map to Male/Female, and ethnicity codes 0/1 map to Hispanic/Not Hispanic. The donor Asian race category includes Pacific Islander.[2] eICU used gender, age and ethnicity. MIMIC-III used GENDER and ETHNICITY, with age derived from ICU admission and birth dates. Texas age was a coarse discharge-age proxy, while ICU ages over 89 were top-coded. Section S1 specifies prediction roles; Sections S8 and S9 distinguish current threshold policies from historical reweighing.

Leakage and numerical repetition checks¶

What was checked for leakage and cross-device reproduction? Stored partition-overlap and preprocessing checks are rechecked above. Raw timestamp audits and device-replay evidence are recorded results here. Texas patient linkage and prospective timing remain unavailable; CPU/GPU differences are not hidden.

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Leakage and numerical repetition checks

The audit covered the current Texas admission-diagnosis view, corrected eICU cohort and corrected MIMIC vital cohort. It retained two additional Texas XGBoost seeds. The historical three-field and end-of-encounter Texas analyses were not substituted for this evidence. Frozen models, stored predictions and calibration thresholds remained unchanged. The checks assess the implemented pipeline and do not establish that every possible source of leakage is absent.

All outcome-independent seeded partitions were reconstructed. Forty-eight required cross-partition identifier checks found no shared identifiers. Six MIMIC hospital comparisons intentionally involved the same institution. The eICU extraction had excluded 3,596 records from patients crossing assigned hospital partitions. Repeated patients within partitions remain a source of dependence. Texas lacks patient linkage, so patient-level separation could not be tested there. Eligibility and outcome labels were independently reconstructed from source administrative tables. The eICU target uses recorded hospital discharge status and offsets beyond the 24-hour landmark. Its extraction has no separate exact death-time variable. MIMIC checks additionally used admission, discharge and recorded death times.

Actual feature columns excluded outcomes, length of stay, discharge fields and record identifiers. Texas included age code, admission type, admission source and admitting diagnosis. Its age code is recorded at discharge and the diagnosis-entry time is unverified. This feature view therefore remains retrospective. The ICU predictors excluded discharge and quality-control fields, and the eICU view excluded untimed height and weight. Age deliberately served as both a predictor and an audit dimension. Across the three views, training-only refits exactly reproduced all 133 numeric features' fitted statistics and the saved categorical vocabularies. The saved preprocessing objects were retained. These checks cannot remove the exploratory selection of the Texas diagnosis view.

The independent eICU rescan parsed 39,132,531 laboratory, 146,671,642 periodic-vital and 25,075,074 aperiodic-vital rows. It reproduced the source hashes and timing counters. The availability filter excluded 31,805 selected laboratory rows drawn within 24 hours but entered after the landmark. The scan also recorded 576,739 selected laboratory rows with revision times preceding their draw times. All 88 clinical summaries were reconstructed for 1,024 systematically selected cohort records without using outcomes. Values matched within the prespecified float32 tolerance, with no missingness discrepancies. Every source row was scanned, but numerical feature reconstruction covered the stated sample.

The MIMIC rescan parsed all 330,712,483 chart-event rows for item, patient linkage and chart/store-time eligibility. It excluded 1,234 selected item/stay rows with identifier mismatches. Among measurements charted within the window, 1,197,446 failed the storage-time condition. The accepted multiset of 5,255,145 raw row identifiers exactly matched the retained event buckets, without duplicate accepted identifiers. All bucket timestamps and patient links passed. Independent aggregation reproduced all 40 vital summaries for 32,315 patients exactly, including the discard of 14,962 invalid latest revisions. Raw numerical values and units were not independently re-extracted from the complete chart-event source during this audit. Source timestamps describe recorded availability and do not prove that clinicians observed each retained value at the same instant.

All 34 calibration thresholds were reproduced from calibration-positive score order statistics. All 2,458,166 stored model-record class decisions reconciled with their score, threshold and split metadata. The core audit replayed 768 records for each of 32 model-seed fits. Full replay covered two additional Texas XGBoost fits, with maximum CPU score differences of $4.17\times10^{-7}$ and $5.96\times10^{-7}$. Tuning logs and saved split hashes also reconciled. These checks did not retrain the models or independently select hyperparameters again.

The initial 136-check suite retained six failures of the fixed $2\times10^{-6}$ CPU score tolerance, all from attention checkpoints. The tolerance was not relaxed. A subsequent complete same-device replay reproduced all 192,126 attention scores exactly on the recorded NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Laptop GPU. CPU replay had maximum absolute score difference 0.0001347959 and changed 11 frozen-threshold decisions across tuning, calibration and test. Three changes occurred in test, all reductions in false positives. Two were eICU seed-29 records in the Caucasian, age-40--64 category, one male and one female. The third was a MIMIC seed-29 record in the WHITE, male, age-40--64 category. No test false-negative count or seed-11 test decision changed. Some CPU calibration sensitivities fell below 80% at the unchanged GPU-selected threshold. Numerical backend dependence therefore limits cross-device repetition of the operating point, while the reported evidence remains exactly reproducible on the recorded GPU.

The accompanying audit scripts, aggregate outputs and source hashes distinguish executed checks from static review and unavailable checks. Restricted records and patient identifiers are excluded. Repeating the raw scans requires authorized source-data access. The portable notebook instead verifies hashes and reconciles the aggregate audit outputs. Neither operation constitutes an independent prospective study or resolves the empirical limitations of future-hospital inference.

C1: exact count computation and reference dependence¶

Why does shared-reference integration matter? Each group uses the same reference count, so independent marginal multiplication changes family-event probabilities. Exact integration retains that dependence under independent group-count laws; it does not justify those laws for a new hospital.

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

C1: exact count computation and reference dependence

This section preserves the binary reversal procedures and supplies the three-state extension used in the main paper. Both specialize established finite-region summation and shared-control integration.[6, 7] The direct comparator developed for this study is not a reproduction of the complete Koch-Hothorn procedure. It independently constructs the same decision map and sums every reference-by-group count pair.

Binary procedures retained for continuity

Recorded-verdict reversal instead concerns $P(B'_g\ne b_g\mid R,\eta)$, where $R$ specifies what a repeated audit redraws and $\eta$ supplies its parameters. The following two algorithms evaluate the original binary point verdict; the main paper' s three-state algorithm evaluates the interval states. For fixed independent binomial counts, $X_g\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_g,p_g)$ and $X_0\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_0,p_0)$, the passing event is $|X_g/n_g-X_0/n_0|\leq\delta$. Conditioning on $X_g=x$ turns this event into an integer interval for the reference count. With $T=\lfloor\delta n_gn_0\rfloor$, its endpoints are $L_x=\lceil(xn_0-T)/n_g\rceil$ and $U_x=\lfloor(xn_0+T)/n_g\rfloor$.

$$\begin{split}P(\mathrm{pass})={}&\sum_{x=0}^{n_g}P(X_g=x)\\&\times\{F_{n_0,p_0}(U_x)-F_{n_0,p_0}(L_x-1)\}.\end{split}$$ Write $f,F,S$ for binomial mass, CDF and survival functions. For $L\le U$, $\mathcal B_{n,p}(L,U)=(A,E)$ is evaluated as \[ \begin{aligned} A&=\begin{cases}S_{n,p}(L-1)-S_{n,p}(U),&L>np,\\F_{n,p}(U)-F_{n,p}(L-1),&L\le np,\end{cases}\\ E&=F_{n,p}(L-1)+S_{n,p}(U). \end{aligned} \] For $L>U$, set $(A,E)=(0,1)$. Count laws require positive integer denominators and probabilities in $[0,1]$. The implementation checks finite inputs and integer-product overflow, and clips numerical probabilities to $[0,1]$.

Exact scalar recorded-verdict reversal (C1a)

Inputs: Independent binomial laws $(n_g,p_g),(n_0,p_0)$; tolerance $\delta$; recorded pass $b\in\{0,1\}$

Outputs: Recorded-verdict reversal $r$, pass probability $P_+$, fail probability $P_-$ and less-frequent-verdict probability $v$

• Relabel the two laws so $n_1\le n_2$; $T\gets\lfloor\delta n_1n_2\rfloor$

• $P_+\gets0$; $P_-\gets0$

For {$x=0,\ldots,n_1$}

• $L\gets\lceil(xn_2-T)/n_1\rceil$; $U\gets\lfloor(xn_2+T)/n_1\rfloor$

• $(A,E)\gets\mathcal B_{n_2,p_2}(L,U)$

• $P_+\gets P_++f_{n_1,p_1}(x)A$; $P_-\gets P_-+f_{n_1,p_1}(x)E$

End loop.

• Clip $P_+,P_-$; $r\gets bP_-+(1-b)P_+$; $v\gets\min(P_+,P_-)$

•

Return $(r,P_+,P_-,v)$

Algorithm S1 integrates the event opposite to the recorded verdict using $\min(n_g,n_0)+1$ interval evaluations. Strict acceptance uses $T=\lceil\delta n_1n_2\rceil-1$ instead, and the vectorized implementation uses linear memory. Exactness concerns the supplied fixed-denominator laws, while less-frequent-verdict probability and recorded-verdict reversal remain different targets. Uncertainty in fitted event probabilities remains separate from conditional count-law reversal. Outcome-stratified record resampling can also produce random group denominators, requiring a different repetition law.

For a grid of disjoint comparison groups, let $q_g(x_0)$ denote the conditional probability that comparison $g$ preserves its recorded verdict given $X_0=x_0$. Mutually independent group counts become conditionally independent comparisons once the reference is fixed. This gives the shared-reference reversal probability

$$q_{\mathrm{grid}}=1-\sum_{x_0=0}^{n_0}P(X_0=x_0)\prod_{g=1}^{G}q_g(x_0).$$

Exact shared-reference grid reversal (C1b)

Inputs: Independent reference law $(n_0,p_0)$, disjoint independent group laws $(n_g,p_g)$, finite closed accepted intervals and recorded passes $(b_g)$

Outputs: Grid reversal $r_{\mathrm{grid}}$, marginal risks $(r_g)$ and independence comparator $r_{\mathrm{ind}}$

• $\underline T_g\gets\lceil\ell_gn_gn_0\rceil$; $\overline T_g\gets\lfloor u_gn_gn_0\rfloor$ for accepted $[\ell_g,u_g]$

• $r_{\mathrm{grid}}\gets0$; $r_g\gets0$ for each group

For {$x_0=0,\ldots,n_0$}

• $w\gets f_{n_0,p_0}(x_0)$; $\lambda\gets0$

For {$g=1,\ldots,G$}

• $L\gets\lceil(x_0n_g+\underline T_g)/n_0\rceil$

• $U\gets\lfloor(x_0n_g+\overline T_g)/n_0\rfloor$

• $(A,E)\gets\mathcal B_{n_g,p_g}(L,U)$; $\rho_g\gets b_gE+(1-b_g)A$

• $r_g\gets r_g+w\rho_g$; $\lambda\gets\lambda+\operatorname{log1p}(-\rho_g)$

End loop.

• $r_{\mathrm{grid}}\gets r_{\mathrm{grid}}-w\operatorname{expm1}(\lambda)$

End loop.

• $r_{\mathrm{ind}}\gets-\operatorname{expm1}(\sum_g\operatorname{log1p}(-r_g))$

•

Return $r_{\mathrm{grid}},(r_g),r_{\mathrm{ind}}$, clipped to $[0,1]$

Algorithm S2 conditions on the common reference before combining each comparison's preservation probability $q_g(x_0)=1-\rho_g$. It uses $O(G(n_0+1))$ interval evaluations and $O(n_0+G)$ memory in the vectorized implementation. Its independence assumptions do not extend to overlapping demographic groups or clustered hospital observations. A Gaussian alternative uses covariance $\mathrm{diag}(v_1,\ldots,v_G)+v_0\mathbf1\mathbf1^\mathsf T$, where $v_0$ is reference-rate variance, retaining the classical common-control structure.[8] Neither calculation establishes independence for overlapping demographic intersections or clustered hospital records. Those clinical comparisons instead use common resamples that preserve their shared observations.

Three-state count regions and correctness

For a count $k$ among $n$ trials, the Clopper-Pearson limits at rate error $a$ are $L(0)=0$, $U(n)=1$, \[ L(k)=Q_{\mathrm{Beta}(k,n-k+1)}(a/2)\ (k>0),\qquad U(k)=Q_{\mathrm{Beta}(k+1,n-k)}(1-a/2)\ (k<n). \] For $n=0$ use $[0,1]$ and force review. Set $a=\alpha/(G+1)$, so a union bound covers the $G+1$ independent-binomial rates simultaneously with probability at least $1-\alpha$. Subtracting covered rate endpoints covers each true gap. Thus a wrong conclusive decision requires a rate-coverage failure. This is the standard interval argument; the transition algorithm computes the probability of its decisions under supplied count masses rather than estimating unknown rates.

Proposition P1 (ordered count regions). For the interval decision rule in the main paper, the passing region at fixed reference count is $[A_g,B_g]$, the failing region is $[0,F_g]\cup[H_g,n_g]$, and the review region is their complement. All four boundary arrays are nondecreasing in the reference count. Four two-pointer sweeps therefore require linear work in the combined group and reference supports.

Proof. Both rate endpoints are nondecreasing in the success count. Interval containment requires both $L_g(k)+\delta_g\geq U_0(x)$ and $U_g(k)-\delta_g\leq L_0(x)$. The first defines a suffix beginning at $A_g$ and the second a prefix ending at $B_g$. Their intersection is the stated passing run. Disjointness requires $U_g(k)+\delta_g<L_0(x)$ or $L_g(k)-\delta_g>U_0(x)$, giving the lower and upper failing runs. Because $L_g\leq U_g$ and $\delta_g\geq0$, the failing runs cannot overlap the passing run or each other. Their complement contains at most two review runs if pass is present, and one otherwise. Increasing $x$ increases each reference query, so each group pointer moves only forward. Every pointer visits at most $n_g+1$ positions, and processes $n_0+1$ reference queries. Fixed ineligibility replaces the whole support by review.\hfill$\square$

Proposition P2 (state probabilities and shared reference). Under mutual independence of the count variables, the conditional and marginal probabilities and the main paper' s three reported probabilities equal the probabilities of their declared events.

Proof. Summing $f_g$ over the disjoint runs gives the conditional state mass for each comparison at fixed $X_0=x$. Independence of the remaining counts permits multiplication of conditional preservation probabilities, and separately of conclusive-state probabilities. Averaging over $f_0$ yields the grid events. Linearity of expectation gives the expected number of conclusive comparisons without requiring unconditional independence. A single comparison gives scalar state change as a special case.\hfill$\square$

Numerical safeguards and reproducible boundaries

The machine predicate uses the shifted comparisons printed in the main paper. Reassociating a comparison as an endpoint difference can change machine-equality cases even though the real-number inequalities are equivalent. Independent tests found 74 such differences among 1,325 deliberately constructed equality checks; this is a diagnostic test set, not an estimate of their frequency in clinical data. The dense comparator reconstructs interval endpoints independently and uses the same declared shifted predicate.

Prefix and suffix subtraction can lose tiny interior masses. For example, the central mass of $(0.5,10^{-20},0.5)$ disappears if computed only as a difference of rounded cumulative sums. The implementation detects subtraction susceptible to cancellation and instead queries a tree containing sums of nonnegative masses. Tests retain interior masses down to $10^{-300}$. The tree takes linear construction space and logarithmic work per fallback query. Changes are summed from nonrecorded states rather than computed solely by subtracting a nearly unit preservation probability. Stable log products then combine these changes. Underflowed input masses cannot be recovered, and no uniform relative-error theorem or bit-exact claim is made.

Validation design and complete computation results

Historical three-state implementation. The validation and timings below retain the earlier implementation and direct comparator. Table S12 reports the revised implementation and optimized baseline used in the main text. The frozen protocol used 200 validation cases and 200 independently seeded confirmation cases. Count denominators were drawn from $\{0,1,2,5,10\}$, with one to three comparison groups, binomial or hypergeometric masses, boundary and interior rates, and tolerances $0,0.1,0.25,0.5,1$. All cases were retained. For this earlier implementation, maximum absolute disagreement with full finite enumeration was $1.11\times10^{-15}$. Separate tests reconstruct endpoints, enumerate full Cartesian outcomes for every pair of recorded states, and exercise minimum-count gates, deterministic laws, permutations and rare masses. The probability calculation for a hypergeometric law evaluates a fixed CP decision map; it does not assert CP coverage for that law.

Runtime comparisons use six prespecified count families and seven repetitions per method. The boundary routine has one prior evaluation; no matched warm-up is asserted for the other methods. All methods receive the same masses, tolerances, recorded states and decision event. Rule-setup-inclusive times include interval endpoints and decision-map or boundary construction, while common mass construction is excluded from both. Cached times reuse the rules and masses. The documented amendment retains a three-group case omitted from the original protocol's shorthand list of group counts. An independent numerical review prompted the positive-sum safeguard before the final rerun. Original results are archived, and only the corrected rerun supplies the following timings.

In this historical benchmark, dense integration is faster in four of six cases in both timing regimes. The earlier boundary method becomes faster in the two largest pair-table designs. Its setup-inclusive ratios are 4.55 and 4.39, respectively. The binary algorithms were separately compared in twelve cases. They agreed with direct integration within $1.28\times10^{-15}$ and were faster in ten setup-inclusive and six cached cases, with dense-to-proposed ratios 0.558--30.083 and 0.291--17.154. Binary setup timing includes its mass construction, so it is not pooled with the three-state timing regime. These local measurements do not establish universal superiority over optimized exact software.

Why stability must accompany conclusiveness

Four illustrative binomial profiles fix the law before simulation. Reference rate is 0.15 in the clear, boundary and sparse profiles, and 0.10 in the adverse profile. The tolerance is 0.10 and family error is 0.05. Clear uses reference and group counts of 1,000 and group rates $(0.15,0.16,0.18)$. Boundary uses counts of 500 and rates $(0.24,0.25,0.26)$. Sparse uses reference count 500, group counts $(10,30,100)$ and rates $(0.15,0.18,0.20)$. Adverse uses counts of 1,000 and group rates $(0.30,0.35,0.40)$. The recorded states are all pass, all review, all review and all fail, respectively. Point-rule recorded states are computed separately under the same rates and counts. Thus the binary and interval columns describe different declared events, not competing estimators of one probability.

Each profile also has 200,000 independent Monte Carlo audit repetitions. Monte Carlo any-change estimates were 0.271465, 0.001775, 0.000035 and 0.013930 in table order; the corresponding exact values were 0.272705, 0.001745, 0.00004382 and 0.013752. Low interval-state change in the boundary and sparse profiles largely reflects repeated review. Conversely, an almost certain point-rule decision can coexist with frequent loss of interval support. These are controlled examples, not newly observed clinical outcomes.

Current computational benchmark. This section supplies the current three-state accuracy and timing results. The preceding historical comparison retains the earlier implementation and comparator. The implementation revision validates each supplied probability mass function once, constructs a reusable cumulative and positive-tail index, and batches the state-specific count runs. A positive-sum tree is built at most once per group when needed. Equal-denominator endpoints and boundary structures can be reused within a declared family. No nonzero tail is intentionally truncated. The original binary C1a routine remains unchanged; these changes concern the three-state extension.

Let $N_g=n_g+1$ and $N_0=n_0+1$. After endpoint evaluation, the monotone sweep takes $O(\sum_gN_g+GN_0)$ boundary work. The binary-search variant takes $O(\sum_gN_g+GN_0\log(\max_gN_g+1))$. Positive-tree queries also introduce a logarithmic worst-case range-summation cost. Consequently, the practical timing improvements of the binary-search version are not described as a linear-time guarantee for the entire implementation. Prepared storage is $O(\sum_gN_g+GN_0)$. Direct pair maps have worst-case work and storage $O(N_0\sum_gN_g)$, although equal maps can share storage.

The independently optimized direct baseline reuses endpoint arrays and decision maps, then sums each state's pair probabilities with array contractions without constructing a floating-point outer-product table. It evaluates the same count law and decision map. It is a matched direct-integration implementation, not a reproduction of another paper's complete software package. Both algorithms receive reusable structures in cached timing, and both pay their preparation costs in setup-inclusive timing.

The revised code agreed with the independent Cartesian oracle within $9.99\times10^{-16}$ across 400 original cases. Another 140 profiles covered unequal supports, eligibility gates, tied boundaries and rare masses. Nonzero tested masses down to $10^{-300}$ had maximum relative error $6.66\times10^{-16}$. Four additional tests covered full-family enumeration, subnormal interior mass, clipped ranges, group permutations and invalid input. The largest discrepancy among timed implementations was $4.00\times10^{-15}$. These observed checks do not assert a universal floating-point error bound.

Twenty-four frozen benchmark designs used a single numerical thread, one warm-up and nine shuffled timing repetitions per method and regime. Relative to the previous boundary implementation, the revision was faster in all 24 cases. Against optimized direct integration it won four of six original setup comparisons, including two marginal gains below 4%, and two of six cached comparisons. It won five of 18 imbalance comparisons in either regime. The gain is concentrated in large pair tables. Table S12 reports all 24 designs and their peak traced allocations; replicate orders and individual measurements are retained in the reproducibility archive.

The largest original design used 360,228 bytes of prepared boundary arrays, compared with 13,014,504 bytes of direct maps. Setup peak traced allocation was approximately 1.64 MB versus 41.16 MB. Relative to the older boundary code, however, batching increased peak temporary allocation in 31 of 48 design/regime combinations, by up to 2.49 times. These are traced allocations rather than whole-process resident memory. The storage advantage concerns direct pair maps, not every alternative implementation.

This post hoc deterministic analysis quantifies the dependence contribution using every retained exact clinical family/law row. It includes 39 seed-11 attribute/metric families, comprising 15 Texas, 12 eICU and 12 MIMIC families, each evaluated under empirical-binomial and Jeffreys-predictive laws. All 78 rows use tolerance 0.10, gate one and family error input 0.05. Bootstrap, other seed, tolerance and gate experiments are separate and are not pooled. The six principal rows concern race or source-ethnicity FNR families. The analysis changes neither predictions nor observed audit states and provides no new clinical validation cohort.

Let $p_{gs}$ be the saved marginal state probability and $b_g$ the recorded state. The ablation preserves these margins but substitutes $1-\prod_g p_{gb_g}$ for shared-reference reversal and $\prod_g(p_{gP}+p_{gF})$ for complete-family conclusiveness. Differences are approximation minus exact calculation. Mean conclusiveness remains $G^{-1}\sum_g(p_{gP}+p_{gF})$ and is unchanged by this substitution. A separately evaluated two-group example checks the definitions, and all six principal rows were recomputed from their saved counts.

The largest principal any-change difference was 0.4113 points; the largest principal complete-family difference was 0.0000727 points. Across all 78 rows, the corresponding maxima were 7.6450 points for MIMIC sex-by-age FNR and 0.9334 points for MIMIC age selection rate, both under Jeffreys prediction. Signed differences occur in both directions. Thus the largest secondary dependence effect should not be substituted for the modest effect in the principal families.

The same ablation retained all 72 archived known-law policy/design rows and all four earlier decision profiles. Its maximum absolute error was 3.8342 points in the known-law designs and 0.9049 points in the four profiles. Mean conclusiveness agreed within $2.23\times10^{-14}$ percentage points across the clinical rows. Complete CSVs, source hashes and replay code accompany the notebook. The calculation isolates the effect of shared-reference dependence under each declared law; it does not measure the accuracy of that law for future patients.

Current matched Monte Carlo comparison

The later computational comparison retained all 78 clinical count-law configurations, with identical denominators, recorded states, endpoint rules and a single shared reference draw in each repetition. Five seeds, 230010--230014, used disjoint streams by family; prefixes of 1,000 and 100,000 draws formed the two budgets. For any reversal and complete-family conclusiveness, two-sided 95% Clopper--Pearson simulation intervals classified the probability relative to .05, .10 and .20 as below, above or unresolved. These intervals describe simulation error for the supplied law, not simultaneous clinical inference. Mean-conclusiveness error was assessed separately. The 10,000-draw check in Section S1.2 belongs to the earlier validation.

Both methods reused cached endpoint tables. Endpoint and mass construction, exact warm evaluation, and Monte Carlo generation/lookup were timed separately; shared setup was not repeatedly charged. The main paper's unresolved-call counts and cached timings use this protocol. The existing direct-integration benchmark remains the exact comparator. Cached performance does not establish cold-start superiority over methods that evaluate only sampled endpoints.

Hospital dependence and the population target¶

Does exact computation establish future-hospital coverage? No. Future-unit intervals and random access to a known finite frame target different populations. The tables retain coverage, errors and resolution together, including undercoverage and conservative unresolved outputs.

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Hospital dependence and the population target

A bounded-KL score interval

Let independent identically distributed complete hospital units supply $0\leq K_{hg}\leq N_{hg}\leq B_g$, with bounds specified for the generating population. For positive $E[N_{hg}]$, the patient-weighted target is $p_g=E[K_{hg}]/E[N_{hg}]$. At candidate $p$, define $$ Z_{hg}(p)=p+(K_{hg}-pN_{hg})/B_g,\qquad \bar Z_g(p)=a_g+(1-b_g)p, $$ where $a_g=H^{-1}\sum_hK_{hg}/B_g$ and $b_g=H^{-1}\sum_hN_{hg}/B_g$. At $p=p_g$, $Z$ lies in $[0,1]$ and has expectation $p_g$. The bounded-variable Chernoff inequality therefore supports the retained set $$ \mathcal I_g=\{p\in[0,1]:H\operatorname{kl}(\bar Z_g(p)\Vert p)\leq\log(2M/\alpha)\}, $$ with $\operatorname{kl}(z\Vert p)=z\log(z/p)+(1-z)\log[(1-z)/(1-p)]$, using endpoint limits.[9] Each one-sided error is at most $\alpha/(2M)$. A union bound over both tails and all $M$ declared rates gives simultaneous coverage at least $1-\alpha$. Endpoint subtraction then covers all declared group-reference gaps. Joint convexity makes the accepted set an interval containing the pooled ratio. Zero observed denominators retain $[0,1]$; absent groups remain in the multiplicity budget. This applies an established concentration inequality and is not an additional claimed algorithmic invention.

Within-hospital dependence and overlapping rate columns are allowed. Units must be independent, the audit size fixed, and caps valid for the population. The maximum of the complete finite profile library is valid for draws from that library; a maximum in a sampled clinical audit does not bound future hospitals. No inference for arbitrary future hospitals or optional stopping follows.

Matched evaluation and rare-hospital stress

The 16 October 2026 comparison used 2,000 fresh draws in each of 22 settings, totalling 44,000 simulated audits. It retained the twelve clinical-profile/synthetic settings and six overlapping-group stress settings from the earlier analysis. Four additional settings mixed the Texas/eICU empirical profile law with a rare high-volume type at probability 0.05, at original/fourfold unit counts. The rare type had twice the maximum library denominator for each group, reference error probability 0.05 and comparison probability 0.65. Its errors were binomial. The population ratio was calculated analytically from the mixture, and twice the library maxima supplied valid caps. All methods received identical draws and all groups remained declared.

Bounded-KL and empirical-Bernstein intervals covered every simulated family but resolved none in these settings. For 2,000 successful draws within a setting, the Wilson 95% Monte Carlo lower bound is 99.81%; the mathematical guarantee remains 95%, not 100%. In the rare-hospital eICU setting at 25 units, jackknife coverage was 90.00% (88.61% to 91.24%) with 1.22% mean resolution. The corresponding Texas setting at 66 units covered 94.50% (93.41% to 95.42%) and resolved 30.74%. These results preclude treating the support adjustment as a validated general replacement for bounded-unit inference. Its outputs remain sensitivity estimates, whereas the valid but uninformative bounds retain inconclusive decisions.

Earlier two-stage-profile analysis. Figure S2 preserves the preceding implementation's hospital-profile comparison. It does not depict the bounded-KL experiment above.

Integrity and reproducibility

The main paper also reports the separate 22 October population/fixed-frame evaluation. Rare-hospital eICU jackknife coverage was 90.00% in the 16 October run above and 88.15% in the later run (95% Monte Carlo interval 86.66--89.49); these are separate randomizations, not alternative summaries of one sample. The later 36.53% Texas and 58.47% eICU completion results concern known finite frames reviewed at 60/66 hospitals and 23/25 linked components. They do not repair the future-hospital coverage result. The original table remains the record of its own run.

The 16 October run retained all 3,200 calibration draws, 6,400 stable/shifted forecast comparisons, 1,400 retrospective clinical plans and 44,000 hospital draws. Numerical checks covered the defining inequality, scale and permutation invariance, absent categories, invalid bounds and 84 exhaustive finite-support tail checks. The archived freeze was followed by a documented test-only amendment when a final extreme-cap check was added; the inference formula did not change. Transitive historical dependencies and exact target files matched their earlier frozen hashes, verified after the new evaluation began. The reusable notebook reconstructs summaries and reruns declared numerical examples. Neither these simulations nor notebook replay supplies untouched clinical validation.

Fixed-frame verification and resource selection

The separate access experiment assumes an enumerated cohort with known categories and positive-outcome membership but masked prediction linkage/errors. Within each category, simple random sampling without replacement supports hypergeometric inversion for the fixed error total, with tail error $.05/[2(G+1)]$. Zero denominators remain inconclusive. Randomization of access supplies validity despite dependence among the recorded patients; it supplies no future-hospital guarantee. The comparison used 2,000 replays at six budgets per cohort, matching record-verification cost to complete-unit samples while retaining the number of hospitals or linked components accessed.

The subsequent resource analysis was explicitly post hoc. It retained all 48 design/budget candidates and mean-resolution targets .80, .90 and .95. One-sided Clopper--Pearson lower bounds allocated error .05 across all 240 category-level replay probabilities; averaging these bounds over each declared family supported selection within that tested grid. These are Monte Carlo bounds on resolution under the fixed replay law, not forecast intervals for a new cohort.

Expected cost was $C(\lambda)=R+\lambda A$, where $R$ counts positive-record verifications, $A$ counts distinct units accessed and $\lambda\geq0$ is an unspecified setup cost in record-equivalent units. The analysis retained capped-equal and proportional record review, matched binomial intervals and complete-unit deterministic-completion review. It compared feasible linear cost envelopes and a separate conservative access-cost sensitivity. Frame construction, outcome ascertainment and measured clinical review time were excluded. Table S15 reports the selected 80% target results from this analysis; they are not prospective budget forecasts.
