Predictive constraints across the full existing factorial. The established constrained optimizer and switch were applied without tuning to all 640 existing synthetic records. All constrained problems were feasible. The constrained allocation equaled balancing in 327/640 records; the switch selected saved DP in 130 and balancing in 510. All selected plans were frozen before their new truth evaluation. Recomputed original DP/balancing/greedy/oracle scalar metrics agreed with their saved values.

The constrained mean correct-resolution gain over balancing is .4402 points (stratified MCSE .1296); the switch gain is .4112 (.1275). They retain 138/1,280 and 26/1,280 group losses, affecting 100/640 and 19/640 pilots, with worst losses 10.8864 and .2235 points. These are improvements over unrestricted DP' s observed losses, not a proof of true-law protection. Table S37 includes all six policies and every gap stratum. Constrained gains at gaps $0,.05,.15,.30$ are $0,0,-.0211,+1.7819$ points; switch gains are $0,0,+.0030,+1.6420$. Null and adverse strata remain.

All-group correct probabilities are 18.9722% for balancing, 8.8416% for DP, 18.9713% for constrained and 18.9722% for the switch. Mean minimum-group correct probabilities are 21.5109%, 9.0015%, 21.4826% and 21.5105%, respectively. The minima average a within-pilot group probability, whereas the worst paired loss selects the single most adverse pilot/group difference. Keeping these summaries separate exposes how an average objective can favor some assertions while leaving others unresolved.

{3pt}

Precision, computation and limits. Clinical MCSE describes the 20 pilot-conditional probabilities within each recorded setting; Texas shares pilots across budgets. Synthetic MCSE stratifies over the 64 fixed cells (16 within a gap stratum), with ten independent pilots per cell. The new calculations reuse those pilots; they introduce no new clinical cohort or generating frame. Clinical evaluation took 492.458 seconds, synthetic selection 127.647 seconds and evaluation 9.834 seconds, with no exclusions, failed cases or stage-cap interruption. Independent verification reconciled all 160/640 records, 800 gain bounds and 10,357 summary numeric fields, and checked all eleven CSVs. Fresh rational checks on eight cases and six policies agreed to within $4.44\times10^{-16}$. These are computational checks, not clinical validation, a new method or an economic recommendation.

Historical 23 October allocation policies and finite-frame protocol

The raw DP core in Algorithm S5 maximizes estimated total conclusiveness. Denominator balancing instead assigns each full batch to the smallest capacity-eligible denominator, including the reference, with reference-first stored-order ties. Given their allocations $n^D,n^B$, the groupwise safeguard returns $n^D$ only if $U_g(n_g^D,n_0^D)\geq U_g(n_g^B,n_0^B)-10^{-12}$ for every group; otherwise it returns $n^B$. Both use identical pilot utilities, minima, budget, batch and capacities. This comparison protects estimated utilities, not true groupwise improvement. The historical confirmation-only allocation table below reports raw DP, balancing, uniform increments and the original-rule oracle; its values are separate from the full-frame constrained/switch evaluation above. Uniform increments assigns each full batch to the eligible category with the smallest increment above its minimum, using the same stored-order ties. The oracle uses true remaining error totals only after the other allocations have been frozen and optimizes the original rule on the same grid.

For the current same-frame study, known category sizes $N_g$ determine pilots $m_g=\min\{\mathrm{cap},\lfloor N_g/4\rfloor\}$ with caps 20 or 200. After observing pilot errors $k_g$, confirmation capacity is $C_g=R_g=N_g-m_g$, minima are $a_g=\min(25,R_g)$, batch size is 50 and extra budgets are 250 or 2,000. Twenty pilots per feasible setting compare DP, denominator balancing, uniform increments and an unavailable-total oracle at identical costs and grids. All categories and multiplicity slots remain; zero confirmation denominators have zero utility. The rule retains tolerance .10 and family error .05. Pilot, base and extra confirmation counts are charged, but discovering outcome eligibility is not.

Pilot seeds use $(20261023,8811,\mathrm{cohort},\mathrm{cap},\mathrm{replicate})$; posterior-total and direct-confirmation streams replace 8811 by 8812 and 8813 and include the budget. Each selected plan has 20 paired direct confirmations. The reported mean expected resolution averages exact pilot-conditional probabilities, rather than those direct-confirmation frequencies. Forecasts and allocations were saved before joining their fixed-frame target values.

Confidence projection and target decisions

With $M=G+1$, invert each pilot's hypergeometric tails at error $\eta/(2M)$, $\eta=.05$, to obtain simultaneous full-frame error-total intervals $\mathcal C_g$. Zero pilots retain $[0,N_g]$, pilot censuses $[k_g,k_g]$, and empty categories $[0,0]$ without removing their multiplicity slot. Remaining totals lie in $\mathcal T_g=\mathcal C_g-k_g$. If $Q_g(t_g,t_0;n)$ is the selected plan's conclusive probability under independent within-category samples from the remainder, its lower bound is \[ \underline Q(n)=\frac1G\min_{t_0\in\mathcal T_0}\sum_g\min_{t_g\in\mathcal T_g}Q_g(t_g,t_0;n), \] with maxima for the upper bound. Integer projection retains one common reference total and does not assume extrema occur at corners. One simultaneous pilot event covers every count plan, hence the pilot-selected plan without another selection penalty. Coverage is over pilot randomization for the conditional-resolution target; it is not coverage conditional on each realized pilot or a statement about future hospitals.

The implemented exact-pair guard is 25 million multiply-adds. Above it, pointwise conditional envelopes conservatively relax the group-total constraint. A separate two-million-entry linear-work cap, fixed before target evaluation, triggers the structural enclosure $[0,J/G]$, where $J$ counts comparisons admitting any conclusive configuration. No feasible total is discarded. Computed nontrivial extrema receive outward padding $10^{-10}$; no uniform floating-point error theorem is claimed. The target is met when the lower bound is at least $q_*$, not met when the upper bound is below $q_*$, and otherwise unresolved. This classifies total expected resolution, not incremental benefit or economic authorization. The primary target is .10, with .05/.20 sensitivities. Posterior-quantile bands in the earlier gate experiment are not these confidence enclosures.

Historical CP results and protocol crosswalk

The current allocation evaluation and the earlier forecast protocols have different information budgets. The current finite-capacity study uses 20 randomized pilots per feasible setting and charges pilot outcomes, base confirmation counts and the extra allocation budget. It evaluates the selected plan under the fixed empirical count law. Earlier correction experiments fit a frozen isotonic map; expanded-calibration experiments add information while retaining selected plans. These comparisons cannot be pooled or interpreted as equal-cost clinical confirmation.

At the larger Texas pilot, adaptive allocation achieved 19.06% mean expected resolution versus 12.20% for balancing at matched total cost 2,878 positive-outcome records (paired gain 6.86 percentage points; Monte Carlo standard error 0.74 points). These means average 20 exact pilot-conditional probabilities. At the smaller pilot and total cost 2,223, expected resolution was 10.96% versus 10.85% (gain 0.10 points; standard error 0.81). Comparing the two pilot settings adds 655 observations; it is not an equal-cost improvement. Complete-family resolution remained negligible.

At the primary .10 expected-resolution target, all 160 confidence forecasts left the target decision unresolved. The computational cap was set to two million entries before evaluation against the target probabilities. In all 80 Texas cases, the calculation reached the structural fallback $[0,1]$ rather than completing the count-box enclosure. Those intervals reflect the implemented computational limit and leave forecast informativeness unresolved. The other 80 cases used the exact count-box procedure but also did not settle target attainment. This does not extend to every sensitivity target: all 40 MIMIC pilots supported target not met at .20. A positive point forecast alone supplied no confidence-supported target assertion.

An extra budget of 2,000 was infeasible for both eICU pilots (whole-batch extra capacities 1,500 and 1,300) and both MIMIC pilots (capacities 300 and 250). Those four failures are retained. For MIMIC, 23 categories have no positive-outcome support. The structural maximum resolvable fraction of 0.15 applies to the original CP rule at these confirmation counts; it is not the structural maximum for the different full-frame interval rule below. All counts are positive-outcome eligibility counts, not all-patient screening costs.

Balancing and uniform increments produced identical count vectors in all 160 pilots. Every category eligible for a 50-record increment began at the same 25-record minimum; smaller categories could receive no increment. Thus the two control criteria coincide here. At the headline cost the original-rule oracle reached 23.24%, compared with DP's 19.06%; the saved oracle is an unavailable-information benchmark for that objective.

Post hoc full-frame interval-rule comparison

On 26 October, we evaluated all 160 saved pilots and all four saved allocations under a different interval rule without changing any allocation, cost, predictor, tolerance or clinical record. This post hoc diagnostic targets the complete recorded-cohort gap \[ \Delta_g=K_g/N_g-K_0/N_0. \] A pass is incorrect when $|\Delta_g|>.10$; a fail is incorrect when $|\Delta_g|\leq.10$. Inconclusive outputs are not errors. Zero original denominators define no rate and remain inconclusive, while retaining the original multiplicity and mean-resolution slots.

Conditional on the saved pilot, confirmation counts satisfy \[ X_g\sim\operatorname{Hypergeom}(R_g,T_g,n_g),\qquad R_g=N_g-m_g,\quad T_g=K_g-k_g. \] We applied the existing fixed-time hypergeometric tail inversion to $X_g$ at tail error $\alpha/[2(G+1)]$, $\alpha=.05$, obtaining integer bounds $[L_g(X_g),U_g(X_g)]$ for $T_g$. Adding known pilot errors gives complete-frame rate bounds \[ \ell_g(X_g)=\frac{k_g+L_g(X_g)}{N_g},\qquad u_g(X_g)=\frac{k_g+U_g(X_g)}{N_g}. \] The gap interval $[\ell_g-u_0,u_g-\ell_0]$ yields pass when contained in $[-.10,.10]$, fail when entirely outside it, and inconclusive otherwise. Zero confirmation counts retain deterministic completion bounds; a census gives the exact known total. Integer cross-products implement tolerance equality and true-gap containment without ambiguous floating-point subtraction at the boundary.

For each fixed realized pilot and its selected confirmation allocation, each inverted total interval has coverage at least $1-\alpha/(G+1)$ under within-category simple random sampling without replacement. Bonferroni therefore gives simultaneous rate coverage at least $1-\alpha=.95$. On this event every defined gap interval covers its true full-frame gap and no pass/fail conclusion is incorrect. This is a classical finite-frame design guarantee conditional on the pilot-selected fixed counts, with no optional stopping. Independence among category draws is used for exact joint evaluation, not for the union bound. Known complete outcome-positive membership, correct linkage and the stated random review design are required. No future-hospital, population or prospective spending guarantee follows.

For both interval rules, we integrated pass and fail probabilities over the same exact conditional hypergeometric masses, conditioning on one reference count before taking products across comparisons. Table S39 averages these conditional probabilities over each setting's 20 retained pilots. Mean wrong-pass and wrong-fail probabilities average over all declared comparisons. ``Any wrong'' is the probability of at least one incorrect conclusion in the audit and retains shared-reference dependence. All four allocations remain fixed; notably the saved oracle optimized the original CP objective and is not an upper bound for the new rule.

\normalsize

At cost 2,878, full-frame resolution was 39.13% for DP and 30.23% for balancing/uniform, a paired gain of 8.90 percentage points (pilot MCSE 1.67). The allocation advantage was not uniform: with the smaller Texas pilot it was $-1.47$ points (MCSE 1.08), and with the larger eICU pilot $-4.12$ points (MCSE .63). The original-rule oracle allocation gave 25.78% in the headline setting. This is not evidence that DP outperforms an oracle optimized for the full-frame objective. In small-budget Texas settings, the tiny probabilities of conclusive output are almost entirely incorrect fails and provide no useful resolution advantage.

For the headline full-frame DP plan, mean wrong-pass probability was zero, mean wrong-fail probability .009582%, and any-incorrect probability .038326%, compared with zero, .000088% and .000353% for balancing/uniform. All four true Texas gaps are within tolerance, so every incorrect conclusion there is a fail. Across all 640 plan/policy evaluations, the largest conditional any-incorrect probability was .048888% and the smallest simultaneous full-gap coverage 99.2461%. Across the 32 setting/policy means, any-incorrect probabilities ranged from $6.758\times10^{-10}$% to .048038%, and simultaneous gap coverage from 99.3608% to 99.9460%. These empirical extrema describe the saved pilots; they are not uniform performance guarantees.

For context, applying the original CP rule to the headline DP allocation gave 19.0625% resolution, .009569% mean wrong-fail probability and .038276% any-incorrect probability against the same full-frame target; balancing gave 12.1978%, .000070% and .000280%. Such small observed probabilities do not prove general CP validity for finite sampling. The full-frame and remainder tolerance states differed in eight of 20 eICU pilots at each cap and in seven and 12 MIMIC pilots at caps 20 and 200, respectively; no Texas state changed. The target must therefore be named explicitly.

The large mortality resolution changes between interval rules reflect use of known pilot records, finite-population information and census completion, not new observations or improved allocations. MIMIC retains 40 comparisons including 23 zero-positive categories, so complete-family resolution remains zero under either rule. The full-frame rule does not inherit the original rule's .15 structural resolution ceiling. No confidence-based resolution forecast was recalculated for the new rule. The 160 unresolved decisions concern the primary .10 target under the original CP rule; the .05/.20 sensitivity results also retain that original-rule interpretation.

The diagnostic independently reproduced all 640 saved original-rule expectations to maximum absolute error $1.39\times10^{-16}$. Checks of the new rule covered 1,495 exhaustive finite-sampling coverage cases (minimum .992063 versus nominal .99), 815 exact endpoint-inversion cases and eight independent Cartesian count enumerations, including zero support, zero confirmation, census and exact tolerance equality. Maximum joint-enumeration difference was $1.11\times10^{-16}$. The portable notebook executes these checks and 24 real rule/policy replays drawn from one saved pilot in each cohort; the complete 640-policy diagnostic outputs are preserved separately. This execution is not a rerun of all historical experiments or new clinical validation.

Historical spending-gate crosswalk

The historical spending gate is a separate simulation comparison. Stable-law resolution was 24.38% for the point-estimate gate, 16.25% for the posterior-quantile gate and 24.58% for ungated dynamic programming. The first comparison concerns the two named gates; the ungated value is not its baseline. These historical percentages are not the current matched-cost result in the table.

Forecast design and information cost

The original 12 October validation used 400 pilots in each of 32 settings, or 12,800 pilots per stable/shifted law; its results appear in Table S40 and Figure S5. The separate 15 October follow-up used 100 new pilots per setting, or 3,200 plans, and supplies the expanded-calibration table below. Its raw, frozen and expected-resolution values therefore need not equal the original table. The safeguard experiment also used 3,200 new pilots under its own protocol and is not pooled with either result.

For each of the 3,200 selected plans from the 15 October follow-up, an independent calibration count of 200 eligible outcomes per group was generated. The candidate used those counts alone, so 1,000 additional labelled outcomes were required per plan, beyond that planning pilot. Binomial plug-in prediction used $(k+0.5)/(m+1)$; beta-binomial prediction integrated the corresponding Jeffreys posterior. Both retained the selected counts. The primary contrast was binomial plug-in minus frozen isotonic MSE under stable rates; shifted rates were a separate stress endpoint. The intervention changes both calibration size and its independence from planning, so their individual effects cannot be separated by this experiment. The exact confirmation expectations were already available but were joined only after forecasts were saved and hashed.

Clinical replay instead reused the full calibration partition, including records used in the original pilot and threshold selection. This supplied 42,923 eligible Texas outcomes and 1,303 eICU outcomes, compared with original pilot totals of 100 and 109. No additional clinical records were observed. A third forecast used hypergeometric masses with population error totals estimated by rounding the known confirmation capacity times the calibration rate. Those are plug-in estimates, not known test-population error counts. All candidates used the same information and the same 1,400 fixed allocations. None was selected using confirmation outcomes. The seven feasible settings and all previously infeasible eICU/MIMIC full-family budgets were retained.

The prespecified stable-law MSE difference was $-0.01958$ (95% Monte Carlo interval $-0.02093$ to $-0.01824$). The shifted-law difference was $0.000714$ ($-0.000595$ to $0.002022$). Intervals use within-setting variance of paired squared errors and equal weights across 32 settings. They quantify simulated-pilot/calibration variation within these fixed profiles. Expanded clinical forecasts reduced MSE in all seven settings, but the 2,000-record Texas forecast remained 16.27% against 11.98% expected resolution. Lower error does not establish an equal-cost advantage or future clinical calibration.

C4: intervention targets, errors and review costs¶

What does policy review accept or reject? Reviewed disagreement outcomes bound incremental detections and false alerts under a declared criterion. Acquisition and inference are compared at matched costs. This is a policy-audit conclusion, not a treatment-effect estimate.

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

C4: intervention targets, errors and review costs

For categories with at least 20 calibration deaths and 20 survivors, the group policy takes the highest score threshold achieving at least 80% calibration sensitivity: $$ t_g=\max\{t\in\mathcal S_g:\sum_{i\in g,Y_i=1}\mathbf1(S_i\geq t)/m_g^+\geq0.80\}. $$ Other categories retain the original global threshold. The utility preference and permitted increase in group misses are specified before the paired review. These are evaluated research criteria, not a demonstration that additional flagged deaths would have been preventable.

A symmetric parity failure is not necessarily evidence of harm to the comparison group. In the finite-frame eICU access study, Native American patients had zero misses among ten deaths versus 327 among 1,505 in the reference (signed difference $-21.73$ points). At the 13-unit-derived budget, capped-equal hypergeometric review classified this difference as failing in 1,977 of 2,000 replays because it was outside the symmetric tolerance on the favorable side. Across six comparisons, the same review resolved 86.12% of comparison-replay pairs: 58.77% passed and 27.35% failed. Matched proportional review resolved 3.67% (3.28% passed, 0.38% failed). These are decisions about the declared error-gap criterion, not changes in patient outcomes.

The exploratory protocol was recorded before inspecting the new policy results on 28 September 2026. Earlier baseline test results were already known. The current corrected eICU and MIMIC cohorts, saved XGBoost scores and seeds 11, 29 and 47 were retained. No model was retrained. These threshold results do not establish reweighing effectiveness for the current mortality models. Calibration data alone selected the category thresholds in Supplementary equation S17 and the calibration-budget global comparator. The selection targeted sensitivity, not probability calibration. Threshold adjustment is an established intervention;[11] this evaluation does not claim a new mitigation algorithm.

All seven eICU and 41 MIMIC source categories were declared before policy evaluation, including their reference categories. Four eICU and three MIMIC categories met the requirement of at least 20 calibration deaths and 20 survivors. Every other category used the original global threshold. Native American in eICU had eight calibration deaths; AMERICAN INDIAN/ALASKA NATIVE in MIMIC had none. Their policies therefore remained unchanged. A fitting-support requirement never removed a category from the test audit.

The global budget comparator searched distinct calibration scores plus a threshold above the maximum, minimizing absolute alert-count deviation. Equal deviations favoured fewer alerts, then the higher threshold. Calibration alerts matched exactly in all six fits. Realized test workloads were reported rather than forced to match. This differs from the historical additional-test-alert comparison.

Paired empirical bootstrap draws used seed 928771 for 25 eICU patient-linked components and seed 928772 for MIMIC patients. The same 500 draws were shared by policies and training seeds within each cohort. All records within a sampled component received its integer resampling weight. Contrasts compared group minus original, budget minus original and group minus budget policies. Every plotted overall sensitivity, false-positive-rate and alert-fraction contrast had 500 defined replicates. These intervals describe the empirical resampling distribution of frozen predictions; they exclude threshold selection and model fitting uncertainty.

The maximum-gap metric used the full originally positive-supported contrast set. A replicate losing any required denominator was marked undefined. Only two of 500 MIMIC replicates retained that complete set, so no interval was reported for its maximum gap. Undefined rates were never replaced by zero. Category-specific rates, support counts and the number of defined replicates are retained in the aggregate files.

The family-adjusted binomial endpoint rule retained error input 0.05, tolerance 0.10 and denominator gate one. All 18 cohort/seed/policy evaluations remained entirely inconclusive. Exact plugin-binomial calculations separately evaluated repeated conclusiveness under fixed observed denominators. These supplied count laws do not establish future-hospital validity. In MIMIC, 23 categories lacked positive outcomes, while 11 additional comparisons admitted no conclusive configuration under this family-adjusted binomial endpoint rule at their fixed denominators. The latter limitation is rule-dependent. Only six contrasts admitted any conclusive count configuration; only UNKNOWN/NOT SPECIFIED admitted a pass. These structural checks were unchanged by thresholds.

The seed-11 maximum MIMIC gap fell from 79.30 to 78.23 points, but BLACK/AFRICAN AMERICAN misses rose from 5/26 to 10/26. False positives fell from 128 to 70 in that group. UNKNOWN/NOT SPECIFIED misses fell from 23/72 to 20/72 with false positives increasing from 124 to 151. WHITE reference misses rose from 77/372 to 81/372. Thus reference-relative summaries changed partly because the reference policy changed. Neither the smaller maximum gap nor fewer aggregate false alerts established uniformly improved group outcomes.

Execution checks independently reproduced the original seed-11 audit states, all observed endpoint predicates and count-probability mass conservation. Original raw-score AUROC and average precision were identical across policies. Synthetic checks covered score ties, budget ties, absent categories, fallback rules and confusion-count indexing across 41 categories. The accompanying protocol, source manifest, threshold table, full group confusion counts and paired bootstrap records document this evaluation. No private row-level records were exported.

This supporting RQ4 evaluation retained C1a to C4, predictions and all previously fitted thresholds. It assesses whether an existing policy change satisfies a declared retrospective criterion. It introduces neither a new mitigation method nor an additional contribution. Both cohorts and all three seeds had been examined previously. The local protocol preceded randomized replay but does not make the clinical analysis independent confirmation.

Decision target and original review design

Let $g$ index every category in one exhaustive, mutually exclusive partition, including the reference category used in disparity comparisons. For each category, let $N_{g+}$ and $N_{g-}$ count newly flagged and no-longer-flagged records. An overlapping demographic family is assessed separately; its records are not added again to the same utility sum. Their unknown outcome-positive totals are $K_{g+}$ and $K_{g-}$. Then $$ \Delta TP_g=K_{g+}-K_{g-},\quad \Delta A=\sum_g(N_{g+}-N_{g-}),\quad \Delta FP=\Delta A-\sum_g\Delta TP_g. $$ Unchanged classifications cancel. The criterion requires every $\Delta TP_g\geq0$ and utility $U(w)=\sum_g\Delta TP_g-w\Delta FP>0$. The illustrative primary weight $w=0.1$ values one detection as ten false alerts; weights 0, 0.25 and 1 test sensitivity. In mixed-direction changes, this net-count constraint permits newly missed patients to be offset by newly detected patients in the same category; it is not individual protection. These weights lack clinical endorsement. The utility is a count-based scenario, not a causal care effect or a probability-threshold decision curve. Zero changes in an absent or unchanged category do not establish that category's absolute fairness.

Let $S$ be the number of nonempty category-direction strata. When $S=0$, both policies make identical classifications: all signed changes and utility are exactly zero, so the strict positive-utility criterion is not met with no outcome review. For $S>0$, each active stratum is sampled without replacement. For population size $N$, total $K$, reviewed count $m$ and observed positives $k$, the conditional law is $k\sim\operatorname{Hypergeom}(N,K,m)$. The retained integer totals satisfy $$ \Pr_K(X\geq k)\geq\alpha/(2S),\qquad \Pr_K(X\leq k)\geq\alpha/(2S). $$ The two tails and a union bound give at least $1-\alpha$ simultaneous coverage for the fixed cohort. Unreviewed strata retain $[0,N]$ and census strata $[k,k]$. Group difference endpoints and utility endpoints follow by signed addition. All lower group bounds nonnegative and a positive lower utility bound support a criterion-met result (state A). A negative upper group bound or nonpositive upper utility bound supports a criterion-not-met result; otherwise the decision is deferred. The same covered totals support all four weights simultaneously. The randomization concerns observation of fixed outcomes and does not require independent patients or hospitals.[12] This fixed-budget inversion is not an anytime confidence sequence or a guarantee for future hospitals.

In the original four-budget experiment, uniform review sampled the whole cohort. Targeted review used capacity-capped equal allocation across active disagreement strata, without their outcome counts, and stopped at their census. Both received the same maximum budget, defined as 1%, 5%, 10% or 20% of cohort size, rounded down. Unused budget was reported. A point-estimate uniform comparator deferred if any active stratum remained unsampled; it had no interval guarantee. Each budget was evaluated separately, without optional stopping. There were 2,000 paired review repetitions for each of 18 contrasts and four budgets, or 144,000 review pairs. The policies were category-specific thresholds (G), original global thresholds (O) and the global calibration-alert-matched policy (B).

Original review results and interpretation

At the primary 5% budget and $w=0.1$, targeted review resolved every contrast after inspecting all changed classifications. These records constituted 0.10% to 3.77% of each cohort. Uniform review resolved 21.71%; the paired difference was 78.29 points (95% Monte Carlo interval 77.88 to 78.70), with equal weights across the 18 fixed contrasts. Targeted review averaged 141.78 records versus 635 for uniform review. This is a census advantage from known prediction disagreements, not evidence of a new concentration inequality or prediction accuracy gain. The review workload is simulated because outcomes were already available, and record review time and implementation costs were not measured.

All 18 contrasts were rejected under the primary criterion. Sixteen increased misses in at least one category; the other two failed the utility test. At zero false-alert cost, two contrasts satisfied the criterion and targeted review supported them after its disagreement census. A uniformly sampled point-estimate decision incorrectly endorsed changes in 10.78% of primary replays, versus 0.014% for uniform interval decisions and zero for the targeted census. These are outcomes of the defined comparators, not measured failures of a deployed tool. Across valid methods, fixed settings and weights, the lowest simulated simultaneous coverage was 98.65%. Each coverage estimate used 2,000 repetitions, not 2,000 independent clinical cohorts.

The primary benefit is a supported decision about a particular policy change while absolute parity remains inconclusive. These conclusions do not establish safety for future patients, clinical benefit from care, or that the current global policy is acceptable. Useful future-hospital inference and forecast transport remain unresolved. The requirement of no net increase in subgroup misses and utility weights need intended-user assessment before operational use. Under this net-count rule, every contrast failed at the tested positive weights .1, .25 and 1; the later preference analysis below shows how smaller weights or a .02 FNR allowance change these decisions. Positive-case support is therefore limited under the primary criterion, not absent under every possible preference.

Verification and retained implementation detail

All 432 category-level paired transition rows were reconstructed from six original private prediction files and reconciled with the saved counts. Exact finite-population coverage checks covered 1,784 small-population cases; a separate combinatorial calculation checked 818 cases. Every new summary and 720 randomized review pairs were separately recomputed from the packaged aggregate inputs. A disagreement census recovered every exact criterion decision. All cases, seeds, weights, budgets and deferred decisions remain in the notebook and aggregate files. No patient records are included.

Later partial-review comparison and preference sensitivity

The 22 October extension reused all 18 fixed policy contrasts at maximum review fractions .1%, .25%, .5%, 1%, 2% and 5%; .5% was the primary partial-budget comparison. Each case/budget used 2,000 randomizations seeded by $(20261022,4419,\mathrm{case},\mathrm{budget\ index},\mathrm{replicate})$. Uniform cohort review and capped-equal disagreement review were joined by an outcome-free proportional-disagreement comparator. The latter assigns one record per active stratum when affordable, then distributes remaining reviews in proportion to remaining capacities by largest remainders. If the budget cannot cover every stratum, larger strata receive priority; fixed indices break ties. All three use the same hypergeometric intervals and multiplicity rule. No outcome totals determine allocations, and each fixed budget is evaluated separately.

Actual reviews, unused allowances, coverage and decisions were retained, with a separate subset where the budget is below the disagreement census. In the 15 such contrasts at .5%, $w=.1$ and zero FNR allowance, mean resolution was 82.73% for capped-equal, 82.46% for proportional-disagreement and 2.95% for uniform review, each using 55.2 records on average. These are distinct from the original 5% census comparison. Sensitivity used $w\in\{0,.1,.25,1\}$ and allowed group FNR increases $\tau\in\{0,.02\}$, replacing the group constraint by $\Delta TP_g\geq-\tau M_g^{(1)}$, where $M_g^{(1)}$ is the complete category-positive total and $M_g^{(0)}$ denotes the complete category-negative total. These outcome denominators differ from the disagreement sizes $N_{g+}$ and $N_{g-}$. Covered totals support these scenarios together; the values are unendorsed preferences.

The separate 23 October deterministic analysis used complete counts without new review draws. It defined \[ \tau_{\min}=\max\left\{0,\max_{g:M_g^{(1)}>0}\frac{-\Delta TP_g}{M_g^{(1)}}\right\}, \] and retained all 18 contrasts at $w\in\{0,.05,.1,.25,1\}$ and $\tau\in\{0,.02\}$. The recorded-cohort criterion is met when $\tau\geq\tau_{\min}$ and $\Delta TP-w\Delta FP>0$, retaining strict utility equality as rejection. Zero-positive categories provide no positive-outcome evidence. This map describes observed-cohort trade-offs rather than inference from a partial review. For example, the eICU seed-11 calibration-budget change has six additional detections, 60 additional false alerts and no group loss, so it passes the zero-loss criterion at $w=.05$ but not at $w=.1$. It does not establish clinical endorsement or preventable deaths.

29 October review at matched actual record counts

This extension retained all 18 correlated clinical policy contrasts, categories and frozen classifications. The contrasts comprise three related policy comparisons across three training seeds in two previously inspected cohorts; they are not 18 independent clinical replications. At each maximum budget, every design spent the same actual record count, capped by the disagreement census. Whole-cohort uniform review could therefore spend reviews on unchanged classifications, while capped-equal and proportional-disagreement review sampled known disagreement strata. The protocol used 1,000 randomizations per case/budget and retained all cases, including censuses. This is a fresh randomized replay of inspected cohorts, not independent clinical validation.

The simultaneous fixed-budget hypergeometric event retained error .05 over the nonempty disagreement strata and supported the complete deterministic preference grid: $w\in\{0,.05,.1,.25,1\}$, FNR allowance $\tau\in\{0,.02\}$, and absent, zero or .02 subgroup FPR-increase caps. With $\Delta A_g$ known from classifications, $\Delta FP_g=\Delta A_g-\Delta TP_g$. Consequently no net increase in subgroup misses and zero subgroup FP-count increase require outcomes only in disagreements. A positive FNR allowance additionally needs the complete $M_g^{(1)}$; a positive FPR allowance needs complete $M_g^{(0)}$, or known group size minus $M_g^{(1)}$. Both include unchanged classifications. Absolute PPV changes require complete baseline confusion counts and are reported descriptively, not inferred from partial review. The same simultaneous event supports the preference grid without a separate penalty, but does not give anytime validity across adaptively repeated review budgets.

Equal minus proportional resolution at .5% was .294 percentage points (95% Monte Carlo precision interval $[-.329,.918]$), and equal minus uniform was 83.161 points [82.676,83.646]. These equal-case averages concern the fixed contrasts; their intervals measure replay precision, not clinical generalization. No incorrect conclusion occurred at the .5% primary budget. Across all 11,340 clinical case/budget/design/preference summaries, minimum simulated simultaneous coverage was 98.5% and maximum setting-specific wrong-decision frequency .4%. These are distinct from the 22 October interval-only extrema of 98.65%, .55% wrong acceptance and zero wrong rejection. They do not include the historical point-estimate comparator and must not be pooled with its errors.

At $w=.05$, zero FNR allowance and no FP safeguard, two eICU budget-policy contrasts met the criterion; a zero subgroup FP-count-increase constraint rejected both. At $w=.1$ and .02 FNR allowance, three contrasts met the criterion with or without that zero-FP-increase constraint, each losing detections while reducing false alerts. These choices are unendorsed. Their full-denominator assumption matters: if constructing $M_g^{(1)}$ and $M_g^{(0)}$ requires individually linking and ascertaining every cohort outcome, the entire policy decision is already directly evaluable at that cost. Partial-review savings cannot apply to the same completed ascertainment. A trusted aggregate outcome registry is a separate known-information assumption whose acquisition cost remains external.

Synthetic criterion controls. Four separate fixed frames tested acceptance, added-miss rejection, concentrated false alerts and equality at the strict utility boundary. A concentrated-alert case with 95 added detections and 105 added false alerts satisfied the original criterion but violated a .02 subgroup FPR cap: one group gained 95 false alerts among 800 negatives, an 11.875-point increase. In the boundary case, ten additional detections and 100 false alerts gave utility zero at $w=.1$, requiring rejection. At 100 of 110 disagreements reviewed, equal/proportional designs resolved only .8%/.7%; both recovered rejection at census. These cases verify supported abstention, positive decisions and boundary handling under known truth, not clinical adoption effectiveness. The clinical primary experiment remains all-rejection.

Cost sensitivity and verification. An operational example is illustrative, not observed: a hospital model-governance analyst has a registry of reliable identifiers, categories and two policies' classifications for a closed cohort, but no linked adjudicated outcome field. A reviewer checks sampled disagreement records against source charts. These known fields and perfect outcome verification are explicit assumptions. A criterion-not-met result supports rejection under the specified rule; criterion met leads to independent clinical assessment; inconclusive leaves the decision open. Unverifiable records remain incomplete review, outside the simulated access law, rather than being silently imputed. Outcome-dependent nonresponse can invalidate the sampling law; unresolved sampled records cannot simply be discarded. Registry setup, failed linkage, reviewer disagreement and staff time were not measured. The .10 symmetric disparity tolerance, calibration sensitivity target and utility/rate preferences are research definitions, not patient-benefit thresholds or endorsements of absolute model performance.

The actor is a retrospective model-governance analyst evaluating a frozen policy change for one closed cohort. Predictions and categories are aligned; review verifies masked outcomes/linkage because the experiment assumes that bottleneck. Accept supports only the incremental recorded-cohort criterion, reject rules it out, and inconclusive requests more evidence. None establishes baseline acceptability, overall fairness or patient benefit. The research extracts already contain outcomes and no operational time-and-motion study was performed.

Cost scenarios add frame costs of 0/.01/.1/1 record-equivalents per cohort record and hypothetical unit counts 1/5/25 at costs 0/1/5/20 per unit. Common overhead preserves the matched-cost equality. Differential contacts can remove disagreement-census savings relative to whole-cohort review, but no actual unit mapping is available here; these scenarios must not inherit the C1 known-frame contact counts. No staff-time or empirical access-cost saving follows.

The full extension retains 660 case/preference truths and 13,860 replay-summary rows including the four synthetic cases. Independent checks reconciled all 432 clinical subgroup accounting rows and all saved decisions; exact rational enumeration matched 1,680 small hypergeometric intervals, and 9,720 confidence-box/preference checks found no covered incorrect conclusion. Nine selected case/budget combinations regenerated 810,000 decisions exactly. All designs matched actual record counts. These bounded checks do not reconstruct restricted patient data or establish transportability.

Historical reweighing and protocol separation¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Historical reweighing and protocol separation

The equal-hospital Texas age-selection-ratio increase of 0.505 averages seeds 11, 29 and 47 before the hospital bootstrap; the saved unrounded mean is 0.5047589127. It is a dimensionless ratio change across 31 supported hospitals out of 66, not a probability-point increase in patient benefit. Age/outcome-independence weighting reduced historical XGBoost AUROC from 0.749 to 0.679. All three seeds failed the declared calibration utility screen, which permitted at most a 0.02 sensitivity decrease and a 0.02 alert-fraction increase relative to the matching baseline. Each failed the alert constraint; AUROC was reported separately. The 16 improved, ten worsened and five unchanged counts below refer specifically to demographic-cell weighting at seed 11, not that three-seed average or the age/outcome-independence policy.

This section reproduces existing aggregate evidence from the historical age-localization experiment, rather than adding a new fit. The three-field Texas predictor is separate from the current four-field diagnosis model. All weighted policies and fixed seeds are retained. The selection-rate ratio is the minimum divided by maximum age-category selection rate. A hospital required at least 20 records in every declared age category. Unsupported hospitals remain in the denominator of the support column.

Demographic-cell weights were $\operatorname{clip}(N/(K n_c),0.1,10)$ using observed race, age and sex/gender training cells. Age/outcome independence and uniform age/outcome weighting are separate comparators. Changes below compare each policy with its matching unweighted predictor. Counts describe point changes, not simultaneous hospital-specific certificates. For the highlighted seed-11 Texas XGBoost demographic-cell policy, 16 of 31 supported hospitals improved, ten worsened and five were unchanged. Nine improvement intervals and six worsening intervals excluded zero under the original marginal bootstrap; these exploratory intervals were not multiplicity-adjusted.

The eICU second-stage hospital bootstrap does not model all cross-hospital patient links, so its historical site intervals remain descriptive. These results do not establish a causal explanation, current-model mitigation effectiveness or patient benefit.

Additional retrospective policy and paired-planning validation¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Additional retrospective policy and paired-planning validation

This extension retains the preceding observations and frozen predictors. It adds two analyses specified before their new evaluations: a calibration-defined policy panel and paired confidence projection on existing planning records. Neither supplies an untouched cohort. Original figures, reference entries and numerical result records remain unchanged.

Known prediction direction and clinical-policy decisions

The panel used the six eICU/MIMIC-III XGBoost fits (seeds 11, 29 and 47). For each fit, the highest calibration threshold achieving sensitivity 60, 70, 75, 85, 90 or 95% was compared with its original 80% threshold. The three existing group/global/budget comparisons were retained, yielding 54 correlated policy contrasts. The six calibration partitions contained 1,303/473 deaths in 15,619/4,847 eICU/MIMIC records, respectively; the original thresholds reproduced their stored values exactly. Patient identifiers crossed no stored partition. This check does not establish that all potential leakage is absent.

The protocol, input hashes and calibration thresholds were frozen at 04:35:03 UTC on 30 October 2026, before new test-policy evaluation began at 04:35:22. The primary criterion retained no net increase in subgroup misses and $\Delta TP-.1\Delta FP>0$; weights .05 and .25 were prespecified sensitivities. Budgets were 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100% of each disagreement frame, rounded upward and capped at census. Each case/design/budget used 1,000 randomized reviews. Complete outcome totals assessed truth only, not the zero-loss review decision. The replay took 29.56 seconds on the recorded machine; this is computation time, not staff review time.

Equal and proportional allocation sampled category--direction strata. SRS-D sampled the disagreement frame; SRS-C sampled the whole cohort at the identical total count. Conditional on its realized stratum sample sizes, SRS supplies uniform samples within strata, so the existing simultaneous hypergeometric intervals remain valid. Sampling depends on known predictions and categories, not outcomes. The direction-pooled comparison uses exactly the same SRS-D sampled records; its advantage isolates the inference rule from the sampling allocation.

For a purely negative-to-positive change, $\Delta TP_g\geq0$ follows from classifications before outcomes are reviewed. Write $D$ for total disagreements and $K$ for their positive outcomes. Utility is $U(w)=(1+w)K-wD$. If $[L,U]$ is a level-$1-\alpha$ hypergeometric confidence interval for $K$, positive lower utility certifies the criterion and nonpositive upper utility rejects it. The one-dimensional coverage event suffices for the whole criterion because its subgroup no-added-miss clauses are deterministic. It does not estimate group-specific effect magnitudes or verify subgroup false-alert caps. For a purely positive-to-negative change, zero added misses requires $K=0$ and utility is $wD-(1+w)K$; an upper total of zero with $wD>0$ certifies the criterion, whereas a positive lower total or nonpositive upper utility rejects it. Mixed-direction changes retain separate group bounds. No disagreements imply exactly zero utility and failure of the strict-positive criterion without review.

All 54 policies failed the primary weight-.1 criterion. At 10% disagreement review, mean actual cost was 122.13 records: equal/proportional/SRS-D correct rejection was 46.15/45.78/46.47%, compared with 21.34% for SRS-C. Thus a sensible disagreement-SRS comparator did not support general superiority of the proposed allocation. Only 42 policies had a single direction; pooled results are compared on that matched subset, not against an all-54 average.

The weight-.05 sensitivity contained 20 acceptable and 34 rejected policies. All 20 acceptable policies added positive classifications only. Within this secondary 20-policy subset, at 50% disagreement review (992.20 records on average), correct acceptance was 46.91% with equal allocation, 31.71% with proportional allocation, 31.350% with stratified SRS-D and 71.745% with pooled inference on the identical SRS-D records. The paired gain was 40.395 points (95% Monte Carlo interval [39.781,41.009]); pooled wrong rejection was .01% and deferral 28.245%. These are conditional replay quantities, not independent clinical replications. All targeted census decisions exactly matched complete-cohort truth.

The smallest empirical coverage was 93.8% [92.12,95.21] in eICU seed 47 at the 60% target, pooled inference and 20% review (666 records). Independent finite-law calculation gives 95.3128% coverage for that same setting. The largest primary wrong-decision frequency was 3.1% [2.12,4.37] in MIMIC seed 11 at the 85% target and 20% pooled review (67 records); its exact wrong-acceptance probability is 2.15085%. The displayed intervals describe simulation uncertainty for selected extrema, not simultaneous confidence limits over the grid. Across design cells, pooled empirical coverage averaged 97.896% over its 42 applicable cases; other designs retained all 54. Coverage and error denominators remain explicit in the aggregate files.

The representative example was fixed as the first cohort, first seed and first higher-sensitivity target, rather than selected for its outcome. eICU seed 11 at 85% changes 1,595 of 20,572 classifications, adding 115 detected deaths and 1,480 false alerts. Utility changes from $-33$ at .1 to $+41$ at .05. At 798 random outcome verifications, pooled inference supported primary rejection in 79.7% of replays and deferred in 20.3%; weight .05 supported acceptance in 98.3% and deferred in 1.7%. No wrong decision occurred in these two fixed-example slices. Table S48 retains every recorded category. None gains an additional miss, but the Native American category gains no detection and five false alerts; meeting the criterion is not demonstrated benefit for that group.

The auditor knows categories and both classifications initially. One reviewed record reveals its outcome; no complete positive-outcome denominator is required for the criterion of no net increase in subgroup misses. Frame construction, prediction linkage, access arrangements, failed reviews and staff minutes are unpriced. A 50% disagreement budget therefore means half the census outcome verifications, not a measured 50% reduction in clinical work. The weights and zero-loss constraints remain research choices without clinician endorsement. Existing cohort inspection and correlated policy comparisons preclude independent external-validation claims.

Paired confidence projection and a correctness safeguard

The further planning analysis freezes all 160 primary clinical pilot-budget records and all 640 existing factorial pilots, preserving allocations, count laws, grids and tolerances. The full remaining-total vector is withheld from projection; synthetic design metadata describe the factorial but are not read by the projection function. Deletion/perturbation checks test that separation. No new tolerance, posterior or allocation is fitted to the evaluated truth.

Let the simultaneous pilot region be $\mathcal T_0\times\cdots\times\mathcal T_G$. At candidate totals $(t_g,t_0)$, $H_g$ is one if the original full-cohort gap lies within the closed tolerance, and zero otherwise. For allocation $a$, define correct resolution \[ C_g^a(t_g,t_0)=H_gP_g^a(t_g,t_0)+(1-H_g)F_g^a(t_g,t_0), \] with zero for an unsupported denominator. For comparison plan $b$, take $D_g=C_g^a-C_g^b$ at the same candidate totals, then compute \[ L_{a-b}=G^{-1}\min_{t_0\in\mathcal T_0}\sum_{g=1}^G\min_{t_g\in\mathcal T_g}D_g(t_g,t_0). \] Maxima give the upper bound. At any fixed shared-reference total, the separate group extrema are attainable together because their total sets form a product; the outer reference extremum therefore gives the exact mean-difference range on that region. This separability concerns mean resolution, not multiplication of joint decisions. Minimizing each $D_g$ over both totals gives per-group lower bounds. Substituting $P_g+F_g$ projects conclusiveness instead of correctness.

On the original pilot event, all true totals lie in the region, so these bounds cover every considered allocation simultaneously, including pilot-selected plans. No added comparison penalty is required on that common event. A safeguard prefers DP to balancing only if its mean correct-resolution lower gain is strictly positive and every group lower gain is nonnegative. Otherwise it selects balancing. This confidence statement is over random pilots, not a posterior probability conditional on the observed pilot, an anytime guarantee, or proof that the spending is clinically worthwhile. Identical allocations return zero exactly; nonconstant bounds receive outward $10^{-10}$ padding.

The declared limits were 25 million pair operations and 50 million intermediate entries. A computational amendment, recorded before truth assessment, corrected pass-plus-fail work accounting and replaced oversized conditional-envelope construction with valid separate-extrema mean bounds and $[-1,1]$ group bounds. Earlier files and hashes were preserved. All 800 records remain; no oversized case is silently excluded or called an exact projection.

Against matched balancing, the clinical evaluation contains 71 exact identities and 89 conservative fallbacks; all 640 synthetic comparisons are exact. No positive matched-cost mean lower gain was certified, and the operational safeguard retained balancing in every clinical and synthetic record. Against lower-cost required minima, 42 clinical records (24 eICU, 18 MIMIC) had positive correct-resolution lower gains; 53 had positive conclusiveness lower gains. Each required 250 extra verifications. The correct-gain lower bounds had median .00123 and maximum .03165 percentage points, with minimum about $1.08\times10^{-8}$ points. This tightening is mathematically informative but does not establish a useful spending threshold. Every saved true gain was enclosed. The synthetic comparison against minima is a separate, different-cost diagnostic, not the matched-balancing selection policy.

The earlier predictive floor and switch remain in the study with their observed gains and group losses. The new confidence safeguard evaluates a different requirement: evidence that mean correctness improves without reducing any group's correctness. Its observed lack of switching is retained rather than replaced by a favorable point forecast. C2 likewise returns no supported clinical collection recommendation when no confidence region validated for its unbalanced source design is available. Its fitted sufficient counts and the balanced-design theorem remain conditional illustrations with their distinct assumptions.

Reproducibility and scope¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Reproducibility and scope

The 30 October revision adds the complete 54-policy panel and all 800 paired planning records. Independent calculation reproduced all 5,418 saved clinical decision arrays, assessed 656 planning records directly and verified the recorded bounds. A local input-validation repair rejects Boolean values before mixed-container integer coercion; historical source hashes remain preserved. All 4,800 frozen count vectors were unchanged, and all 800 projections replayed with maximum bound difference $2.22\times10^{-16}$. These are computational checks, not independent clinical cohorts.

The canonical notebook reconstructs aggregate summaries and executes declared probability checks. Its 26 October C3 addition packages the original four-policy controls and post hoc full-frame interval comparison, with separate target definitions, raw probabilities and replay checks. Earlier outputs are preserved, and no original forecast is relabelled as a forecast for the new interval rule. It preserves the preceding notebook, source hashes and historical experiment records. A 25 October input-validation repair rejects fractional or nonfinite counts before integer conversion; valid-count decisions and probabilities are checked against the preceding implementation. No reported clinical outcome or fitted prediction model was changed by that repair.

The historical \nolinkurl{JBHI_Reproducibility_Policy_20261031.zip} included extraction and model-setting documentation, aggregate inputs, protocols, environment specifications, manifests, code and executed outputs. Its contents are preserved in the current \nolinkurl{ICDE_Reproducibility_20261102.zip}, whose added public-Texas rebuild and later experiments have separate entry points. The historical replay excluded patient-level identifiers and restricted clinical records and did not independently extract cohorts or retrain predictors. Fresh simulated draws and randomized access to already examined cohorts do not provide an untouched clinical validation cohort.

The paper's empirical-bootstrap intervals describe their stated resampling laws. The source-model mean intervals are plug-in normal intervals that hold fitted covariance components fixed. Neither establishes full parameter uncertainty for a future hospital. Unsupported categories remain inconclusive; missing protected attributes are not inferred from proxy labels. The tolerance and utility weights are research inputs rather than clinically endorsed cut-offs.

Complete policy panel and computation-only follow-up

This retrospective reporting revision retains all 54 frozen policy contrasts. Known classification direction identifies 42 single-direction and 12 mixed-direction policies before their outcome-based truth is used. The primary false-alert weight is .1; .05 and .25 remain prespecified sensitivities from the original expanded experiment. Every policy is evaluated at the original seven disagreement fractions (1/2/5/10/20/50/100%), with 1,000 randomizations per method and budget. No new predictor, policy, patient or favorable outcome subset was selected for the complete comparison. The reporting plan was frozen before these new summaries, after the original outcomes had already been examined.

For each row, correct acceptance, wrong acceptance, correct rejection, wrong rejection and deferral partition all policy randomizations. Each policy has equal weight. Same-record pooled-minus-stratified comparisons isolate inference from allocation; equal/proportional comparisons use their original independent review substreams. Interval estimates describe pointwise Monte Carlo precision conditional on the retained policies and frames. A fixed-policy, fixed-budget confidence guarantee does not cover searching the panel for a favorable policy or repeated-look stopping.

The lower-cost acceptable subset remains secondary: 20 policies, not the complete 42. At half-disagreement review its pooled correct acceptance was 71.745% versus 31.350%, with .010% versus zero wrong rejection and 28.245% versus 68.650% deferral. Across the complete 42 policies the corresponding total correctness was 85.057% versus 65.821%. Under the primary criterion, total correctness was 80.083% versus 61.688%, with .095% versus zero wrong acceptance. At weight .25 all 54 fail; pooled versus stratified correctness over the eligible 42 was 97.252% versus 86.274%. Full policy-level and every-budget outcomes, pointwise exact Monte Carlo intervals and conservative bounded-outcome intervals are retained in the portable tables. Zero-width normal Monte Carlo intervals at zero empirical variance are not interpreted as proof of absence of errors.

The verifier reconstructed all 162 policy-weight truths, 5,418 saved decision/coverage arrays, 875 summary rows and 1,296 signed subgroup rows from aggregate inputs. Deterministic review replay matched all saved states. Targeted designs were exact at disagreement census; this is not a full-cohort census for whole-cohort SRS, whose informative reviews are recorded separately. Review counts across policies describe separate hypothetical audits and cannot be summed as unique patients. No private patient files were needed for this replay.

Exact paired clinical projection. The computation-only follow-up kept the original simultaneous pilot rectangle, paired same-total design, allocations, error levels and tolerance. Minimum, median and maximum input-work cases within five nonidentical cohort/pilot/budget strata gave 15 selections. Ten met the frozen work caps and completed; five retained skips were all Texas cases, including every selected pilot-20/budget-2,000 case. No nonidentical MIMIC allocation was available. The selected set is computationally stratified, not a random clinical sample.

All ten exact mean-gain intervals straddled zero and the confidence safeguard selected no switch. Mean width decreased from .951858 to .262411 in probability units (72.43%). Every evaluated true mean and group gain lay within its bounds; source expectations matched within $3\times10^{-12}$. An independent rational-probability check covered 91 parameter vectors in four small designs, including identity, census, unsupported groups and closed boundaries; evaluator discrepancy was at most $1.11\times10^{-16}$. The projection stage took 240.48 seconds with no attempted timeout. These results remove computational relaxation as the sole reason for noncertification in ten cases, without establishing a result for the other 79 nonidentical clinical cases or for a different confidence construction.

The existing eight-plan direct-gap diagnostic retains every category. In MIMIC-III, 23/40 slots have zero full-frame positive support; correct resolution of 39.4878--40.0025% over all slots equals 92.9124--94.1235% descriptively over the 17 supported slots. The primary denominator and error correction remain unchanged. In eICU at coarse pilot cap 20, the 5.8373-point improvement comes from incomplete group totals; at cap 200, the 2.6373-point gain comprises 1.4426 points from incomplete and 1.1947 from censused group totals. The latter comparisons still depend on an incomplete shared reference. This decomposition does not rerun or reoptimize the eight plans and does not extend their result to the other 152 records.

Scope of the error guarantees. The exact repeat calculation conditions on its supplied count law and does not estimate coverage for an unknown hospital population. The pilot and confirmation guarantees below refer to different randomizations. Their intersection has probability at least $1-\eta-\alpha$ by a union bound, without assuming independence. With the evaluated separate .05 budgets, this generic bound is .90, not .95. A report requiring joint 95% protection must allocate a common total error budget before evaluation; no such reallocation was used to generate the reported results.

Policy-release provenance and current entry point. The historical policy release used \nolinkurl{JBHI_Reproducibility_Policy_20261031.zip} and \nolinkurl{Journal_Canonical_Evidence.ipynb}. The current entry point is \nolinkurl{ICDE_Canonical_Evidence_20261102.ipynb} in \nolinkurl{ICDE_Reproducibility_20261102.zip}; it preserves those earlier outputs and appends the ICDE evidence checks. Under \nolinkurl{canonical_assets/jbhi_policy_revision_20261031/}, \nolinkurl{clinical/report_panel.py} rebuilds the 42/12-policy tables from saved randomized outcomes, \nolinkurl{clinical/check_report.py} verifies their truth, costs and replay, and \nolinkurl{statistical/portable_check.py} checks exact projection. The input manifest fixes the aggregate files and hashes. Historical protocols retain their dates and targets; they are not alternative estimates of the later comparisons.

Matched comparison of uncertainty-based audit rules¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Matched comparison of uncertainty-based audit rules

Frozen target, sampling protocol and retained scenarios

This additional retrospective experiment compares the UAF Clopper--Pearson (CP) difference rule with a Cherian--Cand\`es (C--C) simultaneous-bootstrap adapter[13] and an Uncertainty Matters (UM) holdout-predictive adapter.[14] Each method receives the same sampled confusion counts, frozen predictions, declared categories and shared reference. The comparison concerns audit conclusions, not patient-prediction accuracy. It does not change the C1 count-integration algorithm or the C2--C4 experiments. The protocol, runner, adapters and aggregate populations were frozen on 2 November 2026 at 03:27:58 UTC, before the new outcome evaluation. The existing clinical test sets had already been studied; this freeze is neither external preregistration nor new clinical validation.

For each declared nonreference category $g$, the target is the signed FNR difference $\delta_g=\operatorname{FNR}_g-\operatorname{FNR}_0$, with acceptable band $[-.10,.10]$ and family error level $.05$. All methods pass when their entire interval lies inside this closed band, fail when it lies strictly outside, and otherwise remain inconclusive. An unissued interval is $[-1,1]$. Categories with no observed positive outcomes, or without positive reference support, remain inconclusive. No category is merged or removed from the decision denominator. Population-undefined gaps are retained as unsupported comparisons; they are excluded only from the supported-family inclusion diagnostic.

Audits are independent draws with replacement from a specified joint law over mutually exclusive group and confusion-matrix category. The 16 synthetic scenarios combine two group-mass vectors, $(.25,.25,.25,.25)$ and $(.65,.25,.08,.02)$, with four comparison-FNR vectors: equal $(.20,.20,.20)$, boundary $(.30,.10,.20)$, violations $(.35,.05,.40)$ and mixed $(.20,.27,.35)$. The reference FNR is $.20$, prevalence $.20$ and FPR $.10$. Every distribution uses 3,000 and 12,000 records and 500 independent audits per size, giving 8,000 synthetic audits. A numerical tolerance of $10^{-12}$ represents exact decimal equality at the specified fairness boundary; it does not relax the decision rule.

The nine clinical scenarios use the empirical joint laws of the existing seed-11 test predictions. Their record counts are $N=169{,}933$ for Texas-100X, $20{,}572$ for eICU and $4{,}848$ for MIMIC-III. Each law is evaluated at $\lceil N/4\rceil$, $\lceil N/2\rceil$ and $N$, with 200 independent replacement audits per size. The respective families contain 4, 6 and 40 comparisons. MIMIC-III retains 23 population-unsupported comparisons, leaving a maximum possible correct-resolution fraction of $17/40=42.5\%$. Cohort-specific category vocabularies are not pooled. Replacement sampling provides a common iid benchmark; it is not without-replacement clinical review and supplies no future-hospital transport guarantee. Observed full-test-count outputs are separately retained as descriptive results, not estimates of future-population correctness.

Implemented intervals, support gates and native targets

The UAF rule uses the unchanged CP rate error $.05/(G+1)$ for $G$ comparisons plus their shared reference. Exact binomial endpoints are combined by subtraction. Its minimum observed positive denominator is one. Its finite-sample interpretation concerns binomial sampling conditional on denominators, whereas C1 computes repeated decisions under an explicitly supplied count law.

The C--C adapter implements the paper's two-sided rescaled process for one fixed FNR/reference family, with $p_*=.01$, $w_0=\infty$ and 1,999 bootstrap draws. It does not execute the authors' complete software. Conditional on the audit's observed positive rows, let $m$ be their total count, $p_g=n_g/m$, $d_g=k_g/n_g-k_0/n_0$, and $s_g=\max(p_g,.01)^{3/2}\operatorname{SD}(L)$ for binary miss loss $L$. A joint multinomial bootstrap over group and miss status is equivalent to iid resampling of these positive rows. Each draw recomputes the shared reference once. Over the admitted comparisons, the bootstrap maximum is \[ T_b=\max_g\left|\frac{p_g p^{(b)}_g(d^{(b)}_g-d_g)}{s_g}\right|. \] The higher empirical $.95$ quantile $c$ gives radius $cs_g/p_g^2$; bounds are intersected with $[-1,1]$. The practical support guard is 20 positive observations in each compared group and reference. Boundary counts, undefined bootstrap rates and degenerate scales or radii also withhold an interval. Calibration uses the data-dependent admitted family, while every declared comparison remains in the reported results. These disclosed safeguards are implementation adaptations, not additional finite-sample guarantees. They differ from the CP support gate. The published inference is asymptotic under iid regularity conditions and does not justify the historical hospital-dependent adaptation.

The UM adapter implements the published two-stage holdout model. For each group with observed full confusion vector $\mathbf c_g=(TN,FP,FN,TP)$, it draws \[ \boldsymbol\pi_g\mid\mathbf c_g\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\mathbf c_g+\mathbf 1), \qquad \mathbf c'_g\mid\boldsymbol\pi_g\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n_g,\boldsymbol\pi_g), \] where $n_g$ is the observed total patient count in that group. Each of 19,999 iterations uses one predictive reference realization for all contrasts. The benchmark adds marginal predictive tails $.05/(2G)$ and the common three-state interval decision rule. This family-adjusted wrapper was prespecified for this experiment; it is not the original paper's KDE highest-density-region procedure. Lower and upper endpoints use outward order statistics. A predictive zero-positive denominator contributes the full interval $[-1,1]$ to that draw, rather than being deleted. Observed zero-positive support always withholds a decision. Full confusion counts are required; padding positive-only data with zero negative-outcome cells would change the model.

The UM interval targets a future same-group-size holdout gap, whereas CP and C--C infer a population gap under their respective assumptions. The common decision benchmark therefore has different native uncertainty targets. UM's empirical inclusion of the fixed population gap is a diagnostic, not frequentist coverage of that gap or coverage of its native predictive target. Wider predictive intervals cannot by themselves establish inferior population inference. All groups are disjoint in this comparison; overlapping subgroups would require another construction.

Complete scenario results and Monte Carlo interpretation

For each audit, correct pass, correct fail, false pass, false fail and inconclusive partition the declared comparisons. Correct resolution is $(\text{correct pass}+\text{correct fail})/G$, retaining unsupported categories. Any wrong assertion is a separate family-level event. Table S53 reports all 25 scenarios without selecting favorable distributions or budgets. Its three columns per method therefore do not sum to 100%: resolution and inconclusiveness are comparison fractions, while any wrong assertion is an audit fraction.

Across the equally replicated synthetic grid, mean correct resolution was 12.28% for UAF, 24.65% for C--C and 13.77% for UM; any-wrong-assertion rates were respectively 0, .56 and .01%. Thus UAF did not have the highest resolution on this grid. At clinical audit size $N$, Texas-100X correct resolution was 62.62%, 55.88% and 54.25%, with no observed wrong assertions. Paired UAF-minus-C--C and UAF-minus-UM gains were 6.75 and 8.38 percentage points, with descriptive 95% Monte Carlo intervals [4.72, 8.78] and [6.69, 10.06]. These intervals condition on the specified empirical population and are not simultaneous claims across the scenario grid. eICU and MIMIC-III remained predominantly inconclusive at every tested budget; the retained nonzero C--C wrong-assertion rates are shown in the table.

Supported-family population-gap inclusion at size $N$ was 99.5/91.5/100% for Texas-100X, 98.5/94.0/100% for eICU and 99.0/96.5/99.5% for MIMIC-III, in UAF/C--C/UM order. This exposes uncertainty behavior that decision errors alone can conceal. In particular, the C--C adapter's 91.5% Texas inclusion is below the nominal 95% target in this finite empirical experiment. UM values retain the predictive-target qualification above. Saved outputs also include issued fractions, widths, all-group correct resolution, error direction and descriptive implementation runtime. Paired differences use the same audits; their standard errors reflect independent audit replications, not independent groups within an audit. Source-population reuse and the shared reference preclude interpreting group cells or clinical scenarios as independent validation cohorts.

Precision sensitivity, independent verification and evidence files

The prespecified precision check used replicate indices 0 and 1 in every scenario, increasing C--C to 4,999 bootstrap draws and UM to 99,999 predictive draws. All 50 checks per method, covering 396 comparison states per method, retained their primary pass/inconclusive/fail states. Maximum endpoint changes were .005537 for C--C and .044673 for UM. These selected checks do not establish Monte Carlo stability for all 9,800 audits. In MIMIC-III's 40-comparison family, the primary UM configuration has only about 12.5 expected draws per tail, increasing to about 62.5 in the sensitivity. Thin-tail warnings are retained and do not alter decisions. Sensitivity outputs never replace the primary outcomes.

Independent verification checked all 9,800 saved audit samples, 29,400 method rows and 162,000 comparison rows against the frozen source and input hashes. Every sampled audit was independently regenerated from its population and seed. The verifier independently reconstructed truth gaps, support bookkeeping, decision predicates and replicate metrics without using the runner's metric or scenario functions. CP endpoints were recalculated with inverse incomplete-beta functions. No declared category was lost, and every population-undefined comparison remained inconclusive. C--C support, boundary and undefined-bootstrap flags and UM support, predictive-undefined and tail-resolution flags were reconciled.

Primary bounds and states were reproduced in 45 API replays: all three methods at indices 0, 1 and 7 for balanced-boundary and sparse-boundary synthetic scenarios of size 3,000, and the three clinical scenarios of size $N$. Twenty higher-draw replays reproduced the saved precision diagnostics at indices 0 and 1 in these five scenarios. This verification establishes implementation and accounting agreement. It supplies neither a new coverage theorem nor independent clinical validation.

The matched-benchmark directory is \nolinkurl{icde_matched_20261102}. Its \nolinkurl{freeze.json} records Python 3.11.9, NumPy 2.4.2, SciPy 1.15.3 and source/input hashes; the verified freeze SHA-256 is \nolinkurl{92c8d604d750e89e391ac8816ad1f1dab273f82312d19767a2b49ab4ee00fc13}. \nolinkurl{PROTOCOL.md}, \nolinkurl{CC_IMPLEMENTATION.md} and \nolinkurl{UM_IMPLEMENTATION.md} record the frozen design and adaptations. \nolinkurl{summary/all_scenarios.csv} contains every scenario metric and Monte Carlo standard error, \nolinkurl{summary/paired_comparisons.csv} the paired differences, and \nolinkurl{summary/precision_sensitivity.csv} every higher-draw check. Scenario directories retain \nolinkurl{audit_counts.npz}, \nolinkurl{cells.csv}, \nolinkurl{replicates.csv}, \nolinkurl{precision.csv} and output hashes for replay. \nolinkurl{INDEPENDENT_VERIFICATION.json} records the complete check inventory. These aggregate records export no patient identifiers. The experiment compares the declared interval adapters on frozen predictions; it does not train new mitigation models or establish patient benefit.
