Additional numerical detail retained from the conference condensation¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Additional numerical detail retained from the conference condensation

These records preserve secondary experimental settings and numerical diagnostics condensed in the conference main text. They do not replace the primary protocols or change any result.

The factorial crosses gaps $0,.05,.15,.30$, sizes $(40,20,20)/(20,40,40)$ and reference rates $.3/.5$: 16 frames with two comparison groups. Pilot fractions $.1/.3$, confirmation fractions $.3/.85$ and ten pilots yield 640 records; policies share zero minima, integer grids and costs. Constrained/switch policies reuse these and the 80 fine-grid clinical records. All 160 primary records retain no-confirmation/minimum-review controls and same-region gain bounds. Eight mortality direct-gap sensitivity plans keep pilot caps, grids and allocations fixed. Historical confirmation-only corrections remain diagnostic. The isotonic forecast correction is our adaptation of classifier calibration [15], not a validated forecast protocol. Paired conclusiveness/correct-resolution projections compare all 160 clinical and 640 synthetic records with balancing and minima, preserving unequal versus matched costs. Oversized projections use conservative bounds fixed before truth assessment. A separate computation sensitivity retains 15 minimum-/median-/maximum-work nonidentical pairs within cohort/pilot/budget strata, allowing 100 billion estimated operations, 50 million entries and 120 seconds per case; only computation limits change.

Primary review retains 18 correlated contrasts (three policies, three seeds, two cohorts). Equal/proportional disagreement allocation and whole-cohort uniform sampling share actual counts capped by disagreement census, with 1,000 randomizations per case/budget. Sensitivities use false-alert weights $0/.05/.1/.25/1$, FNR allowances $0/.02$ and absent/zero/.02 FPR caps. Four synthetic controls test acceptance, added misses, concentrated false alerts and utility equality. Costs count records, not observed staff time or frame construction.

The expanded panel freezes sensitivity targets 60/70/75/85/90/95% against 80% for each mortality fit; original contrasts give 54 correlated comparisons. Weight .1 and prespecified .05/.25 sensitivities use 1/2/5/10/20/50/100% disagreement review and 1,000 randomizations. Equal/proportional allocation, disagreement SRS and whole-cohort SRS share actual counts. Stratified inference conditions on realized stratum counts; single-direction pooling uses identical disagreement-SRS records. Complete-cohort truth defines correct acceptance/rejection/deferral. Randomizations do not create new clinical cohorts.

eICU's guard was finite in 81.0% of hospital-pairs versus 32.9% of two-stage draws; hospital variance was zero in 46.35% of pairs draws. Finite pairs guards had 2.5th/median/97.5th percentiles 175.5/569.5/3,701.3. Near-boundary binomial-cell tests with nonfinite benchmark Gaussian guards nevertheless returned finite fitted counts in 40.67% of nine-hospital and 18.33% of 58-hospital repetitions. These are sensitivity frequencies, not clinical confidence or recommendation-validity probabilities: the two-stage law can double-count outcome variation and serves as an overdispersion stress test.

Across 30 recovery repetitions, variance-component relative bias ranged from $-23.33\%$ to $+9.52\%$. Balanced Gaussian refinement added one risk-threshold decision in 26,000 confirmations despite reducing median risk width by up to 36.75%. A recovered horizon of 8.987 model units gave 4.997% reversal versus 5% predicted; these checks establish neither clinical collection advice nor calendar-time monitoring intervals.

Fine-grid eICU DP achieved 40.76%/49.29% correct resolution at costs 475/661 versus balancing/greedy 37.36%/49.79%; groups lost resolution in 16/20 and 15/20 pilots. Predictive floors returned balancing in all 80 mortality records, removing losses and gains together. Primary-grid Texas constraints retained 2.97/4.79-point gains but reduced true-law resolution in 11/80 and 18/80 pilot-group comparisons. Posterior floors therefore did not protect true-law outcomes.

Paired projection retained all 160 clinical/640 synthetic allocations and certified gains over minimum review in 42 clinical records (24 eICU/18 MIMIC), each costing 250 extra verifications. Lower gains had median .00123/maximum .03165 points, with none certified over matched balancing; the mean-and-every-group confidence safeguard therefore retained balancing, surrendering unsafeguarded gains. Clinical comparisons comprised 71 identities/89 conservative fallbacks; all 640 synthetic comparisons were exact. Of 15 complexity-selected nonidentical clinical pairs, ten completed exact projection (three eICU/seven Texas) and five Texas pairs exceeded the frozen cap: average width fell 72.43%, from .952 to .262, but every interval crossed zero and supported no safeguard switch, implicating pilot-region uncertainty as well as computation. The remaining 79 pairs retain their bounds; all evaluated true gains were enclosed, without establishing an independently validated collection policy.

At unchanged eICU replicate-00 coarse-grid allocations, direct-gap tests raised correct resolution from 24.23% to 30.06% and 37.77% to 40.40% at pilot caps 20/200; fine-grid gains were smaller and MIMIC-III nearly unchanged. This eight-plan sensitivity changed neither allocations nor forecasts. MIMIC-III's 23/40 unsupported comparisons remained: 39.49--40.00% resolution over all 40 equaled 92.91--94.12% among 17 supported comparisons, without changing multiplicity. The 5.84-point eICU gain at cap 20 involved incomplete verification; even a fully verified group can retain reference uncertainty, so inconclusiveness is not an intrinsic evidence lower bound.

All 54 policies failed the primary criterion of no net subgroup miss increase and positive utility at $w=.1$. Among 42 single-direction policies, pooling raised correct rejection from 61.69% to 80.08%, with .095% wrong acceptance and less deferral (the corresponding main-paper result table). For 12 mixed-direction policies, half-disagreement review averaged 91.83 verifications: equal/proportional/disagreement-SRS/whole-cohort SRS rejection was 98.20%/97.13%/97.41%/6.17% under both weights, without observed errors. The original 18-policy and all-54 10%-review experiments likewise favored targeting disagreements, without a general equal/proportional advantage over disagreement-SRS.

At prespecified $w=.05$, correctness across the same 42 policies rose from 65.82% to 85.06%; paired panel gains were 18.395 points [18.181,18.609] at the primary weight and 19.236 [18.943,19.528] at .05, with intervals describing conditional Monte Carlo precision. All 20 acceptable changes only added positives, so no added misses were known before review; this secondary subset's acceptance was 71.745% versus 31.350%, a 40.395-point gain [39.781,41.009]. Median per-policy gain was zero at both weights, concentrating improvement in a subset. Expanded-grid maximum error was 3.1% [2.12,4.37] and minimum coverage 93.8% [92.12,95.21], selected extrema without simultaneous guarantees; census decisions were exact.

The eICU seed-11 85%-sensitivity change added 115 detected deaths/1,480 false alerts across 1,595 changed classifications without additional subgroup misses, giving utility $-33$ at $w=.1$ and $+41$ at $w=.05$. At 798 outcome verifications, primary rejection/deferral was 79.7%/20.3% versus sensitivity acceptance/deferral 98.3%/1.7%; Native Americans gained no detections but five false alerts. Conversely, the original MIMIC-III seed-11 group-versus-budget change gained one detection and removed 21 false alerts while adding four misses among 26 Black/African American positives, requiring at least 15.38 FNR-loss points. The original eICU budget-versus-baseline change added six detections/60 false alerts, giving utility equality at .1. These are classification trade-offs, not measured care benefits or preventable deaths.

Further retained protocol and diagnostic detail

C1 combines group-state probabilities at each common-reference count, then averages over that count. Exact integration requires independent disjoint groups; overlapping comparisons use common resamples. Population coverage is evaluated separately. C2's Gaussian binary-risk analysis concerns hospital-by-sex variation, not C1's three-state race audit or validated collection advice. C2 source shares do not determine C3 allocations, and C1 forecasts do not select C4 policies.

C3 uses one full-frame rule for predictive utility, allocation and evaluation. Predictive floors compare groupwise utility with balancing; complete totals assess correct and incorrect conclusions. A simultaneous pilot region classifies the total-conclusiveness target as met, not met or unresolved. Incremental review value is assessed separately. C4 fixes the known disagreement frame, budget and subgroup-error/alert criterion before outcome review. Its bounds support criterion acceptance, rejection or deferral, with acceptance informing subsequent clinical assessment. Repeated favorable-look stopping would require sequential inference.

C3 charges prediction-linkage/error verification among known positives; C4 charges completed outcome reviews among known disagreements. Frame construction, denominator acquisition, failed reviews, access and staff time are unpriced. Fully linked, verified predictions and outcomes permit direct calculation. Positive FNR/FPR allowances require whole-group outcome totals. The 80% sensitivity point, .10 tolerance and detection/false-alert weights are research choices without clinical endorsement. Neither parity nor criterion acceptance establishes adequate absolute care.

C2 uses 30 recovery repetitions and 13 balanced Gaussian scenarios with 1,000 validations/2,000 confirmations each. Historical seed-11 sex-FNR thresholds (.390873 Texas; .073716 eICU) differ from the principal analysis. Requiring 20 positives per sex/cell and five hospitals leaves 58/nine cells. Each cohort uses 2,000 hospital-pairs and 2,000 two-stage resamples. Six binomial-cell stress scenarios use 300 repetitions, sex denominators 20--300, male miss probability .2 and latent normal female effects, testing the Gaussian approximation rather than exact Gaussian recovery.

Full-frame planning retains 160 feasible pilot-budget records from 120 clinical pilots; four infeasible larger-budget mortality settings are excluded explicitly. Pilot caps are 20/200, minima $\min(25,R_g)$, batch 50 and extra budgets 250/2,000. Texas reuses 40 pilots at both budgets; eICU/MIMIC each supply 40 at one feasible budget. All 80 mortality pilots also use a matched expanded grid: group increments of five plus terminal capacities and integer reference increments. Forecasts use $q_*=.10$, $\eta=.05$; evaluation retains correct/wrong conclusions, group/all-group resolution and forecast bounds. Primary computational limits are 25 million pair operations and 50 million fallback entries.

All cohorts were inspected before additional protocols were chosen. Factorial/allocation plans were frozen before truth evaluation; an already-saved eICU plan had an earlier numerical check after code/protocol freeze, without design changes. This preserves replay integrity, not independent validation. Monte Carlo intervals describe precision conditional on retained frames; differing vocabularies, information and targets prevent treating cohorts or C1--C4 as interchangeable replications.

Rare-hospital jackknife coverage was 88.15% at nominal 95% (Monte Carlo interval [86.66,89.49]); bounded-KL/Bernstein alternatives resolved nothing, leaving future-hospital inference unestablished. In fixed frames, capped-equal review reached 80% mean resolution with 19,400/932 Texas/eICU verifications versus 57,058/1,720 proportional verifications, contacting 64.45/22.52 versus 65.86/23.95 units. Reductions of 66.0%/45.8% still involved most units and exclude frame construction, so do not establish workflow savings. At matched samples, hypergeometric intervals added 4.59/8.93 resolution points over binomial intervals; coverage over 12 settings was 98.95--100%.

Correct resolution excludes wrong P/F outputs; forecast bias concerns total conclusiveness, and family error any wrong assertion. At 2,878 Texas verifications, DP achieved 41.64% correct resolution versus balancing/greedy/oracle 30.23%/22.55%/43.58% (the corresponding main-paper table), a paired 11.42-point gain (Monte Carlo standard error, MCSE, 1.13), positive in 19/20 pilots but uncertified by pilot evidence. eICU gained less at cost 475 and nothing at 661; MIMIC-III controls also coincided, and both small Texas budgets yielded almost no correct conclusions. Posterior optimality therefore did not ensure an advantage over simple controls.

In the larger Texas setting, balancing-to-DP correct resolution changed from 53.918% to 75.906% for Black, .180% to .040% for Other, and .002% to .138% for Native American comparisons. At eICU cost 475, African American resolution fell from 3.797% to 2.385%. Correct resolution includes both tolerance directions: eICU's Native American gap was $-21.728$ points, so its correct failure meant fewer misses than the reference, not minority disadvantage or patient benefit.

At total-conclusiveness target .10, nine decisions were supported as met, five as not met, and 146/160 unresolved; all 160 exact expectations were enclosed with no wrong supported decision. Mean widths were .724 in larger-budget Texas and .996/.929 in eICU, while Texas point forecasts over-/underestimated by 12.79/12.74 points at costs 2,223/2,878. Separate-extrema bounds certified no positive gain over minimum review or balancing. Pilot-only resolution was zero, but mortality minima already supplied resolution: total attainment does not establish incremental spending value.

Across 640 factorial pilots, unrestricted DP gained 5.41 correct-resolution points (MCSE .37), but harmed a group's resolution in 356 pilots and more than halved all-group correctness (the corresponding main-paper table). In the worst verified case, transferring six confirmations to the reference changed group correctness from one to zero. Predictive constraints/switching limited losses while surrendering most gain. Forecast mean bias was +17.82 points; confidence projection supported 262 target decisions, left 378 unresolved and made no observed wrong supported decision, separating optimization from reliable forecasting.

C1 distinguishes repeated agreement from sufficient evidence: mortality audits can repeatedly remain inconclusive. Missing outcome support and interval conservatism differ, as direct-gap tests improved resolution on unchanged records. Exact shared-reference probabilities preserve joint dependence, but computational gains favor large maps/reuse and do not validate the repetition law for future audits.

Comparator and matching ledger

Extended interpretation

C1's advance is the reusable three-state count map, not a new Clopper--Pearson interval or the invention of common-control conditioning. Ordered regions handle unequal and zero support; reference-conditioned products compute joint events without enumerating all group-count tuples. Existing direct integration remains competitive on small or imbalanced maps. Repeatability and statistical validity remain separate: sparse audits may repeatedly be inconclusive, and a correctly integrated law need not predict future hospitals.

The matched benchmark also makes rule choice part of the evidence question. C--C resolved more synthetic comparisons, whereas Texas ordering changed with audit budget and mortality evidence remained sparse. These results support no all-purpose best rule. UAF and C--C assess population-gap decisions under different inferential constructions; UM propagates uncertainty into a future holdout and consequently answers a different native question. Its decision wrapper can be compared empirically, but its predictive inclusion cannot be relabeled population coverage. Reporting correct resolution beside family errors, support gates and retained inconclusive categories makes these trade-offs visible. The iid empirical exercise does not repair the unresolved hospital-dependence result.

C2--C4 address source sensitivity, confirmation allocation and paired policy evidence, not an integrated clinical decision system. The unbalanced clinical source design lacks a validated confidence region, so C2 supports no collection recommendation. C3's predictive safeguards traded mean gain for fewer group losses without true-law protection; confidence safeguards retained balancing, certifying only tiny gains over minimum review and none over matched balancing. Optimization therefore informs a declared objective, with group priorities supplied externally.

C4 evaluates a fixed recorded-cohort criterion. All 54 policies failed at $w=.1$; pooling improved rejection across 42 single-direction policies with some wrong acceptance, while $w=.05$ improved total correctness. Its 20 acceptable changes only added positives, but median per-policy gain remained zero. The four additional Black/African American misses under mixed changes and Native American false alerts show why net utility cannot establish benefit for every group.

Practical value requires incomplete prediction linkage among known positives (C3) or incomplete outcomes among known disagreements (C4); verified linked data permit direct calculation. Counts exclude frame/denominator acquisition, failed-review overhead, access and staff time. Prior cohort inspection, unverified Texas linkage/timing, single-institution MIMIC-III, bounded simulations and unresolved future-hospital coverage limit transfer. Applications must prespecify missing information, priorities, budget and error/alert criteria, then measure verification effort and decision impact; patient-benefit claims require care-outcome evaluation.

Additional structural, support-gate and bounded scalability checks¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Additional structural, support-gate and bounded scalability checks

These checks dated 2 November 2026 retain the primary experiment and all preceding supplementary material. The structural audit examines existing outputs; the support-gate diagnostic was selected after reviewing the primary results; the additional computational grid was fixed before its new timing observations. None provides independent clinical validation.

Structural inconclusiveness and the mortality-table identity

Let $M$ count conclusive comparisons in a repeat. When every recorded verdict is inconclusive, as in the principal mortality families, $$ r_{\rm any}=\Pr(M\geq1),\qquad Gc_{\rm mean}=E[M],\qquad Gc_{\rm mean}-r_{\rm any}=E[(M-1)_+].

$$ The last expression equals $\sum_{m=2}^{G}(m-1)\Pr(M=m)$ and is nonnegative. This identity needs no independence assumption. Equality holds only when two or more simultaneous conclusions have zero probability. Low any-change and low mean conclusiveness therefore describe the same predominantly inconclusive repeats, rather than independent empirical discoveries. Table S55 reports the unrounded-output check: the four exact-law rows have positive differences, while the retained bootstrap samples have equal integer counts of conclusive cells and repeats with any conclusion. Sample equality does not establish equality under the underlying resampling law.

An independent exhaustive scan of CP endpoint decisions at the observed positive denominators, tolerance .10, family error .05 and minimum support one separates three cases. All six eICU comparisons admit at least one conclusive count configuration, although three admit failure only. MIMIC-III has 23 zero-denominator comparisons, eleven further comparisons with positive denominators but no conclusive count configuration, and six potentially conclusive comparisons; five of the latter admit failure only. Thus 34/40 MIMIC comparisons are forced inconclusive under this fixed-denominator rule, giving zero all-family conclusiveness and a mean-conclusiveness ceiling of $6/40=15\%$ irrespective of the supplied miss-count law. This is a rule-specific restriction, not an information-theoretic lower bound or impossibility under every valid interval procedure.

The new matched replacement audits vary their positive denominators across draws, so their corresponding zero-population-support ceiling is $17/40=42.5\%$, not the fixed-denominator 15% ceiling. Structural scanning uses the rule and observed denominators without miss counts; the clinical denominators themselves require observed outcomes and membership. Accordingly, it is a check before using prediction errors conditional on those denominators, not a finding obtained before seeing any clinical data. The evidence files are \nolinkurl{reviewer_structural_check.py}, \nolinkurl{reviewer_structural_check.json}, \nolinkurl{reviewer_structural_probabilities.csv} and \nolinkurl{reviewer_structural_support.csv} in \nolinkurl{icde_matched_20261102}.

Post-review C--C minimum-support diagnostic

After the primary results and a concern about method-specific support withholding were inspected, a separate diagnostic lowered only C--C's observed-positive minimum from 20 to one. It retained all 9,800 primary audits, all declared groups, the same seeds and 1,999 bootstrap draws, reference, tolerance and error level. Boundary-count, undefined-bootstrap and degenerate-scale/radius withholding remain. The protocol and code were frozen before this rerun; its post-review selection makes it diagnostic rather than confirmatory. It does not replace the primary benchmark or implement every feature of the original publication.

Across the complete grid, 185/54,000 comparison states changed, including 133 in sparse synthetic size-3,000 scenarios. Texas verdicts were unchanged at every budget; at $N$, its supported-family inclusion remained 91.5%, so this gate change did not remove the observed inclusion shortfall. eICU at $N$ retained its decisions but changed supported-family inclusion from 94.0% to 94.5% and mean width from .784846 to .644566. MIMIC at $N$ improved correct resolution by .375 percentage points and remained 99.55% inconclusive. The eICU and MIMIC half-budget rows retain unfavorable changes. Lowering the gate can enlarge the admitted calibration family and change its common bootstrap critical value; it is not simply the issuance of extra unchanged intervals, and resolution need not improve monotonically.

Independent verification reconstructed every truth gap and all replicate/summary metrics from saved cells, checked all 54,000 cell states and support records, and confirmed unchanged hashes for 152 primary-release assets. Both gates reproduced saved states, endpoints and diagnostics at indices 0 and 17 in five design-selected scenarios, giving 20 method replays. \nolinkurl{POST_REVIEW_CC_SUPPORT.md}, \nolinkurl{support_sensitivity/summary.csv} and \nolinkurl{SUPPORT_SENSITIVITY_VERIFICATION.json} retain the protocol, all scenarios and verification. This check concerns the C--C adapter only. UM remains a future-holdout predictive distribution with a declared interval wrapper; its inclusion of a fixed population gap remains a diagnostic rather than population-confidence coverage or validation of its native predictive target.

Additional bounded scalability experiment

The additional 24-case computational grid crosses reference denominator $n_0\in\{10^3,10^4,10^5,10^6\}$, $G\in\{3,10,40\}$ and two support patterns. Balanced-scale supports cycle ratios $(.5,1,2)$ and severe-imbalance supports cycle $(.0001,.0003,.001)$, with $n_g=\max\{1,\operatorname{round}(n_0\rho_g)\}$. These are count supports, not newly collected clinical cohorts. The unchanged searchsorted implementation and optimized direct pair-map integration use tolerance .10, family error .05, gate one and recorded states cycling P/I/F. Each query $q=0,\ldots,9$ supplies independent binomial masses with reference rate $.20+.002(q-4.5)$ and group rates evenly spaced from $.12$ to $.36$, shifted by the same amount. Both methods return the full conditional/marginal arrays and joint outputs; identical-size reuse is allowed for both. The direct comparator is an implementation comparator, not Koch--Hothorn's original software.

Each method/case runs in a separate sequential child with one numerical thread. The frozen limits are a conservative estimated working allocation of 768 MiB per child, 12 seconds per complete worker and 600 seconds for the timing pass. Cold time is the first rule/map preparation plus first evaluation; it excludes common mass generation and process startup. It is a single observation, not a repeat median. The worker timeout includes imports, mass generation, checks and subsequent workloads. After a warm evaluation, cached $Q=1$ and $Q=10$ workloads have three planned repetitions each; incomplete workloads and repetition counts remain recorded. Table S57 preserves all 48 attempts: 24 complete, eight timed out and 16 excluded by the memory estimate. The timing pass used 185.31 seconds.

Four small Cartesian profiles passed before timing. Full cold-output comparisons were available for twelve cases, with maximum discrepancy $1.33\times10^{-15}$; the verifier also checked all 24 saved conditional arrays against reassembled marginal/joint outputs. Search was faster in the three matched balanced cold phases, all at $n_0=1,000$, by 2.87--4.39 times; direct integration was faster in all nine matched severe-imbalance cold phases by 1.09--2.28 times. Search's three fully measured balanced ten-query workloads were 5.95--9.18 times faster. Larger balanced direct cases were excluded before allocation and provide no measured speed ratio. No exclusion or timeout bound is counted as a speedup, and selected large-case slice checks do not substitute for full independent enumeration.

The recorded environment was Windows, Python 3.11.9, NumPy 2.4.2 and SciPy 1.15.3, with 24 logical CPUs but one numerical thread per sequential worker; no CPU-model comparison was performed. Windows peak working-set measurements include Python/import overhead. The million-reference, three-group imbalanced search worker completed its cold phase in 5.673 seconds and recorded 719.50 MiB peak working set against a 129.95 MiB import baseline before a later timeout. A timed-out worker's last snapshot is a lower bound on its final peak, not a completed-workload memory guarantee. The conservative preflight estimate is neither measured peak usage nor a formal upper bound. Supplied floating-point binomial masses can already underflow; the experiment does not establish real-arithmetic exactness, universal runtime superiority or future-hospital validity.

All phase records, statuses and missing comparisons remain in \nolinkurl{icde_scalability_20261102}: \nolinkurl{status_and_cold.csv}, \nolinkurl{cached_replicates.csv}, \nolinkurl{cached_summary.csv}, \nolinkurl{matched_speed_ratios.csv}, \nolinkurl{memory_summary.csv}, \nolinkurl{numerical_comparisons.csv} and \nolinkurl{VERIFICATION.json}. Frozen hashes confirm that copied kernels match their original environment. These additional 24 cases do not replace the earlier 24-design results.

Post-review blocked direct comparator¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Post-review blocked direct comparator

The full pair-map comparator in Section S14 was memory-intensive. This separate exploratory follow-up, frozen after that result and the comparator criticism, uses direct integration in blocks of reference-count rows. It caches CP endpoints and evaluates every group/reference count pair, regenerating P/I/F masks for each query. It uses no monotone boundary search, CDF shortcut, support truncation or zero-mass skip. The temporary pair-buffer budget is 64 MiB; for a group of size $n_g$, each block has at most $\lfloor64\,2^{20}/[4(n_g+1)]\rfloor$ rows, allowing three Boolean buffers and a fourth temporary. Both implementations share upstream CP endpoint code and final output assembly; this is an implementation comparator, not a reproduction of Koch--Hothorn software or an independent large-case derivation.

The same 24 cases, supplied laws, recorded states and full conditional/marginal/joint outputs are retained. The unchanged search method and blocked direct method each receive a fresh sequential child with one numerical thread. A frozen 768 MiB estimated-allocation cap admits 40 of 48 attempts; a 30-second complete-worker limit and 1,200-second total limit apply. The pass used 570.50 seconds. Cold timing includes first endpoint/rule preparation and first full evaluation, excludes common mass generation/startup, and is a single observation. The timeout covers the whole worker, including subsequent cached workloads. After warm-up, $Q=1$ and $Q=10$ have three planned repetitions each; paired cached ratios require all three in both methods. These limits differ from the earlier experiment, which remains reported in full.

There were 26 complete workers, 14 timeouts and eight preflight exclusions. All 16 paired full cold outputs agree within $3.56\times10^{-15}$. Search is faster in all six measured balanced cold phases (blocked/search ratios 2.67--65.56); the three $n_0=10,000$ blocked workers complete those cold phases but subsequently time out. No balanced cold ratio is available at $n_0\ge100,000$. Blocked direct is faster in eight of ten paired imbalanced cold phases; the full ratio range is .343--2.076, including the two cases favoring search. Thus replacing the full pair map removes several memory exclusions and supplies larger measured balanced comparisons, but the timings still do not support a universal speed advantage.

Independent verification checked frozen hashes, the five unchanged upstream Python files, every worker/status/cached record, all 36 saved output arrays, all 16 full comparisons, timing ratios and memory accounting. Five separately constructed small Cartesian enumerations agreed within $4.19\times10^{-14}$, including zero support and nonzero joint conclusiveness. Saved conditional arrays were independently reassembled into all reported marginal and joint outputs. Large-case slice checks are additional diagnostics, not full independent enumeration.

The recorded machine was an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX with 24 logical processors, Windows 11 Home 10.0.26300, Python 3.11.9, NumPy 2.4.2 and SciPy 1.15.3. Hardware/free-memory metadata was recorded during the run; no controlled idle-load claim is made. Windows peak working set includes the Python/import baseline. A timed-out worker's last saved peak is a lower bound on its final peak, and the allocation estimate is not a measured-memory guarantee. Floating-point law underflow is not recovered. This post-review check supplies computational evidence conditional on supplied laws, not new clinical validity or confirmatory evidence. The full records, including partial cached repetitions, are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_blocked_direct_20261102}, with \nolinkurl{INDEPENDENT_VERIFICATION.json} and \nolinkurl{INDEPENDENT_VERIFICATION.md}.

Complete family inventory and deterministic tolerance sensitivity¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Complete family inventory and deterministic tolerance sensitivity

This post-review reporting extension retains the complete saved universe rather than selecting families by their results. The source archive contains 228 family/law or rule-sensitivity rows and 1,104 comparison/law rows. It represents 39 distinct cohort/attribute/metric families: 13 attribute families crossed with FNR, FPR and selection-rate difference (SPD). There are 276 distinct non-reference comparisons. The 228 rows comprise 78 exact-law rows (39 each for EB and JP), 78 archived bootstrap rows (unit and row resampling for each family) and 72 observed-rule sensitivity rows. They are not 228 distinct families. Texas has five attribute families and 57 metric-specific comparisons; eICU has four and 66; MIMIC has four and 153. Each family retains its own multiplicity count and reference category.

The additional deterministic grid includes all 39 families at tolerances .05, .10 and .15, family error .05 and support gate one: 117 rule configurations and 234 EB/JP forecasts. The .10 results reproduce all 78 saved exact forecasts, with maximum absolute discrepancy $2.23\times10^{-15}$. The .05/.15 forecasts are newly computed post-review sensitivity analyses, not previously collected or confirmatory results. No new bootstrap simulation is performed. The 72 saved race-FNR observed-rule sensitivity rows (three cohorts, three tolerances, four gates and two error levels) are retained separately, including overlaps with this grid; all recorded P/I/F counts reconstruct exactly.

Definitions, fixed supports and complete feasibility

``Metric-defined'' means both the comparison and reference have positive denominators. ``Rule-computable'' means that the declared rule and supplied count law return a probability, including a forced I outcome at zero support. Consequently every declared comparison here is rule-computable, while only $G-Z$ are metric-defined, where $Z$ counts zero support. A computable probability is not an estimable clinical error rate or evidence that a conclusive result is possible. Pass-incapable ($P^-$) and fail-incapable ($F^-$) count comparisons for which no count configuration at the fixed denominators can produce that state; these counts include zero support. $U$ counts positive-support comparisons for which neither P nor F is possible. These are structural statements conditional on the observed denominators, family size, tolerance, error level and gate. They do not mean simply that the observed interval was wide. The maximum possible mean conclusive fraction is $(G-Z-U)/G$; attainability of all such conclusions simultaneously is not asserted.

Feasibility uses monotone scans of CP endpoint arrays, without dense count-pair matrices. Thirty-six small exhaustive count-grid checks reproduce the scan. At the primary race-FNR rule, Texas has $(G,Z,U)=(4,0,0)$, eICU $(6,0,0)$ and MIMIC $(40,23,11)$, giving individual-capability ceilings of 100%, 100% and 15%. The 15% bound fixes the observed positive-outcome denominators. The separate matched empirical replacement audit varies those denominators, leaving only the 17/40=42.5% zero-population-support ceiling; those bounds concern different repetition designs. Denominators require observed outcome and category data, so this check is prior to using prediction-error counts, not prior to seeing any data.

Table S59 includes every family and tolerance. All rows use gate one and error .05. Race abbreviates the source field \nolinkurl{race_ethnicity}; Texas uses recorded race with White as reference and keeps Hispanic ethnicity as a separate family. Cohort category vocabularies are not equated. The observed-state columns concern the current rule at that row's tolerance. {3pt}

Complete exact-law forecasts

Table S60 lists all 234 exact-law forecasts, with EB and JP side by side for each of the 117 configurations. Entries are percentages; very small nonzero values retain scientific notation. The .10 rows are saved-primary replays; the .05/.15 rows are post-review extensions. Each any-change probability uses that row's own recorded P/I/F vector, which may change with tolerance. Thus reversal probabilities across tolerances do not by themselves measure a monotone improvement. The mean and all-conclusive outputs are reported alongside them. These probabilities condition on fixed observed denominators and the supplied independent count laws. Exact evaluation does not validate those laws for arbitrary hospitals or future clinical populations. {3pt}

Archived bootstrap rows and Monte Carlo provenance

Table S61 preserves the 78 bootstrap rows from the same all-family input archive at tolerance .10, gate one and error .05. Unit means hospital resampling for Texas/eICU and the source's one-unit-per-patient resampling for MIMIC; the parallel row law is also retained. These Monte Carlo rows are archived outputs, not newly simulated results at .05 or .15. Missing bootstrap forecasts at those tolerances remain missing.

The principal main-paper Texas hospital-bootstrap row uses the independently seeded stream in \nolinkurl{review_revision_20260928/diagnosis_replication/results/race_fnr_family.csv}, subsequently exported to \nolinkurl{jamia_revision_20261004/texas_seed_transitions.csv}. For seed 11 and 9,999 resamples, it gives 72.0872087%, 55.9455946% and 4.8304830%, rounding to 72.09%, 55.95% and 4.83%. The all-family archive instead gives 72.1372137%, 55.5930593% and 4.2904290%. These are distinct resampling streams on the same frozen predictions, not interchangeable numerical copies. Both sources are preserved, and \nolinkurl{TEXAS_BOOTSTRAP_LINEAGE.json} records the exact source and prediction hashes. No result is silently replaced or pooled across streams. {3pt}

Aggregate participant flow and comparison counts

The following aggregate tables reproduce the cohort-flow and partition sources. Texas starts with 925,128 discharge records, excludes 1,200 records with suppressed hospital codes and 174 exact duplicates, and retains 923,754 records at 439 hospitals. It has no patient linkage or usable calendar-period field in this extract. eICU retains 111,214 stays after its staged landmark and cross-partition exclusions; MIMIC retains 32,315 after first-stay selection and timing/outcome eligibility. Selection order is preserved in the original flow CSV and is not reconstructed from the later test subset.

Per-comparison counts are in \nolinkurl{comparison_counts276.csv}: each row includes the group/reference labels, numerator $k_g$, denominator $n_g$, reference numerator $k_0$ and denominator $n_0$. FNR uses missed positive outcomes over all positive outcomes; FPR uses false-positive classifications over negative outcomes; SPD uses positive classifications over all records. These are classification metrics, not clinical adverse-event counts. \nolinkurl{test_category_composition.csv} reports all 105 category/attribute rows including references, with records, positive/negative outcomes, misses, false positives and positive classifications. For every attribute family, positives plus negatives reproduce records, positives minus misses plus false positives reproduce positive classifications, and category totals reproduce its cohort's test counts. Rows from different attribute families reuse the same people or records and must not be summed across families. The reference category is part of composition but is excluded from the declared comparison count $G$. {3pt}

{3pt}

The complete machine-readable inventory is retained in \nolinkurl{icde_reporting_20261102}: unmodified inputs, 117 family feasibility rows, 828 comparison/rule rows, 234 exact family/law rows, 1,656 comparison/law probability rows, 72 saved observed-rule sensitivity rows, category composition, participant flow and split counts. \nolinkurl{freeze.json} records the protocol, source aggregates and unchanged transitive kernel hashes before computing the new tolerances. \nolinkurl{completion.json} records checks and output hashes. This reporting extension neither refits a model nor accesses patient identifiers, and does not supply new clinical validation.

Separate wide-family computational stress check¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Separate wide-family computational stress check

This exploratory follow-up varies the number of comparisons separately from the million-reference grid. It fixes $n_0=1,000$, crosses $G\in\{100,1,000\}$ with the same two support patterns, and retains the unchanged search and blocked-direct kernels, complete outputs, 64 MiB temporary pair budget and 768 MiB estimated-allocation cap. The separately frozen limits are 30 seconds per worker and 300 seconds overall. Cached $Q=1,10,100$ workloads each plan three repetitions. The four cases are not evidence that 1,000 groups and one million reference counts are jointly tractable.

The 201.55-second pass retains all eight attempts: two complete workers (both at $G=100$, imbalanced support) and six timeouts. Every cold phase completed. Table S64 reports all values, including phases before later timeouts. Search wins both balanced cold comparisons, whereas blocked direct wins both imbalanced comparisons. Only $G=100$ imbalanced completes all three $Q=100$ repetitions for each method; its cached medians are 2.851 and 1.808 seconds. The balanced $G=100$ search worker completes two $Q=100$ repetitions (median 7.632 seconds), while blocked direct completes none. Neither $G=1,000$ case completes any $Q=100$ repetition. Missing work is neither extrapolated nor counted as a speed win.

Independent verification checked frozen hashes, six unchanged upstream kernels, all statuses and phase-accounting records, and all eight saved output arrays. The four full paired cold outputs agree within $1.89\times10^{-15}$; every saved array was independently reassembled into marginal/joint summaries. Five small Cartesian checks add independent numerical evidence. The copied hardware snapshot retains its earlier timestamp. Shared endpoint/assembly code, uncontrolled load, single cold observations, floating-point masses and lower-bound memory snapshots for timed-out workers limit the conclusions in the same way as Section S15. All records and \nolinkurl{INDEPENDENT_VERIFICATION.json} remain in \nolinkurl{icde_wide_family_20261102}.

Separate pass/fail error-allocation sensitivity¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Separate pass/fail error-allocation sensitivity

This second post-review addendum changes the audit rule rather than the evaluator. It is frozen separately after the complete reporting extension and is not part of the original confirmatory design. At family error budget $a=.05$ and $G$ non-reference comparisons, define \[ \alpha_P=a(G+1)/G,\qquad \alpha_F=a(G+1)/(2G),\qquad \alpha_P<1. \] The split rule uses the P region from the unchanged endpoint rule with family parameter $\alpha_P$ and the F region with parameter $\alpha_F$; the remainder is I. Thus the pass endpoints are narrower and the fail endpoints wider than the primary $\alpha=a$ rule. The P region contains the primary P region, while the F region is contained in the primary F region. The two regions are disjoint. This is a directional tradeoff, not uniform improvement.

For a truly outside-tolerance comparison, false P requires one of two relevant one-sided endpoint failures. Each has probability at most $\alpha_P/[2(G+1)]=a/(2G)$, so false P is bounded by $a/G$. For a truth inside or on the tolerance boundary, false F requires at least one of four endpoint-tail failures, each bounded by $\alpha_F/[2(G+1)]=a/(4G)$; false F is also bounded by $a/G$. Summing the relevant wrong-assertion probability over $G$ comparisons bounds any wrong conclusive assertion by $a$. This union bound does not require independence among comparison events despite their shared reference. It does require the binomial sampling assumptions underlying the CP endpoint tail bounds. A JP repetition forecast is not a frequentist coverage guarantee, and neither law establishes clinical independence.

For every one of the same 39 families at tolerance .10 and gate one, the addendum recomputes the recorded vector under this split rule, its structural feasibility and all 78 EB/JP forecasts. The existing count evaluator is unchanged: the conditional P probability is taken from the first rule, F from the second, and I is the complement (roundoff-scale negative residuals are clipped after a conservation check). The recorded vector is also computed from those two regions; any-change forecasts therefore refer to each rule's own observed decisions. Cross-rule reversal differences alone do not measure improved informativeness. For split-rule outputs at or below $10^{-12}$ absolute probability ($10^{-10}$ percent), the numerical interpretation is only ``below the precision floor. The I complement can contain cancellation residuals at this scale; smaller printed values are retained raw arithmetic outputs, not validated rare-tail probabilities. This limitation does not affect the displayed substantive changes in mean conclusiveness.

Across 276 observed comparisons, P/I/F changes from 20/197/59 to 20/200/56: three F states become I, and no observed P is added. The three principal race-FNR families retain their recorded states and structural capability counts. At fixed denominators, MIMIC retains 23 zero-support and 11 positive-support comparisons incapable of P or F, hence its 15% mean-conclusiveness ceiling. Across all 39 families, mean conclusiveness increases in 13 EB forecasts and decreases in 19 (seven equal within $10^{-12}$); for JP the counts are 12 increases, 20 decreases and seven equal. Preserving the unfavorable changes is essential: more permissive P does not overcome more conservative F in every setting.

For principal race-FNR, Texas EB mean conclusiveness changes from 59.365% to 60.878%, whereas eICU changes from .06022% to .02940% and MIMIC from .012688% to .010499%. JP changes from 56.872% to 58.053% for Texas, from .57773% to .40194% for eICU and from .071008% to .051434% for MIMIC. These are conditional deterministic sensitivities, not a new matched empirical coverage experiment. No bootstrap rerun is claimed.

Table S65 reports every family's observed and feasibility changes; Table S66 retains all 78 forecasts. The zero-support and recorded-vector definitions match Section S16. $P^-$, $F^-$ and $U$ refer to the split rule; every row has error budget .05, tolerance .10 and gate one. {4pt}

{4pt}

Before clinical calculations, 72 exhaustive configurations covering 157,188 count pairs checked attainable states, containment, zero support and disjointness; 48 additional endpoint-derived equality cases checked the shifted non-strict P and strict F predicates. Four direct Cartesian profiles agreed within $1.23\times10^{-15}$. A finite grid of 144 independent-binomial truth configurations, including inside/outside and boundary cases, had maximum any-wrong probability .008062; this is a diagnostic consistent with the bound, not its proof. Conditional probabilities were checked for mass conservation. The frozen source and all outcomes are in \nolinkurl{icde_reporting_20261102/split_rule}. The analytic bound and numerical checks do not turn this post-review rule choice into confirmatory evidence or a new confidence-interval method.

C4: acquisition and auxiliary-prediction comparators¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

C4: acquisition and auxiliary-prediction comparators

The contribution labels organize separate analyses: C1 evaluates rule-dependent decision stability and computation; C2 examines evidence limitations and conditional sources of variation; C3 evaluates allocation; C4 examines intervention verification. They do not denote a single validated clinical framework. This C4 addendum extends the fixed-policy evidence while retaining the earlier 54-policy report and the 42-policy comparison in Section S11.1.

The design was frozen after the test cohorts and policy frames had been inspected and reconciled, but before drawing these new review samples. It is a retrospective post-review follow-up, not independent clinical confirmation. All 42 eligible single-direction policies retain their thresholds, original XGBoost scores, category vocabulary and full-information criteria. The 12 mixed-direction policies are outside this pooled-target comparison; they are not relabeled as the earlier 18-policy historical subset. Each policy receives $\lceil D/2\rceil$ verified outcomes from its $D$ prediction disagreements, repeated 1,000 times. The 42,000 decisions per method/weight use fresh deterministic samples because the earlier saved simulations did not retain sample indices. Mean charged reviews are 756.52 (range 10--2,989), identical across methods within policy. Frame/prediction acquisition, access work and staff time are excluded from this charge.

Source methods, adapters and decision rule

SRS exact pooled, SRS exact stratified and Gaussian finite-population PPI use the same uniformly sampled records without replacement. The first two reuse the original hypergeometric count inversion and its group-stratum Bonferroni variant. The Gaussian PPI comparator uses the finite-population construction in \href{https://www.stat.ubc.ca/ john/papers/AngelopoulosScience2023.pdf}{Angelopoulos et al., Science (2023), Corollary S14 with Proposition S4}: for frozen scores $f$ and outcomes $y$, its mean estimate is $\bar f_D+\overline{(y-f)}_n$ and its standard error is \[ \sqrt{\frac{D-n}{D}\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_n(y-f)}{n}}. \] The residual variance uses denominator $n$. The full-frame score mean includes sampled and unsampled records; no independent-unlabeled-sample variance term or fitted predictor coefficient is added. The native \nolinkurl{clt_swr} source at commit \nolinkurl{74c2da5d4c0673263e7145549edffc874664335e} calls the normal CDF where the paper requires a quantile. The retained adapter documents the \nolinkurl{norm.cdf} to \nolinkurl{norm.ppf} repair (at .05, 0.8352 becomes 1.9600). It is a repaired source adapter matching the paper, not unmodified original software. Its normal interval remains asymptotic.

The two Equal methods share a separate capacity-capped equal allocation across nonempty strata and independent SRS within strata. Equal exact retains the original stratified exact intervals. The equal-allocation Gaussian stratified comparator (archived as ``Equal Neyman'') uses a design-based variance, not Neyman allocation. It estimates the positive total by $\widehat K=\sum_hD_h\bar y_h$, with variance \[ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat K)=\sum_hD_h^2(1-n_h/D_h)s_h^2/n_h, \] where $s_h^2$ uses denominator $n_h-1$ and census strata contribute zero variance. This is a Gaussian interval for a weighted stratified estimator, not a pooled hypergeometric interval applied after unequal sampling. SRS-versus-Equal contrasts change acquisition while matching charged review counts; within-acquisition contrasts use identical records.

Every method applies the same criterion: no added missed deaths in any group and strictly positive $\Delta\mathrm{TP}-w\Delta\mathrm{FP}$. Primary $w=.10$ and sensitivity $w=.25$ each have zero acceptable policies; conditional correct acceptance is N/A. At $w=.05$, 20 policies are acceptable and 22 are rejected. Addition-only utility changes sign at positive fraction $w/(1+w)$; removal-only acceptance additionally requires no positive outcomes in the disagreement frame. This is a policy criterion, not measured clinical benefit or protection against added subgroup false alerts.

Zero disagreements and full censuses are handled exactly. Noncensus Gaussian intervals defer for insufficient sample sizes, missing or one-observation noncensus strata, nonfinite variance or zero estimated SE. The zero-SE safeguard is an adapter choice. Intervals are intersected with $[0,D]$, then projected by ceiling the lower and flooring the upper count; disjoint or integer-empty intersections defer. This never manufactures a support-boundary singleton and does not make Gaussian coverage exact.

At $w=.10$, exact pooled SRS correctly rejects 79.9476%, with .0952% wrong acceptance. PPI correctly rejects 80.1071% but wrongly accepts 1.4929%. The paired correct-decision difference, PPI minus exact pooled, is .1595 percentage points (pointwise Monte Carlo 95% interval $[-.0309,.3499]$). Similar correct-rejection rates therefore do not establish interchangeable error behavior. Equal Neyman correctly rejects 75.4857%, compared with 71.2857% for Equal exact: a 4.2000-point gain on the same records $[3.9368,4.4632]$. Exact pooled SRS remains 4.4619 points above Equal Neyman $[4.1609,4.7629]$ at equal charged cost but different acquisition. This narrows the earlier claim: its 18.0952-point advantage over SRS stratified isolates inference on identical records, whereas its 8.6619-point advantage over Equal exact also changes acquisition and falls to 4.4619 points against the stronger Gaussian comparator. The new 79.95% estimate is kept separate from the earlier randomization stream's 80.08% estimate.

PPI's all-repetition total-count inclusion is 92.7333%, versus 96.6238% for exact pooled; this does not violate an exact finite-sample PPI guarantee because no such guarantee is asserted for its Gaussian construction. Equal Neyman's 91.0286% all-repetition inclusion includes 4.0238% invalid/deferred intervals; inclusion among valid intervals is 94.8450%. At $w=.05$, conditional correct acceptance among the 20 acceptable policies (20,000 decisions) is 71.275% for exact pooled, 66.485% for PPI, 55.280% for Equal Neyman, 47.170% for Equal exact and 31.050% for SRS stratified. These denominators differ from the complete-panel table; they are not substitutes for it. Zero observed errors do not imply zero error risk.

The retained descriptive maximum illustrates the Gaussian limitation: the eICU seed-47 calibration-budget-global removal-only frame has $D=20,n=10,K=1$. PPI makes 453 wrong acceptances in 1,000 reviews, with 503 count-interval inclusions and 44 empty projected intervals. This was found after inspecting all cases; it is not a separately prespecified hypothesis or a simultaneous worst-case guarantee. All 42 cases remain in the denominator.

Pre-freeze reconciliation reconstructed all 42 disagreement frames, strata and 126 weight-specific truths from unchanged private predictions. Independent aggregate verification then reconstructed 630,000 decisions and 210,000 intervals, including every state, inclusion, invalid status, charged count and summary denominator. PPI and Neyman formulas were independently coded; the maximum native-formula endpoint discrepancy was $8.33\times10^{-17}$. The public aggregate verifier does not reconstruct patient records or sampled identities. All per-policy outcomes, interval diagnostics and contrasts remain in \nolinkurl{icde_c4_comparators_20261102}, together with source/commit/license provenance and \nolinkurl{independent_check.json}.

Exact validity concerns one fixed policy and review budget under its stated sampling design. Coverage of the scalar total, or simultaneous coverage of the required stratum totals, supports every deterministic weight transformation on that same event, including the three reported weights. It does not protect selection among the 42 policies or repeated-budget stopping. The Gaussian methods retain their asymptotic status. Neither construction establishes future-hospital validity, staff-time savings or patient benefit. The Monte Carlo intervals condition on these fixed, reused policy frames; the contrasts are not independent clinical cohorts.

Texas principal-model rebuild and portable source check¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Texas principal-model rebuild and portable source check

This reproduction starts from the public donor's processed \nolinkurl{texas_100x.csv}, not the original complete discharge database. Its SHA-256 is \nolinkurl{12b842d893ff245513aeb8e1187ac2729cdc517121aa2c0435b663b6704e7e74}. The entry point rebuilds the cohort, hospital split (seed 7319), training-only preprocessing, LR/XGBoost tuning and fitting, calibration-threshold choice and seed-11 principal test predictions, then reconstructs the principal race-FNR audit. The explicit model view is \nolinkurl{admission_diagnosis}: age category, admission type, admission source and admitting diagnosis. The inherited three-field \nolinkurl{primary} view omits diagnosis and is a different experiment.

From 925,128 donor rows, the rebuild excludes 1,200 suppressed-hospital records and 174 exact duplicates, retaining 923,754 discharges at 439 hospitals. It reproduces 169,933 test records and 75,316 stays longer than three days, the complete five-category confusion counts, the recorded P/P/I/P comparison vector and both exact-law forecasts. The Native American miss count is 12/75, versus the White reference's 8,496/52,770; the reconstructed denominators and counts are in Table S69.

EB reproduces 53.80385244% any-change and 59.36502403% mean conclusiveness; JP reproduces 59.81588733% and 56.87168689%. Corresponding all-conclusive probabilities are $6.98146523\times10^{-8}$ and $.000137916654$ in probability units. Supplied PMFs are normalized before kernel evaluation; the recorded maximum normalization corrections are $3.56\times10^{-15}$ for EB and $1.12\times10^{-10}$ for JP. These are numerical mass corrections, not new statistical assumptions or a change to the observed counts.

Both the working-tree rebuild and a run from a clean extracted copy of the source package produce predictions byte-identical to the original file, with SHA-256 \nolinkurl{0289424fa8fab32ff8a1dbf670fe54811221d99baf684ba7762ea52c80f54be7}. The extracted-copy run used the same installed environment, not a newly created environment: Python 3.12.14, NumPy/pandas 2.3.3, SciPy 1.16.2, scikit-learn 1.7.2, XGBoost 3.0.5 and PyTorch 2.8.0+cu128 on Windows 11 with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Laptop GPU. Its measured run time was 61.74 seconds. Agreement is measured for this environment; differing numerical/GPU libraries may change fitted scores.

The 17-file public manifest contains source and aggregate validation, excluding donor rows, fitted model objects, individual predictions and patient identifiers. The complete feature/code hashes, command-line instructions and dependency versions are in \nolinkurl{icde_texas_pipeline_20261102}; \nolinkurl{validation/PORTABLE_VALIDATION.json} explicitly records the same-environment limitation. Aggregate confusion counts also reconcile to the complete reporting inventory. This is a Texas donor-to-principal-audit rebuild, not end-to-end reproduction of all C1--C4 studies or a credentialed ICU rebuild. The previously inspected features/splits remain exploratory evidence. This check establishes neither prospective feature availability, patient linkage, calendar generalization, nor external clinical validity. Creating a source package does not itself establish a public repository deposit or DOI.

Runtime and memory curves from the frozen blocked-direct run¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Runtime and memory curves from the frozen blocked-direct run

Figure S6 visualizes the complete 24-case, 48-attempt blocked-direct follow-up in Section S15. It introduces no new measurements or fitted scaling law and does not pool the earlier full-matrix or separate wide-family timing streams. Colors distinguish $G=3,10,40$, while solid/circle and dashed/square marks distinguish search and blocked direct. Cold time is rule preparation, including CP endpoints and method-specific structures, plus first evaluation; it excludes process startup, law generation and validation. Each cold phase is a single observation.

Independent reconciliation retains 36 completed cold phases, including ten from workers that later time out. The memory panels contain 26 final whole-worker process peaks and 14 unconnected timeout snapshots interpreted only as lower bounds, four containing only the saved process baseline. All values are within the plotted axes. Eight estimated-allocation exclusions are shown separately and are not measured memory failures or timing wins. Process peak working set includes Python/imports and cached workloads, so it is distinct from the 768 MiB allocation estimate. No missing phase or timeout limit supplies a runtime or ratio. The curves show support-dependent performance within this one machine/load; they establish neither universal speedup nor successful completion of every million-reference workload.

The four copied source tables/reports match their independently verified originals byte-for-byte. Every plotted row was additionally reconciled to saved worker records; all 16 eligible cold ratios use completed phases. The vector figure, plotting source, all 48 data rows, exclusions and independent verification are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_runtime_curves_20261102}. The figure is a descriptive post-report visualization of a post-review experiment, not additional clinical evidence.

Figure S6 — Complete runtime and memory view of the frozen blocked-direct follow-up. Open runtime markers denote completed cold phases followed by later worker timeout. Only final memory peaks are connected; triangles are timeout lower bounds (filled: search; open: blocked direct). The separate table contains estimated allocations for excluded attempts, not measured peaks. Hardware, caps and definitions are retained in the figure and Section S15.

What the 160 forecast decisions establish¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

What the 160 forecast decisions establish

The 160 entries are pilot--budget planning records from 120 pilots, not 160 fairness passes or independent clinical populations. Their forecast target is expected mean conclusiveness of at least .10 under the retained confirmation rule. Pilot-derived bounds certify attainment in nine records, nonattainment in five and neither in 146. The 14 resolved forecasts therefore comprise nine supported collection targets and five targets ruled out; they are not 14 successful fairness audits.

Complete recorded-frame evaluation, unavailable to the planner, gives a second quantity: whether the chosen allocation's true expected conclusiveness exceeds .10. It does so in 120 records, comprising the nine certified cases and 111 unresolved cases. The remaining 40 comprise five certified nonattainments and 35 unresolved cases. All supported forecast classifications agree with this exact conditional evaluation, but that agreement does not turn unresolved forecasts into certificates. At unchanged allocations, tightening inference alone cannot honestly yield 146 target attainments, because 35 of those 146 allocations actually fall below the target. Neither target attainment nor correct resolution constitutes evidence of equitable clinical outcomes.

Per-record bounds, true mean and correct resolution, costs, pilot identifiers and source hashes are retained in \nolinkurl{original_target_truth.csv} and \nolinkurl{original_target_truth_audit.json}. The same threshold classifications happen to hold for expected correct resolution in these records, but mean conclusiveness and correct resolution remain different endpoints. This is a reconciliation of existing outputs, not a new clinical validation or a forecast improvement.

The full-information oracle also reaches the .10 target in 120/160 records on the original grid. All 40 Texas records with extra budget 250 remain below it, including 35 unresolved and five ruled-out forecasts. Thus improving confidence calculations alone cannot make all of the original plans meet the target; even changing allocation within that particular rule, pilot and grid does not remove this resource limit. This is not an impossibility result for other rules or pilot designs.

More pilot evidence at the same total verification cost

A separately frozen exploratory protocol retained every original pilot and its total charged cost. It shifted 25% or 50% of the original confirmation budget, rounded down to 50-record batches, into additional pilot verification. Additional pilot records were balanced across the smallest current category counts subject to capacity. Error counts were simulated without replacement from the known remaining finite frame, using deterministic independent seeds for three extensions per record/fraction. The full totals generated those hypothetical observations and evaluated the resulting allocations; they were not supplied to the planner. Updated minima and residual batch costs were charged before replanning, with exact equality of old and new total costs checked in every row. Enlarging the pilot also changes the remaining capacities, minima and feasible confirmation choices; the comparison therefore combines information and allocation-design changes rather than isolating a narrower forecast bound. Tolerance .10, target .10 and both declared error levels .05 were unchanged.

All original nine supported attainments remained supported in their 27 extensions per fraction; the five original nonattainments became unresolved in all 15 extensions per fraction. The exact expected-conclusiveness value lay within its forecast enclosure in all 960 simulations. The underlying total-count region contained the complete totals in 97.8125% of simulations. Neither empirical frequency proves conditional coverage: the enlarged-pilot region treats the combined original and added sample as a random sample of the full frame, so its nominal coverage averages over both sampling stages. Holding an original pilot fixed, as this replay does, is a different conditioning event. Confirmation assertion bounds remain conditional on the enlarged pilot because confirmation samples its remaining frame.

The additional information has an opportunity cost. Mean correct resolution at 25%/50% pilot diversion was 34.92%/27.22% in Texas, 30.60%/34.87% in eICU and 39.95%/39.75% in MIMIC-III. Therefore the fraction with more supported forecasts did not maximize confirmation performance in every cohort. No fraction was selected after inspecting outcomes, and the original 9/5/146 result remains unchanged. The repeated simulations share pilots and Texas budget records; they are not 960 independent clinical observations. Protocols, all 960 outcomes, costs, groupwise correctness and the inference clarification are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_completion_planning_20261102}.

Native audit components and matched allocation adaptations¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Native audit components and matched allocation adaptations

The additional external comparison distinguishes execution of a published target from adaptation to the present audit. VFR-Audit's original seven-metric calculator and Fleiss-kappa function were extracted unchanged from the author notebook [16]. The three principal frozen predictors produce 91 metric--attribute cells over 13 attribute families. Each uses 500 outcome-stratified replacement bootstraps of 10,000 rows; the sample size is a repetition-law choice and can exceed the observed cohort size. The size-axis calculation uses 30 samples without replacement at each feasible actual size, retaining 413 metric/attribute/size rows. Census variation is zero by construction. Cross-hospital diagnostics use frozen predictions in 66 Texas and 32 eICU hospitals; this adapts the author notebook's GroupKFold retraining experiment. MIMIC-III's single hospital supplies no cross-hospital agreement estimate. The complete historical 12-model training and mitigation notebook was not rerun.

Nine cells distinguish minority frequency from reversal relative to the full-cohort recorded binary verdict. Texas race equal-opportunity auditing gives minority VFR .104 and recorded reversal .896 under the same 10,000-record law. The source calculator assigns zero to TPR/FPR/PPV when the corresponding within-group denominator is zero and drops categories absent from a resample. These original behaviors are retained and documented; they do not supply interval coverage. A separate matched reference-FNR adaptation retains all 50 principal contrasts at denominator fractions .25/.5/1, with 10,000 conditional draws per configuration. It uses the inclusive .10 threshold and retains unsupported groups. It is an explicit change from native max-minus-min metrics, not a coverage competitor or clinical-outcome improvement.

Yan--Zhang Algorithm 3 was implemented with exact finite-class extrema and a consistent surviving-hypothesis online oracle [17]. Its native target is female-minus-male selection-rate disparity. The target predictor is an anonymous member of a known finite class formed from the existing fitted candidates; target inclusion is checked, but its index is withheld. That strong prior information is part of the comparison. Fifty seeds at each $\epsilon=.01/.05$ and $\delta=.05$ yield 300 native runs and 600 comparator rows. The exponential sampling rate was checked against the paper as $\log(|\mathcal H|^2M/\delta)$. All runs completed within the requested error in this restricted class. The paper's released linear-surrogate implementation was inspected but not represented as executable on a nonrealizable frozen XGBoost target; the finite-class code is an authored implementation of the published algorithm.

At $\epsilon=.01$, mean query counts were 57.60 (Texas), 47.36 (MIMIC-III) and zero (eICU). eICU's full candidate-class disparity diameter was already .016896, below $2\epsilon$, so no query was needed. This is not a clinical efficiency gain. Random queries with the same candidate class and realized count gave mean absolute errors .000432/.000158 for Texas/MIMIC-III, compared with zero/.000128 for the active algorithm. A separate equal-group IID estimator had errors .112031/.117193 at those small query counts; it lacks the candidate-class information and is not an information-matched superiority test. Zero-query IID estimates remain unavailable. Other recorded sex categories lie outside this native binary target.

For the C3 setting, an explicit adapter minimizes the mean diameter of unrestricted possible FNR gaps. With $G_s$ supported nonreference groups, an additional reference review reduces this diameter by $1/N_0$, while reviewing group $g$ reduces it by $1/(G_sN_g)$. Greedy largest reduction solves this linear objective on the equal-cost batch grid. It uses neither unknown errors nor confirmation outcomes. All 160 inherited pilots retain their minima, capacities and exact charged costs; uniform within-group confirmation is evaluated by the existing finite-population family rule. This is a diameter-objective adaptation inspired by active auditing, not native Algorithm 3, and the latter's guarantees do not transfer.

The adapter's Texas zero resolution reflects its different objective; it cannot establish that DP outperforms native active auditing. Family wrong-assertion probabilities remain below .05 under the declared fixed-allocation law. The 640 family and 8,640 group evaluations retain errors as well as correct resolution. Portable aggregate reruns, with private prediction access disabled, reproduced four output files byte for byte. Native patient-row replays still require authorized predictions. Source hashes, method mappings, all comparator rows and verification are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_completion_external_20261102}; neither a full historical retraining nor new clinical confirmation is claimed.

Texas policy eligibility for the same pooled comparison

The unchanged Texas policy panel was checked before extending the five-method review. It contains group-sensitivity thresholds, utility-constrained thresholds and race/outcome reweighing versus an unweighted predictor, for LR and XGBoost at seeds 11/29/47. All 18 contrasts include both added and removed alerts. For example, historical seed-11 XGBoost group thresholds add 563 alerts and remove 1,319; the signed change $-756$ is not a single-direction change. Each comparison aligns with 169,933 held-out records and 75,316 length-of-stay outcomes. These historical predictors differ from the current admission-diagnosis principal fit.

With both change directions, the TP change depends on $K_{\rm added}-K_{\rm removed}$, and the no-added-misses constraint depends on their subgroup allocation. One pooled total of positive outcomes cannot identify those quantities. The inherited single-direction helper rejects direction zero; replacing it with the sign of the net alert change would be invalid. Scores are available, but none of these existing contrasts is eligible for the unchanged pooled/PPI experiment. No new review samples or selected replacement policies were generated. Thus the 42-policy five-method comparison remains explicitly limited to the two mortality cohorts; mixed-direction Texas inference needs a separately specified design.

All 18 added/removed counts, outcome and group-alignment checks, source hashes and the untouched 44-file mortality-comparator manifest are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_completion_texas_ppi_20261102}. The portable eligibility check confirms every exclusion without exporting patient records. This check establishes a scope limit, not a completed Texas PPI comparison.

C1 boundary reuse: invariant, cost and cache scope¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

C1 boundary reuse: invariant, cost and cache scope

Algorithm 1 in the main paper distinguishes preparation from a new probability-law query. Preparation fixes the comparison family, interval rule, family error allocation, denominators, tolerances and eligibility. Each eligible denominator/tolerance type shares endpoint-induced boundary vectors, but each comparison retains its own probability mass. Recorded states may change between queries without changing these boundaries.

For a type $t$, write the four integer boundary vectors as $A_t,B_t,F_t,H_t$. Let $\mathcal R$ be the maximal intervals of consecutive reference counts on which every vector is constant. Conditional pass, fail and inconclusive probabilities depend only on these boundaries and the supplied comparison mass. Hence they are constant on each $R\in\mathcal R$, as are products for recorded-state preservation and all-group conclusiveness. For any such term $h$ and representative $x_R\in R$, \[ \sum_{x=0}^{n_0} f_0(x)h(x) =\sum_{R\in\mathcal R}\left(\sum_{x\in R}f_0(x)\right)h(x_R). \] This finite-sum identity proves the reuse step independently of the chosen normalized count law. It does not establish that the law models a future clinical audit. Zero denominators give the constant inconclusive term and introduce no boundary changes. Strict failure and inclusive passing endpoints retain the main paper's conventions.

Each monotone integer boundary has at most $n_t+1$ changes; their union therefore has at most $4\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}(n_t+1)$ changes. With $K=|\mathcal R|$, this gives $K\leq\min\{n_0+1,1+4\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}(n_t+1)\}$. The bound counts potential runs, including zero-mass runs. The implementation skips only runs with supplied mass zero; it does not apply an arbitrary tail cutoff. Upstream floating-point PMF evaluation can underflow, so exactness is the mathematical finite-sum claim and numerical agreement is tested separately.

Preparation uses endpoint generation and searches for the four boundaries. The present implementation stores dense boundary vectors per unique type, so reference memory remains linear in $n_0$ for each type; it is not a sublinear-memory index. Per query, full-support mass generation and comparison-mass indexes remain necessary. Conditional lookups fall from the full-grid $G(n_0+1)$ count to $GK$, with prefix/suffix lookups and logarithmic positive-mass-tree fallbacks. Probability-zero reference counts can reduce both implementations' evaluated work. Many denominator/tolerance types or dense boundary changes can eliminate the reuse advantage, and full-support PMF generation can dominate even when $K$ is small.

Caches must be rebuilt after a change in denominators, family error allocation, tolerances, eligibility or interval rule. A changed probability mass or recorded state alone does not require rebuilding. The scaling extension varies these preparation inputs across designs and probability laws within a design. It compares unchanged implementations; none of the computational changes alters the clinical forecasts or the C2--C4 statistical targets.

Joint thousand-group, million-reference scaling¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Joint thousand-group, million-reference scaling

This extension evaluates $G=1{,}000$, $n_0=1{,}000{,}000$ and 100 varying repeat-audit laws. It changes the output storage contract, not the three-state probabilities: all marginal triples and family scalars are retained, while conditional rows are reduced during evaluation rather than stored in a $G(n_0+1)\times3$ tensor. Exactly identical group laws are combined with integer multiplicities. Exactly zero supplied float64 masses are omitted; positive masses are never deliberately truncated. Any underflow already present in generated PMFs therefore remains a numerical limitation. The direct comparator uses the same law classes and zero-weight omission, classifies positive-mass count pairs, and uses neither cumulative nor boundary lookup.

The original heterogeneous probability grid and a separately declared repeated-law grid are both retained. The repeated-law workload has only three distinct denominator/probability classes per query ($U=3$), whereas the heterogeneous workload has $U=1{,}000$. Thus repeated laws form a favorable workload, not a substitute for arbitrary heterogeneous groups. Endpoint construction, boundary construction, PMF generation, integration and whole-process time have separate scopes. The machine is the same shared Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX workstation; no isolated-machine replication is claimed. Initial and follow-up attempts, including a Windows status-file sharing error and changed time cap, remain separately identified.

For repeated imbalanced laws, the completed indexed/direct integration times were 6.274/26.789 seconds; adding setup gives 8.778/29.521 seconds, and adding PMF generation gives 27.457/51.176 seconds. The resulting ratios are 4.270, 3.363 and 1.864, respectively, for one varying-law trajectory. Repeated balanced indexed integration completed in 16.103 seconds, 26.423 seconds including setup and 124.434 including law generation; its censored direct run supplies no 100-law speed ratio. The heterogeneous workloads did not complete 100 laws within their declared caps. Prefixes at 1, 10 and 100 queries are reported only when observed, not as independent timing replicates.

Independent output reconstruction checked 309 saved complete outputs and 103 matched indexed/direct outputs, with maximum absolute discrepancy $2.59\times10^{-12}$. Eight additional 1,000-group small-support profiles included distinct group laws and nonsaturated joint probabilities, with maximum discrepancy $9.02\times10^{-17}$. These tests supplement the earlier Cartesian enumeration checks; they do not provide a uniform floating-point error theorem. All initial failures, censored attempts, frozen retry protocols, portable source and output checks remain in \nolinkurl{icde_completion_scale_20261102}.
