Hospital-binomial source sensitivity¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Hospital-binomial source sensitivity

The historical C2 illustration estimates hospital variation after substituting working binomial variances into a Gaussian model. To assess that substitution, we retained the same supported hospital-by-sex counts and fitted an established binomial-normal model. For hospital $h$ and sex $s$, $K_{hs}\mid p_{hs}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n_{hs},p_{hs})$, conditionally independently, with \[ \operatorname{logit}(p_{hm})=\beta_m+a_h-d_h/2,\qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_{hf})=\beta_f+a_h+d_h/2, \] where $a_h\sim N(0,\sigma_a^2)$ and $d_h\sim N(0,\sigma_d^2)$ are independent across effects and hospitals. The contrast variance $\sigma_d^2$ describes heterogeneity in the female-minus-male log-odds contrast. It is not the variance of the rate difference used in the historical Gaussian guard. We also integrate the mean and variance of $p_{hf}-p_{hm}$ over the fitted random effects. A shared intercept can make this rate difference vary even when $\sigma_d^2=0$.

Maximum likelihood uses two-dimensional adaptive Gauss--Hermite integration and multiple starts, including variance boundaries. The 95% profile interval for $\sigma_d^2$ uses the asymptotic $\chi^2_1$ cutoff, not a finite-sample or distribution-free guarantee. Such variance estimation is sensitive to the number of clusters [18]. Fits at 9, 15 and 25 nodes per dimension were checked; the reported clinical intervals use 25 nodes. The same inclusion criterion leaves 58 Texas and nine eICU hospitals. MIMIC-III supplies one institution and therefore no between-hospital variance estimate. The target is the supported-hospital distribution, not the omitted hospitals or arbitrary future sites.

For calibration, 200 new simulated count datasets per cohort retained the recorded denominators and drew hospital effects from the fitted model. Each replicate refitted both the unrestricted and true-contrast-variance-constrained likelihood. The nominal profile rule retained the generating variance in 92.5% of Texas and 99.5% of eICU simulations; exact binomial intervals quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty in these frequencies. The Texas point estimate is below 95%, and the eICU zero-variance boundary is conservative. These fitted-model tests cannot establish that the clinical hospital distribution is Gaussian or exchangeable. The percentile intervals propagate uncertainty through 200 parametric refits but are not calibrated clinical recruitment intervals.

Numerical checks recover the zero-variance binomial likelihood, preserve sex-label symmetry and agree with direct numerical integration on three small count configurations. Twelve selected simulation fits, including two eICU optimizer warnings, were rerun with 25-node quadrature and multiple starts. All coverage calls were unchanged; the largest likelihood-ratio change was $1.01\times10^{-5}$. The two warnings remain in the primary log rather than being silently removed. An earlier optimizer failure was rejected before the reported analysis and retained separately as an invalid attempt. The portable aggregate verifier reconciles all 400 simulations and both profile intervals.

This analysis adds uncertainty estimates under a stated hospital model; it does not establish a new hierarchical estimator, validate the 621-outcome collection recommendation, or repair future-hospital coverage under other dependence structures. The eICU boundary estimate and broad upper limit particularly caution against interpreting a small fitted component as evidence that hospital variation is absent. C2 remains a conditional sensitivity contribution alongside C1's exact count computation. Source, protocol, aggregate inputs, rejected-attempt provenance, simulations and verification are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_completion_sources_20261102}.

Complete comparator and operating-point reporting¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Complete comparator and operating-point reporting

These exploratory reporting additions use unchanged predictions, repeated audits and declared categories. They add no validation cohort. The bootstrap support-one sensitivity retains the same 1,999 draws, $p_*=.01$, $w_0=\infty$, boundary/degenerate-scale withholding and admitted-family calibration as the support-20 adapter. UAF uses rate error $.05/(G+1)$ and positive support one. UM uses 19,999 Dirichlet--multinomial predictive draws and tails $.05/(2G)$ with a shared reference. UM interval inclusion below concerns the fixed empirical-population gap; it is not native future-gap predictive coverage. Future targets were not retained for that separate evaluation.

The 600 clinical group--scenario--method rows retain all-audit inclusion, interval issuance, conclusiveness and wrong assertions. Unissued intervals are $[-1,1]$, so inclusion may be trivial. Issued-only inclusion, all numerators/denominators, pass/fail errors and Monte Carlo intervals are in \nolinkurl{per_comparison_clinical.csv}; the 792-row all-scenario file also retains synthetic groups. Across defined clinical groups, bootstrap support-one inclusion ranges from 93% to 100%, compared with 99% to 100% for UAF. At full Texas size, simultaneous inclusion is 91.5% for either bootstrap gate and 99.5% for UAF. A nominal level and zero wrong tolerance decisions do not establish interval coverage. Unsupported true gaps have no inclusion denominator.

{2pt}

Attainable states and probability of reaching them

The following table separates structural possibility from probability under a supplied law. P/F means both states are possible; F means failure alone is attainable; a dash means neither state is possible. Zero support and positive-support incapability remain distinct in the feasibility inventory. EB's zero-miss empirical law fixes that group's count at zero, whereas JP retains uncertainty; neither is asserted to predict future hospitals. Extremely small computed tails are below the displayed numerical threshold, not proven zeros. In mortality, fail-only cells produce asymmetric decisions by construction of this rule, not by a general impossibility of establishing acceptable disparity. {2pt}

Feasibility concerns possible count configurations, not probability that a population is fair. Unsupported groups remain inconclusive. Display-floor probabilities are numerical outputs, not independently validated rare-tail bounds.

The split rule changed exactly three recorded failures to inconclusive: eICU FPR for Male aged 65--79 versus Male aged 40--64 ($1025/3318$ versus $705/4217$); MIMIC FNR for age 80+ versus 40--64 ($23/196$ versus $58/150$); and MIMIC selection rate for Female aged 65--79 versus Male aged 40--64 ($282/637$ versus $290/1153$). FPR denominators are negative outcomes and selection-rate denominators are all records.

On the original coarse-grid MIMIC plans, 16 of 17 supported comparison groups reach census. UNKNOWN/NOT SPECIFIED contributes 43/72 reviewed positives; the White reference contributes 295/372 or 368/372 for caps 20/200. Total review is 435/541 (80.4%) or 508/541 (93.9%). The 23 zero-positive categories do not become census-supported groups. These flags describe this grid, not every new sensitivity.

Clinical operating points, ascertainment and calibration

These models predict recorded length of stay over three days or subsequent hospital mortality. The intended use here is retrospective review before changing an alert policy; no care intervention was deployed. The 80% calibration sensitivity fixes a common operating point across predictors, and the ten-percentage-point disparity tolerance defines a common research comparison. Neither choice has clinician endorsement. Tolerances .05/.15, policy weights .05/.25 and complete denominators expose their influence. A conclusive audit does not authorize a clinical action without further assessment; inconclusive comparisons do not establish fairness.

Outcome labels are the recorded source outcomes, without independent chart adjudication. Thresholds reproduce every saved principal prediction: .4219199717, .07371558994 and .08344839513 for Texas, eICU and MIMIC. Across these cohorts, PPV is 64.706/21.672/22.480%, sensitivity 82.332/78.404/77.079%, specificity 64.253/72.961/66.613%, and alert fraction 56.394/31.514/38.263%. Brier scores are .176461/.064614/.084590; ten-bin expected calibration error is .016751/.005233/.010195. These summaries are descriptive and prevalence-dependent, not guarantees of calibration or acceptable workload.

For each of the 105 declared category rows, \nolinkurl{all_declared_groups.csv} retains confusion counts, positive/negative denominators, PPV, sensitivity, specificity, alerts, mean probability, prevalence, Brier score and calibration error. The 1,080 bin rows retain all ten bins per group and pooled cohort, including empty bins. Bins are $[0,.1),\ldots,[.9,1]$; ECE is the count-weighted absolute difference between mean score and event frequency. Every attribute partitions its cohort, all counts and bins reconcile, and absent or undefined rates remain N/A. Sparse-group ECE can be unstable. The following tables show every race category, with Texas ethnicity separate; vocabularies are not harmonized across cohorts.

{2pt}

{2pt}

Support-ratio sensitivity of the streamed evaluator

At $n_0=10{,}000$, ten distinct group laws and ten changing queries, a frozen grid crossed eight group/reference denominator ratios with both evaluators and three repetitions, alternating method order. All 48 runs completed; 240 matched outputs agreed within $5.33\times10^{-15}$. Integration was nearly tied at ratio .001 and favored indexing at .003 and above. Total-time medians favored indexing at every tested ratio, with only a .0008-second difference at .001. This small shared-workstation grid does not establish a universal crossover. RSS is a common-process snapshot, not a method-specific peak; prior isolated-worker memory measurements remain separate.

All-cohort rule and allocation continuation¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

All-cohort rule and allocation continuation

This exploratory continuation retains all 160 original pilot--budget records from 120 saved pilot configurations (Texas reuses 40 configurations at two budgets). The original 50-record grid and the additional 25-record grid use identical pilots, category order, minima, capacities and total charged costs. The 25-grid is a finer matched grid for every cohort; it does not replace the separately retained reference-step 1/group-step 5 grid with terminal capacities. All comparisons remain in the family, including unsupported groups; $G=4,6,40$ for Texas, eICU and MIMIC-III, respectively. Tolerance remains .10, the family wrong-assertion budget .05, and the recorded mean-conclusiveness target .10.

The frozen manifest accounts for every requested row. Original 120-second cold-start timeouts are retained before a separate 600-second continuation; the exact identity $U(x;R,n,\alpha)=R-L(n-x;R,n,\alpha)$ avoids duplicate upper-tail inversion and reproduced 4,632 endpoint integers. Timings are shared-machine wall times, not isolated speed benchmarks. Input caps, stage limits and every incomplete row are in completion_matrix.csv. No incomplete row is imputed as a tie, zero, or failed target.

The finest grid is a distinct candidate family because it includes terminal capacities. Under the primary rule, Texas small-budget allocations actually meet the .10 mean target in 39/40 DP cases and 40/40 oracle cases, compared with 0/40 on either the 50- or 25-record grid. This exact full-frame diagnostic is not a certified forecast; it shows why an oracle ceiling must be indexed by its candidate family. Texas $B=2000$ finest-grid rows remain input-capped.

All 160 fresh primary-grid DP, balancing, greedy and oracle results reconcile exactly with the saved historical values and allocations (maximum difference 0). Cyclic uniform allocation equals balancing on all 160 original-grid records; the duplicate entries make this equivalence explicit. The baseline cycles equal grid moves; these are equal numbers of reviews on the 50/25 grids but differ on the 1/5 grid. This distinction prevents interpreting the latter as equal per-category review increments.

The split finite-population rule uses category error $.05/G$ for pass endpoints and $.05/(2G)$ for fail endpoints. A wrong pass requires one of two relevant endpoint-tail errors; a wrong fail requires one of four. Each comparison therefore has wrong-assertion probability at most $.05/G$, and a union bound gives family error at most $.05$. Pass and fail regions are disjoint. This directional tradeoff is not a uniformly sharper interval, and no single split-rule gap-coverage interval is reported.

The machine-readable results retain wrong pass, wrong fail, any wrong assertion, all-group resolution, all-family and supported-only means/minima, raw group losses at threshold $10^{-12}$, losses above one percentage point, and every group change. These distinguish definition/support limits from rule limits and objective tradeoffs. In the fixed MIMIC frame, 23/40 groups lack positive-outcome support, so they remain inconclusive even at a complete census; the supported-family ceiling for all-comparison mean resolution is 17/40. This is a fixed-frame statement, not an intrinsic lower bound on future data requirements. Mean-oriented reallocation can improve the mean while lowering individual-group correct resolution.

The original unrestricted composite-null direct-gap comparator and the later support-aware variant are distinct. The former completes 80 mortality primary-grid replans; the latter completes 40 MIMIC primary-grid replans within its bounded inventory. Their incomplete Texas/eICU or finer-grid cases do not establish all-cohort support-aware optimization, and the prior eight fixed-allocation support-aware checks remain historical sensitivity. Full nuisance ranges are retained wherever a run completes; dense state maps are compressed only after exact reconstruction. Thus the all-cohort support-aware DP/oracle comparison and the excluded finest-grid cases remain open rather than being renamed completed.

These direct-gap results do not establish a valid less-conservative replacement across all three cohorts for the repeated-verdict, feasibility and allocation analyses. The split directional rule preserves assertion error but is not a uniformly tighter gap interval. Asymptotic intervals are not presented as replacements for the stated finite-population guarantee.

Source freezes, complete manifests, costs, memberships, group outcomes and verification are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_completion_planning_20261102}. These computations use inspected data and supply neither new clinical confirmation nor a certified gain over balancing.

Historical cold-resource inventory. The original resource grid had 24 completions, eight timeouts and 16 allocation-estimate exclusions; blocked direct had 26/14/eight. Sixteen matched cold outputs agreed within $3.55\times10^{-15}$. Indexed computation was 2.67--65.56 times faster in six balanced pairs; blocked direct won eight of ten imbalanced pairs. With 1,000 groups/reference outcomes, indexed/blocked cold times were .738/5.433 seconds balanced and .186/.119 seconds imbalanced. Four wide-family cold pairs agreed within $1.89\times10^{-15}$, but six of eight workers later timed out; that implementation completed no 1,000-group 100-query workload. The original million-reference/three-group imbalanced indexed cold phase took 5.673 seconds. Censored phases supply no speedup ratio.

Predictive-target check for the Uncertainty Matters adapter¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Predictive-target check for the Uncertainty Matters adapter

The fixed-gap diagnostic in the matched comparison is not native predictive coverage. We therefore evaluated the retained Uncertainty Matters holdout adapter [14] against its future same-group-size FNR-gap target. For each of the 200 retained audits at each of nine cohort-size settings, 100 independent future confusion tables were drawn from the empirical within-group multinomial laws. Future group sizes equalled those in the conditioning audit, and one reference realization was shared across comparisons. Existing intervals and adapter parameters were unchanged. No model was refitted.

Undefined future gaps were represented by $[-1,1]$ and required set inclusion. They were not dropped from the family. The table reports full-family set inclusion; per-comparison inclusion among defined future gaps and all category-level denominators are retained in the artifact. Monte Carlo standard errors are computed across 200 audit-level fractions, retaining dependence among the 100 future draws using each interval. These exploratory diagnostics evaluate the predictive adapter under an empirical generating law, not independent clinical coverage or a frequentist guarantee.

Texas and eICU family inclusion ranged from 94.77% to 95.88%. MIMIC-III inclusion was higher (98.98--99.65%), but only 22.04--34.16% of future gaps were defined. High inclusion there therefore includes broad intervals and undefined-target sets rather than informative conclusions. These results support reporting the predictive comparator on its intended target, without treating its fixed-population-gap resolution as a native-method performance ranking.

Earlier repeated-law-class implementation. A streamed extension, retaining aggregate outputs rather than conditional tensors, completed 100 laws at 1,000 groups and one million reference outcomes with three distinct group-law classes. Imbalanced indexed/direct totals including preparation and law generation were 27.46/51.18 seconds (1.86$\times$), with process peaks 247.2/221.0 MiB. The then-current 1,000-distinct-law workloads remained censored. The 103 matched outputs agreed within $2.60\times10^{-12}$. That earlier reuse advantage concerned repeated law classes, not arbitrary heterogeneous workloads.

Exact reference-run aggregation at large scale¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Exact reference-run aggregation at large scale

The conditional pass, inconclusive and fail probabilities are constant whenever their cached integer count boundaries are unchanged. We partition the reference support at the union of those change locations across eligible comparisons. For a run $R$, its representative $x_R$ and mass $w_R=\sum_{x\in R}p_0(x)$, each conditional state probability $c_{g,s}$ satisfies \[ \sum_x p_0(x)c_{g,s}(x)=\sum_R w_R c_{g,s}(x_R). \] The recorded-state preservation and all-conclusive products are also constant within each run, so the same replacement preserves their integrals. This implementation reuses the partition across probability laws without discarding positive mass or merging distinct group laws. Floating-point results remain conditional on the supplied PMFs, including any underflow present when those PMFs were generated.

We repeated the previously censored heterogeneous imbalanced workload without changing its inputs. It contains $G=1{,}000$ comparisons, $n_0=1{,}000{,}000$, group denominators cycling through $100$, $300$ and $1{,}000$, and $Q=100$ queries with $U=1{,}000$ distinct group probability laws per query. The reference and group probabilities follow the previously frozen trajectories; recorded states, tolerance and family error remain unchanged. There are three denominator/tolerance boundary types. Their union contains 5,005 runs, with 165--210 positive-mass runs per query rather than 30,204--37,456 positive reference-count rows.

The completed boundary-run trajectory took 2.426 seconds for setup, 34.639 seconds for PMF generation and 23.349 seconds for integration. On the first ten identical queries completed by both indexed implementations, the total setup, law-generation and integration ratio was 18.490. These finite ratios concern completed matched prefixes only. All 23 current-run completed output pairs agreed within $6.00\times10^{-15}$ for probabilities and $2.56\times10^{-13}$ for expected conclusive count. Direct integration completed three full queries, providing a full-scale numerical comparison rather than only a small-support check.

The implementation passed 84 small direct-evaluation profiles, boundary atoms, a 1,000-group heterogeneous profile, and nine explicit deterministic-state and unsupported-count checks. The hardware was an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX with 24 physical/logical CPUs and approximately 31.4 GiB memory. Library thread counts were fixed to one. Three fresh-process first-query pairs during a coordinated pause of the other team experiment took 4.103--5.794 seconds with run aggregation and 20.626--22.411 seconds with the preceding index, including setup and law generation. Their paired total-cost ratios were 3.560--5.137. Pre-worker system-CPU samples still ranged from 3.2% to 47.2%, so these are shared-desktop measurements, not exclusive hardware isolation. A final direct repeat took 96.426 seconds but overlapped resumed computation and is labelled separately. All repeated outputs agreed within $2.28\times10^{-13}$.

The gain arises when many reference counts induce identical group-state boundaries. It does not imply acceleration when large or diverse group supports change nearly every reference row. The earlier balanced large-support workload remains censored. This computational improvement leaves the audit rule, coverage, clinical forecast uncertainty and patient-outcome claims unchanged.

Independent nonsaturated joint-probability checks. Four additional cases were frozen before execution, retaining 1,000 groups, a million reference outcomes, and group denominators cycling through 100/300/1,000. The reference probability was .001, the first group's probability varied over .22/.25/.28/.31, and the other 999 distinct group probabilities ranged from .70 to .80. Recorded states were failures. All eight compressed/direct workers completed. Any-change probabilities were .731584844300, .461671132081, .219804363006 and .077633547225; all-conclusive probabilities were .268415155716, .538328867919, .780195636994 and .922366452775. The largest probability discrepancy was $2.27\times10^{-14}$ and expected-count discrepancy $2.28\times10^{-13}$. These checks address joint outputs away from zero/one saturation; their timings are diagnostic, not a separate speed claim.

Earlier cold and Monte Carlo checks. All conclusive Monte Carlo calls matched exact computation; some remained unresolved at 100,000 draws. Historical cached and balanced timings favored indexed computation, while direct integration won 13 of 18 imbalanced designs. In the later original-scale cold grid, all seven completed imbalanced pairs favored direct integration; the median prior-index/direct preparation-plus-evaluation time ratio was 1.509 (range 1.089--2.284), excluding probability-mass generation. These are completed comparisons, not ratios against timeout caps. Wide-family cold outputs agreed within $1.89\times10^{-15}$; most workers later timed out. Censored phases supply no speedup ratio.

Earlier support-aware sensitivity, a different rule. At unchanged eICU replicate-00 allocations, direct-gap tests raised correct resolution from 24.23% to 30.06% and from 37.77% to 40.40% at pilot caps 20/200. MIMIC-III changed little: its 23 unsupported comparisons remained, while 39.49--40.00% resolution across all 40 represented 92.91--94.12% among the 17 supported comparisons. Collection requirements therefore depend partly on the retained interval rule. This eight-plan calculation restricts nuisance totals using observed-confirmation logical support. It is distinct from the unrestricted-null follow-up below.

Unrestricted-null exact finite-frame rule sensitivity¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Unrestricted-null exact finite-frame rule sensitivity

The original 160 pilots were retained to separate the effect of the decision rule from the collection design. We reapplied the unrestricted-null exact unconditional gap test to the primary-rule DP allocation and matched balancing allocation of every pilot. This test maximizes over every pilot-consistent nuisance total; it does not apply the observation-dependent logical-support restriction of the separate support-aware sensitivity. The target remained the complete recorded positive-outcome frame, and the confirmation sample remained uniform without replacement within each category. The tolerance was 0.10 and the family wrong-assertion level was 0.05. No previously unexamined patients were introduced.

The original exhaustive test was accelerated without changing its decision map. Its ordering statistic is $A X_g-B X_0$, with nonnegative integer weights. Along a composite-null frontier the group total increases with the reference total. For a reference-total interval $[a,b]$, the upper-tail probability at the corner $(a,T_g(b))$ bounds all upper tails on the interval; $(b,T_g(a))$ gives the corresponding lower-tail bound. A branch is discarded only after its upper bound falls below the original rejection threshold. Otherwise an admissible null point can establish non-rejection, or the interval is subdivided. Binary search over the ordered statistic then finds the four decision boundaries. This retains every nuisance value while avoiding p-values that are unnecessary for the three-state decision.

Rule validity does not imply uniformly greater resolution. Correctly resolved comparisons and wrong assertions are therefore reported alongside total resolution. The original forecast uncertainty is unchanged by this sensitivity: the 146 unresolved forecasts refer to a different question, whether the pilot evidence supports a specified expected-resolution target before confirmation. The additional reoptimization study uses the first five recorded replicates in each cohort/pilot stratum at 250 extra reviews and the unchanged 50-record allocation grid. It reports DP, balancing, uniform, greedy and the unavailable full-total oracle separately; it does not replace the original full set of grid comparisons.

The new computation matched 466 exhaustive decision maps and reproduced 100 previously completed clinical policy evaluations with maximum probability difference 0. Four DP solutions matched exhaustive allocation enumeration exactly. These checks support the implementation and the declared optimization objective. They do not establish forecast calibration, independent clinical benefit or future-hospital validity.

Numerical edge correction. At $\alpha/(2G)<10^{-12}$, an empty-null shortcut could differ from the exhaustive code's inherited numerical guard. The separately retained boundary_gap_validated.maps wrapper restores that convention; 35 maps and 940 binary cells checked three corrected extreme-alpha cells. All clinical evaluations used $\alpha=.05$ and are unchanged. The frozen source, corrected wrapper and verification record are retained separately.

Scaling regimes for reusable boundary integration¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Scaling regimes for reusable boundary integration

This extension fixes 21 designs before timing and runs two fresh-process repetitions of each of three unchanged implementations. Table S89 includes balanced supports, increasing numbers of denominator/tolerance types, one million reference outcomes and up to 1,000 comparisons. Every query has a distinct probability law for every group. Ten queries use reference probability $.20+.002(q-4.5)$ and group probabilities $\operatorname{linspace}(.12,.36,G)+.002(q-4.5)$ for $q=0,\ldots,9$. Recorded states cycle P/I/F and family error is .05. Query order and deterministic rotation of method order are frozen; no design or repetition is selected by its result.

All methods receive a 20-second cumulative query budget, 60-second worker-wall cap and 1 GiB resident-memory cap. Only one benchmark worker runs at a time, with numerical-library threads set to one. The Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX workstation is shared; background activity and preworker free memory are retained. Windows platform build 26300, Python 3.11.9, NumPy 2.4.2 and SciPy 1.15.3 were used. Two repetitions provide descriptive ranges, not timing confidence intervals. The earlier 100-query workload uses a different 300-second budget and remains separately reported.

Setup includes endpoints, boundary construction and any run partition. Cold cost adds the first completed query's law generation and integration. Reuse cost adds all ten completed queries. Process wall time additionally includes imports, output writing and unfinished censored work; it is retained in the CSV. Peak memory combines parent sampling and the operating-system peak counter. Censored peaks are attained lower bounds, not successful completion requirements. No speed ratio is assigned to an incomplete trajectory.

Across all 126 workers, 110 completed ten queries. All 931 shared-query output comparisons met the frozen tolerances; maximum differences were $5.11\times10^{-15}$ for probabilities and $2.84\times10^{-14}$ for expected conclusive counts. The copied engine files retained their earlier hashes. Run counts satisfied the bound in Section S24. Full phase costs, process status, output arrays and paired completed costs are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_scaling_grid_20261104}. These are computational tests under supplied laws, not new clinical observations.

Across the 20 designs with two completed paired indexed trajectories, the median of the design-level paired cost ratios (prior index/run index) was 1.366. Four medians favored the prior index: denominators 3,000 or 10,000 at reference 10,000; 40 distinct denominator types; and 100 groups cycling three denominator types. Their run/prior cost ratios were 1.208, 1.163, 1.079 and 1.078. The 1,000-distinct-denominator design was nearly tied (prior/run 1.020), with repetition-specific timing variation. A single favorable median does not establish a stable speed ordering on shared hardware.

Direct integration completed ten queries in both repetitions for 15 designs; its median design-level direct/run cost ratio was 9.503 (range 1.832--20.878). The two indexed engines completed both trajectories in 20 designs. Balanced million-count groups allowed one completed query per indexed worker and none for direct integration under the declared budget; no ten-query speed ratio is assigned. Boundary-run peak memory reached 420.3 MiB in the 1,000-distinct-denominator design. The support-ratio sweep at $G=40,n_0=10^4$ favored the prior index at .3 and 1, whereas the run index's median reuse cost was lower at .001--.1. Cold costs and both individual repetitions are retained rather than inferring a universal crossover from this small grid.

Historical review interpretation retained from the main text. The historical panel remains separate. Pooled review correctly rejected 80.08% versus Equal's 71.16% at the same cost, an 8.92-point gain. On identical disagreement-SRS records, changing stratified to pooled inference increased rejection from 61.69% to 80.08%, isolating removal of the scalar criterion's unnecessary error-budget split. Wrong acceptance was .095% for pooling and zero for both controls. All 54 policies failed the primary criterion; 12 mixed-direction policies retained stratification.

At $w=.25$, all 42 policies remain unacceptable; fresh pooled/Equal--Neyman correct rejection was 97.22/92.18%, with no wrong acceptance, versus PPI 95.60% with 1.43% wrong acceptance. At prespecified $w=.05$, historical correctness across the same 42 policies rose from 65.82% to 85.06%. Paired panel gains over stratified SRS were 18.395 points [18.181,18.609] at the primary weight and 19.236 [18.943,19.528] at .05; intervals describe conditional Monte Carlo precision. Among the 20 acceptable add-only changes, correct acceptance was 71.745% for pooling, 46.910% for Equal and 31.350% for stratified SRS. With no acceptable primary policy, truth-conditioned acceptance is undefined. Median per-policy gain remained zero at the two historical weights.

Implementation contract and constructed clinical query traces¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Implementation contract and constructed clinical query traces

Same-target execution contract and implementation costs

The three timed engines return the same aggregate quantities under the same fixed rule, supplied laws and recorded states. The preceding index and run index share the four count boundaries, numerical range-sum machinery, positive-mass filtering and exact-law-class reduction. Run aggregation changes only the reference rows at which those quantities are evaluated. It preserves heterogeneous group laws and does not supply a new interval-coverage or population-law guarantee. The direct evaluator recomputes the same state predicates at positive-mass count pairs; it is our reference implementation, not a timing of Koch--Hothorn software [6].

Let $N=n_0+1$, let $\mathcal T$ contain every distinct denominator/tolerance type prepared, and let $\mathcal T_e$ contain the eligible types. Write $L_t=n_t+1$, $E=\sum_{d\in\mathcal D}(d+1)$ for the distinct-denominator endpoint payload, and $C_{\rm CP}$ for endpoint-generation cost. The frozen implementation uses compiled binary searches, giving setup cost \[ O\!\left(C_{\rm CP}+N\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\log(L_t+1) +N|\mathcal T_e|+G\right). \] The last reference scan constructs the run partition. The linear two-pointer argument establishes an alternative boundary cost $O(\sum_tL_t+N|\mathcal T|)$; it is not the binary-search implementation timed here. Ineligible types are omitted from the run union but their endpoint/boundary arrays are still prepared. The preceding index omits the run-partition scan. Direct preparation constructs endpoints and metadata in $O(C_{\rm CP}+G)$ time with $O(E+G)$ persistent storage.

For query $q$, let $U_q$ denote identical rule/PMF classes, with support lengths $L_c$ and memberships $m_c$; let $K_q$ count positive-mass runs, and $M_{0q}$ count positive-mass reference rows. Let $F_{qc}$ count range requests invoking the positive-sum tree and $V_q=\sum_c m_c\log(m_c+1)$ account for duplicate-index checks. Excluding separately reported PMF generation, run integration costs \[ O\!\left(N+\sum_cL_c+V_q+U_qK_q+ \sum_c F_{qc}\log(L_c+1)\right). \] Full-support validation, cumulative construction and any lazy tree construction are included. On the ordinary cumulative path $F_{qc}=0$. The preceding index replaces $K_q$ by $M_{0q}$, with its own fallback count. If $M_{cq}$ is the positive support of class $c$, direct evaluation instead has pair work $O(\sum_c M_{0q}M_{cq})$. Singleton law classes give $V_q=O(G)$; in general $V_q=O(G\log(G+1))$. Grouping equal laws reduces computation, not the assumed independence of their count variables.

Prepared storage is $O(E+N|\mathcal T|+K+G)$. Streamed query peak is $O(E+N|\mathcal T|+N+K+G+\max_c L_c)$, excluding caller-retained inputs and runtime overhead; direct evaluation additionally uses bounded count-pair temporaries. Four dense boundary vectors per type remain stored. Reference aggregation creates a dense length-$N$ equivalent PMF, so the implementation does not have $O(K)$ memory. A caller retaining all group laws adds their total support storage. Full-support law generation remains necessary even when most supplied machine probabilities are zero. The preceding index omits the partition payload. Direct peak storage is instead $O(E+N+G+\max_c L_c+B_{\rm pair})$, where $B_{\rm pair}$ is its bounded pair-temporary payload; it has no dense boundary cache.

Reuse identity and provenance. An endpoint cache key includes denominator, interval construction and per-tail error allocation. A boundary key additionally identifies reference endpoints, tolerance and strict/inclusive machine predicates. The enclosing prepared object fixes those fields, the ordered family and eligibility; therefore its internal $(n,\delta)$ keys suffice. A reusable object is invalidated by changing family size (hence $\alpha/(G+1)$), reference, denominators, rule or eligibility. PMFs and recorded states may change without rebuilding. Binomial law classes use $(n,p,\delta,\mathrm{eligible})$; arbitrary-law classes require identical complete PMFs. Saved outputs additionally identify their law parameters, recorded states and engine hash. These are in-memory reuse rules, not a claim of a persistent automatic cache or of cache reuse throughout C2--C4.

Additional independent implementation check. A new Cartesian enumeration check covered 180 small rules and two changing arbitrary/sparse-law queries per rule. The direct, preceding-index and run-index outputs agreed with enumerated events within $1.12\times10^{-15}$, including unsupported counts, eligibility/minimum support, unequal supports, tolerance endpoints and all recorded states. The same 360 queries also verified a separate validation-only entry point. It rejects fractional/out-of-range class IDs and normalizes valid integer-valued recorded-state arrays before forwarding to the unchanged engine. Twelve input-boundary checks passed. Frozen source hashes match the original manifest; the validation entry point does not change the reported algorithm timings. These checks establish tested-input numerical agreement, not exhaustive correctness or a new inferential guarantee.

Frozen retrospective workload

We constructed an exploratory retrospective query trace from the released principal race/ethnicity counts, retaining every group. It crosses three FNR tolerances, a family-error change, and an FPR denominator change. Each configuration evaluates native empirical-binomial and Jeffreys-predictive laws followed by ten deterministic fitted-rate sensitivities; two queries revisit the first configuration. The 62-query cohort trace has five cache misses and 57 hits. These are hypothetical analyst queries, not measured clinical usage.

The complete trace used the unchanged engines and matched output contract. Texas prior-index/run and direct/run total-cost ratios were 1.400 and 9.482; eICU prior-index/run and direct/run total-cost ratios were 1.748 and 6.607; MIMIC-III prior-index/run and direct/run total-cost ratios were 0.754 and 0.755. Run compression lost 13 of 45 paired configuration comparisons against the prior index; no universal gain is implied. All 27 workers completed, and matched outputs agreed within $4.0\times10^{-15}$ absolute error. Identical law-generation and endpoint routines have variable measured times on this shared host; the three repetitions support descriptive costs, not significance or a reliable crossover. Full prefix costs, physical run/support counts, peak memory and undefined break-even cases are retained in the artifact.

All queries use released aggregate counts. The five configurations cross FNR tolerances .05/.10/.15, the FNR family error level .10, and FPR at tolerance .10/error .05. Ten hypothetical log-odds shifts in $[-.5,.5]$ use rates $(k+.5)/(n+1)$; they are not fitted drift. Native EB/JP summaries include all five two-law prefixes: median run/index/direct costs were 1.220/1.885/6.297 seconds for Texas, .0807/.1396/.3147 for eICU and .1431/.1172/.1004 for MIMIC-III. Each includes five preparations and ten queries. These prefixes are derived from the same trace, not additional independent timing trials.

The final 27 workers had no censored query. Peak resident memory medians (run/index/direct, MiB) were 142.1/141.1/197.1 for Texas, 98.4/99.2/123.5 for eICU and 97.6/97.0/96.7 for MIMIC-III. Total runs across configurations ranged 41,179--54,463, 693--8,338 and 261--2,289, respectively; strictly positive-mass runs ranged 3,442--12,129, 401--3,425 and 261--1,883. Thus the clinical trace does not rely on the synthetic test's three boundary types. Fourteen of 45 paired configuration comparisons had no positive mean query saving, making their stationary-mean break-even estimate undefined. Observed prefixes, extrapolated estimates and all losses are retained separately.

The host was shared. Preparation uses identical endpoint/boundary code and law generation uses identical arguments in all engines; observed differences in these common phases cannot be credited to run aggregation. Rotating engine order and retaining three repetitions describe variation rather than establish a significance test. Component medians need not sum to the median total. The first frozen attempt stopped because raw SciPy beta-binomial masses exceeded the engine's normalization tolerance. Its errors remain archived. The complete trace was refrozen and rerun using the existing clinical helper's full-support normalization for all engines, timed within law generation. Independently regenerated raw mass sums differed from one by at most $1.87\times10^{-10}$.

A separate check reproduced 100 released FNR/FPR counts, observed states and empirical-binomial outputs within $1.55\times10^{-15}$. The trace verifier checks 1,488 matched outputs, cache identities, count conservation, phase totals, statuses and manifest hashes. This aggregate replay does not reconstruct patients or establish production query frequencies.

Supporting historical and sensitivity detail

For all-inconclusive recorded families, let $M$ count repeated conclusive comparisons. Then $Gc_{\rm mean}-r_{\rm any}=E[(M-1)_+]$. The excesses in percentage points are $.0000482224/.0187131$ for eICU EB/JP and $.0000153158/.0121170$ for MIMIC EB/JP; retained bootstrap counts have zero excess. Both quantities describe the same predominantly inconclusive repeats.

Direct integration won 13/18 historical imbalance designs. Across seven completed imbalanced cold pairs, the median prior-index/direct preparation-plus-evaluation ratio was 1.51. Censored phases supply no speedup ratio.

Historical resource tests cross reference counts $10^3$--$10^6$, 3/10/40 groups and balanced/imbalanced support. Blocked-direct temporaries are capped at 64 MiB; four separate wide cases use 100/1,000 groups and reference 1,000. Estimated allocations above 768 MiB are excluded; original/follow-up caps are 12/30 seconds. Phase costs and memory are retained. One-thread timings use an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX, Windows 11, Python 3.11.9, NumPy 2.4.2 and SciPy 1.15.3. Timeouts supply no speedup ratio.

Binomial-normal sensitivity fixes observed denominators and models male/female logits as $\beta_m+a_h-d_h/2$ and $\beta_f+a_h+d_h/2$, with independent Gaussian hospital effects. Using adaptive quadrature for binomial-normal models [18], we profile the contrast variance $\operatorname{Var}(d_h)$. Log-odds and rate-gap variances differ; asymptotic intervals and fitted-model simulations do not supply distribution-free hospital inference.

Exploratory replays shifted 25%/50% of confirmation spending to pilots at fixed total cost, using three conditional simulations per record/fraction. Target attainment was supported in 262/480 and 319/480 simulations, and 235/438 and 292/438 within originally unresolved records. No supported classification was wrong. Texas mean correct resolution nevertheless fell from 34.92% to 27.22% between fractions as confirmation evidence decreased. Correlated replays do not validate universal pilot fractions. Coverage averages over original-plus-extension sampling, not conditional on a fixed original pilot.

Historical comparisons distinguish the source of improvement: pooling increased correct rejection from Equal's 71.16% to 80.08% at matched costs, and from 61.69% on identical stratified-SRS records. The latter gain removes an unnecessary error-budget split; median per-policy gain remained zero. All 54 primary policies failed, with 12 mixed-direction policies retaining stratification. At $w=.25$, the current pooled/equal Gaussian comparison correctly rejected 97.22/92.18% with no wrong acceptance, versus Gaussian PPI 95.60% and 1.43% wrong acceptance. Results at different weights concern different policy criteria.

Age reweighing improved mean selection parity by .505 across 31 Texas hospitals/three seeds, but AUROC fell .749 to .679 and sensitivity .830 to .781. Every seed failed the alert screen; two original eICU contrasts passed the .05 utility rule but violated the constraint of zero additional subgroup false positives.

Additional protocol and sensitivity details¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Additional protocol and sensitivity details

C1 secondary pass/fail error-allocation derivation Error-allocation sensitivity uses rate-tail probabilities $\alpha/(2G)$ for pass and $\alpha/(4G)$ for fail. Outside tolerance, false passes cost at most two pass-tail errors; inside tolerance, false failures cost at most four fail-tail errors. Each is bounded by $\alpha/G$; a union bound controls wrong assertions without contrast independence. Nested bands preclude simultaneous pass/fail. This variation expands pass but contracts fail regions, without uniformly improving conclusiveness; recorded states are recomputed.

C2 sufficient-guard derivation and unevaluated time-growth horizon For sampling variance $c/n$, retained variance $v_P$ and accepted mean's nearest-boundary margin $m>0$, the sufficient guard is $m\geq z\sqrt{c/n+v_P}$, $z=\Phi^{-1}(1-\beta/J)$ for $J$ finite boundaries ($J=2$ for the clinical symmetric tolerance). With $c>0$, it gives $n\geq\max\{1,\lceil c/[(m/z)^2-v_P]\rceil\}$ if the denominator is positive, otherwise no finite sufficient count. With $c=0$, test $m\geq z\sqrt{v_P}$. Fixed growth $v(t)=v_{\rm init}+qt$, $q>0$, gives pointwise horizon $[(m/z)^2-v_{\rm init}]/q$; a negative horizon excludes nonnegative times.

C3 allocation recurrence details Total cost is $\sum_{g=0}^G(m_g+a_g)+B$, including pilots, minimum confirmations $a_g$ and extra budget $B$. main Algorithm 2 enumerates reference increments, using additive prefix optimization over feasible $E_g$ for the grid optimum. On a batch-$h$ grid it takes $O(G(B/h)^3)$ transitions plus utility construction. Empty maxima are $-\infty$; infeasible budgets return no allocation.

Predictor architecture and tuning details Tuning average precision selected depth-six XGBoost from $\{3,6\}$, with 1,000/377/142 trees for Texas/eICU/MIMIC. Comparators are logistic regression and ICU two-layer MLP, two-block residual and two-block/four-head attention networks. Separate calibration selects the highest threshold reaching 80% sensitivity. All 12 seed-11 fits remain; XGBoost adds seeds 29/47. Principal FNR families retain four/six/40 comparisons, including missing identities/zero outcomes; wider families have 57/66/153 cells. The .10 tolerance and 80% sensitivity fix common research operating points, not clinically endorsed cutoffs; .05/.15 tolerances test sensitivity. Family error is .05, with 500 predictive and 9,999 principal-audit hospital/component/patient resamples.

Secondary native-target adapter details We also execute VFR's original seven-metric calculator, bootstrap and size diagnostics [16], and Yan--Zhang's active-auditing algorithm with exact finite-class oracles on its native sex-demographic-parity target [17]. Its known candidate class must contain the target predictor. Frozen-fit site diagnostics adapt the author notebook's hospital retraining; active auditing omits the released linear surrogate. A separate diameter-minimizing allocation adapts its objective to C3 without transferring native guarantees. UM predictive-target diagnostics used 100 independent same-group-size future confusion tables per retained clinical audit, generated from empirical within-group laws.

Historical 18-policy comparison protocol The original 18 correlated contrasts compare equal/proportional disagreement allocation, disagreement SRS and whole-cohort SRS at matched costs. Full-frame outcomes assess correct acceptance/rejection/deferral; synthetic controls test acceptable changes, added misses, concentrated false alerts and utility equality.

Fresh C4 adapter explanation Fresh review retains all 42 eligible policies, half-disagreement budgets, 1,000 randomizations and three weights. Gaussian finite-population PPI [19] combines the frozen full-frame score mean with reviewed outcome residuals and the published Gaussian standard error, sharing SRS records with exact methods. Equal allocation with Gaussian stratified intervals uses design-weighted totals and variance on the Equal samples; ``Equal--Neyman'' in the archived outputs denotes this interval construction, not Neyman allocation. Both Gaussian adapters are asymptotic; unsupported variances and empty integer intervals defer. The native PPI quantile-call repair is documented. The original PPI framework also provides nonasymptotic bounded-residual finite-population inference [19], which that historical comparison did not evaluate. Section S37 reports the matched extension.

Historical cold timing comparison Direct integration won 13/18 historical imbalance designs; the median cold prior-index/direct ratio was 1.51 across seven completed pairs.

Matched-rule results The inference comparison asks which assertions the rules support on identical audits; it does not test computational reuse. Across 8,000 synthetic audits, the C--C support-one adapter correctly resolved 24.388% of comparisons versus UAF's 12.275%, with family wrong-assertion frequencies .550% and zero (the main comparison of matched inference rules). The frozen support-20 adapter resolved 24.654% with .5625% family error; UM resolved 13.771% with .0125% family error on this population-gap diagnostic. C--C therefore resolved 1.99$\times$ as many comparisons at support one and 2.01$\times$ at support 20, with observed family error below the nominal 5% level. UAF/C--C compare population-gap decisions; UM's native target is a future gap, assessed separately below.

C3 secondary rule/grid completion and oracle-ceiling detail Across all 160 records, the split pass/fail rule raised Texas DP correct resolution from 17.67% to 18.59%: .79 points came from changing the rule at fixed allocations and .13 from replanning. eICU declined from 31.65% to 31.51%; MIMIC-III remained 39.95%. Rule changes did not yield uniform gains. Both rules completed all 160 cases on 50-/25-record grids with five policies. Finest-grid terminal capacities let the unavailable-total oracle attain .10 true mean conclusiveness in 40/40 Texas $B=250$ cases; the oracle ceiling therefore depends on the allocation grid.

C3 forecast interpretation Among 160 pilot--budget records from 120 pilots, bounds supported the 10% mean-conclusiveness target as met in nine, not met in five and unresolved in 146. Unresolved bounds span the target without implying incorrect confirmation. Full-frame truth classified 111 of those 146 allocations as meeting the target and 35 below it; these planner-unavailable totals cannot certify forecasts. All exact expectations were enclosed. Texas point forecasts over-/underestimated by 12.79/12.74 points at costs 2,223/2,878. Separately, no correct-resolution gain over balancing was certified. Mortality minima already resolved comparisons; target attainment does not establish incremental value.

C3 secondary unrestricted-null exact-gap rates At the same 160 primary-selected allocations, unrestricted-null exact gap tests changed Texas correct resolution from 29.03/41.64% to 33.45/43.20% at $B=2{,}000$ and pilot caps 20/200. eICU fell from 26.08/37.23% to 22.33/31.51%; MIMIC-III changed from 39.89/40.00% to 39.14/40.00%. Maximum per-pilot family error was .224%. Separate reoptimization on 30 preselected $B=250$ pilots showed no correct-resolution advantage over balancing. Exact tests therefore change the rule's trade-offs without establishing a universally better collection strategy.

C2 cell-variance formula; target and validation assumptions retained Clinical sex-FNR sensitivity estimates only hospital/sampling components, using stabilized variance $\sum_s\widetilde p_s(1-\widetilde p_s)/n_s$, $\widetilde p_s=(k_s+1/2)/(n_s+1)$. The hypothetical target $Y_n=\mu+H+\varepsilon_n$ has variances $v_H$ and $c/n$ for $n$ positives/sex. Hospital-pairs/two-stage resampling gives sensitivity ranges. Separate confidence-projection validation assumes balanced additive Gaussian sampling, independent effects, homogeneous residuals, no interactions and one-boundary risk. It excludes the unbalanced clinical fit; unsupported fits return no report.

Secondary tolerance-specific audit rates and repeated rule interpretation Across all 276 contrasts, the split pass/fail rule changed three observed failures to inconclusive and created no new passes. At fixed denominators, EB mean conclusiveness increased in 13 families, decreased in 19 and was unchanged in seven; JP counts were 12/20/seven. Texas EB rose from 59.37% to 60.88%, whereas eICU fell from .0602% to .0294%. Reallocating error changes attainable conclusions at the same family bound. Texas EB mean conclusiveness at tolerances .05/.15 was 50.13/89.09%, with observed P/I/F counts 1/2/1 and 4/0/0.

Native VFR example Native VFR replay produced both outcomes in 29/91 cells, and nine distinguished minority frequency from recorded reversal, including Texas race equal opportunity (.104 versus .896). C1 instead targets change from the recorded state, including inconclusiveness.

Source-result target and guard qualifications combined C2's historical seed-11 sex-FNR analysis targets binary Gaussian risk for one random supported hospital, rather than C1's three-state race/ethnicity audit. At the mean stabilized cell variance, hospital variation accounted for 65.29%/2.59% of Texas/eICU conditional incremental risk (the main source-component analysis). These shares are neither causal contributions nor averages of hospital-specific risks. The fitted sufficient guard was 621 positives/sex for eICU's nine hospitals and nonfinite for Texas. Neither supplies a minimum or recruitment advice: eICU's exact two-tail risk was .032978 at $n=500$, and nonfiniteness does not prove exact-risk impossibility.

C4 criterion comparison C4 tests one fixed policy criterion: no net subgroup miss increase and positive detection--alert utility. All 42 eligible single-direction mortality-policy changes fail it at the primary weight $w=.1$. Their known direction permits exact pooling; mixed-direction changes retain stratification. At matched half-disagreement review counts, exact pooling correctly rejected 79.95% versus 75.49% for equal allocation with Gaussian stratified intervals, a 4.46-point difference [4.16,4.76] (1.06$\times$), with wrong acceptance .095% versus .033% (2.86$\times$). Gaussian finite-population PPI reached 80.11%, differing by .16 points $[-.03,.35]$ from pooling, but wrongly accepted 1.49% (15.68$\times$ pooling). Pooling improved rejection over the equal-allocation Gaussian comparator without dominating every error measure; that contrast changes acquisition, whereas the SRS rows share records.

C4 Gaussian failure qualification The Gaussian PPI adapter wrongly accepted 45.3% in one removal policy with 20 disagreements and ten reviews. This retained sparse-frame failure concerns the evaluated Gaussian approximation, not all prediction-powered inference procedures; nonasymptotic bounded-residual alternatives were outside this historical comparison; Section S37 adds the matched betting construction [19]. At $w=.05$, correct acceptance among 20 acceptable policies was 71.28%/66.49%/55.28% for exact pooling/Gaussian PPI/equal Gaussian.

Controlled paired integration on native clinical laws¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Controlled paired integration on native clinical laws

This follow-up isolates integration from the common preparation and probability-generation costs in Section S33. It retains all 30 native queries (three cohorts, five configurations and EB/Jeffreys laws), including unsupported groups. One identical prepared object and identical full-support normalized PMF arrays are supplied to all three unchanged engines. One warmup per case and engine precedes 20 paired repetitions, giving 90 warmups and 1,800 timed calls. Query order and the within-case method permutation are randomized using seed 2026110403 before timing. All calls are serial in one fresh, single-thread worker. Inputs, source hashes and the schedule are frozen before measurement; rule/law hashes agree before and after all calls. Warmups are retained separately; no timed observation is discarded.

Complete integration calls include probability validation, mass indexing, run aggregation where used, shared-reference combination and aggregate output construction. Preparation, external law generation, verification and logging are outside the timer. The worker completed within the fixed 480-second and 768-MiB caps; total wall time was 108 seconds. Host CPU and memory observations accompany every block. These warmed, shared-host kernels are not a replacement for the cold end-to-end experiment.

Median paired index/run ratios were 1.025 [1.005,1.060], 1.204 [1.095,1.258] and 1.046 [.952,1.129] (interquartile ranges) for Texas, eICU and MIMIC-III. The run engine lost 5/20, 3/20 and 7/20 cohort repetitions, respectively. Median direct/run ratios were 45.352, 8.044 and 1.145. Ratios are computed within each repetition before summarizing; they need not equal ratios of the separately summarized times. Across all calls, the largest output discrepancy was $2.665\times10^{-15}$. All source, schedule, input-integrity and probability-conservation checks passed. The result supports modest, heterogeneous kernel improvements over the preceding index, not attribution of cold common-phase timing differences to run aggregation.

The complete protocol, warmup and timed observations, randomized schedule, host observations, per-case and per-cohort distributions, and verification receipt are retained in \nolinkurl{icde_clinical_kernel_pairing_20261104}. The earlier complete traces and their failures remain unchanged.

Current grid, guard and reproduction evidence¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Current grid, guard and reproduction evidence

This reporting reconciliation uses the frozen studies already described in Sections S28 and S6.2. It introduces no allocation experiment, inference rule, model fit or clinical cohort. The portable helper \nolinkurl{review/submission_revision_20261105/evidence/reconstruct_evidence.py} checks 1,126 input hashes and reconstructs the current tables from saved outcomes; the preceding historical results remain unchanged.

Both rules and all grids. Table S93 reports all 18 cohort/rule/grid summaries. Primary uses equal-tailed category intervals with error $.05/(G+1)$. Split uses category error $.05/G$ for passing and $.05/(2G)$ for failing; it changes the directional assertion regions while retaining the family wrong-assertion bound, and is not a uniformly narrower gap interval. Section S28 retains the derivation, all five policies and fixed-allocation versus reoptimization attribution. DP maximizes predictive total resolution, and the unavailable-total oracle maximizes true-law total resolution; the reported evaluation is correct resolution.

All 640 requested 50/25-grid records completed. The finest grid completed 240/320 records across both rules. Its exact exclusions are the same 40 Texas $B=2{,}000$ records per rule: predicted allocation-pair counts of 958,120--994,023 exceed the frozen 250,000 cap. These 80 requests were not attempted, not timed out or assigned outcome zero. The 40 completed Texas finest-grid records per rule all have $B=250$. Consequently, their 19.788% primary and 20.619% split DP means must not be compared as matched estimates against the 80-record Texas 50/25 means, which pool two budgets. On the same 40 small-budget records under the primary rule, the .10 mean-conclusiveness target is attained in 39/40 DP and 40/40 oracle cases on the finest grid versus 0/40 for both policies on either coarser grid. This is full-frame attainment, not pilot-supported certification.

Guard instability beside the fitted-count illustration. The sufficient 621-positive-outcomes-per-sex illustration remains conditional on the fitted hospital model. Table S19 reports the separate 1,800 binomial-cell stress draws. Against a nonfinite Gaussian benchmark guard, fitted guards were finite in 122/300 (40.67%) nine-hospital and 55/300 (18.33%) 58-hospital repetitions. For finite benchmark guards, the fractions of finite proposals satisfying the benchmark were 145/234 (61.97%), 85/201 (42.29%), 184/244 (75.41%) and 117/203 (57.64%). Thus a finite fitted count does not itself establish sufficient evidence. These frequencies concern a Gaussian sufficient guard, not patient harm, exact clinical-risk failure or calibrated recruitment advice. The reconstruction verifies the saved draw-level classifications and benchmark formulas; it does not rerun fitting.

Computation and fresh-environment scope. The main combined workload table draws on Sections S25, S32, S33 and S35. Full-computation costs include preparation, law generation and integration; warmed paired costs include integration only. The synthetic ten-query ratio 18.49, clinical full-computation ratios 1.40/1.75/.75 and warmed paired ratios 1.025/1.204/1.046 therefore describe distinct workloads. All losses and censored workers remain reported, and common-phase timing variation is not attributed to boundary-run aggregation.

Five checks passed in a newly created Python 3.11.9 virtual environment on the same Windows host, with system site packages disabled and pinned NumPy 2.4.2, SciPy 1.15.3 and pandas 2.3.3 installed from PyPI wheels. They cover 360 independent Cartesian C1 queries, 12 input-contract cases, the saved 126-worker scaling grid, the C4 aggregate reconstruction of 630,000 decisions and 210,000 intervals, and the current revision evidence reconstruction. All 11 regenerated revision CSV/LaTeX files match their earlier hashes byte for byte. Commands, requirements, logs and the receipt \nolinkurl{FRESH_ENVIRONMENT_VERIFICATION.json} are under \nolinkurl{review/submission_revision_20261105/repro}; the evidence helper remains under the adjacent \nolinkurl{evidence} directory.

This fresh package installation establishes the stated aggregate and small computational replay on the existing host/base interpreter, not reproduction on independent hardware or in a separate operating system. The historical notebook was not rerun in that environment. Its ten appended reporting cells, including five code cells, were executed separately, preserving all 366 preceding cells and outputs. The fresh-environment replay did not rerun experimental timings, train models, extract credentialed ICU data or independently validate clinical outcomes. The next subsection reports a separate new timing experiment. The access and reconstruction limits in Sections S11 and S20 remain; no public repository, DOI or deposit is claimed.

Declared analysis workload and matched small-budget grid comparison

The existing complete-inventory analysis in Section S16, implemented by \nolinkurl{icde_reporting_20261102/build_reporting.py}, supplies a natural sequence: 39 cohort/attribute/metric families, three tolerances and native EB/JP laws, giving 117 preparations and 234 forecasts. Each fixed rule receives exactly two laws; no fitted-rate shifts, artificial revisits or deployment query frequencies are added. The law cache across tolerances follows that driver. We measured one fresh single-thread process per unchanged engine on the shared host, in Run/Index/Direct order, with 180-second worker and 1-GiB resident-memory caps. All three processes completed the full sequence.

Run did not improve the observed complete-workflow total against Index; 53/117 two-law configurations had higher total cost and 56/117 had higher integration cost. This single ordered pass does not estimate timing uncertainty or establish a robust performance difference. Every engine's 234 forecasts matched the frozen study within $3.45\times10^{-15}$; 468 matched cross-engine output comparisons agreed within $5.78\times10^{-15}$. Sequential global and per-cohort prefix costs retain only the actual queries and charge each preparation when first used. They describe this analysis order, not a forecast of usage frequency or an extrapolated reuse threshold. Raw observations, frozen source/input hashes and reconstruction are under \nolinkurl{review/submission_revision_20261105/natural_workload}.

These matched means isolate the grid change on the completed small-budget subset; they do not replace the separate 80-record Texas summaries. The 40 larger-budget finest-grid records remain uncomputed per rule. Input-only preflight counts 958,120--994,023 pair utilities and 679,104,711--707,157,604 DP transition entries per planner; a full record also requires the oracle and evaluation. No raised-cap attempt was made, so these work counts establish neither completion time nor impossibility.

Matched finite-sample prediction-powered review¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Matched finite-sample prediction-powered review

This exploratory extension completes the nonasymptotic comparison left open in the historical Gaussian-PPI sections. It preserves all 42 eligible single-direction policies, frozen predictions, half-disagreement review budgets, 1,000 original-seed SRS repetitions and weights .10/.05/.25. Every reconstructed sample has the same positive count and residual mean as the saved comparison. No patient records, sampled identifiers or individual scores are exported.

Published construction and implementation

Finite-population prediction-powered inference adds the known full-frame prediction mean to a confidence set for the reviewed residual mean [19]. We use Corollary S14 with the nonasymptotic bounded-variable construction in Proposition S3. Write $z_i=(y_i-f_i+1)/2\in[0,1]$, with the predictor fixed before review. For candidate positive total $K$, the transformed residual mean is $m_K=(K/N-\bar f+1)/2$. At review step $t$, the putative remaining mean is \[ \mu_t(m_K)=\frac{Nm_K-\sum_{j<t}z_j}{N-t+1}. \] Predictable bets follow the archived authors' wsr_swr implementation: the initial base bet is one; subsequent bets use the previous regularized running variance and the fixed review horizon. For each direction, bets are clipped to keep factors nonnegative. Candidate totals remain when neither directional capital process exceeds $2/\alpha$ at any observed prefix. Calculations use cumulative log factors to avoid product underflow or overflow. Putative means outside $[0,1]$ are impossible under that candidate and are excluded.

Positive-bet factors decrease with the candidate mean, while negative-bet factors increase. Thus each directional rejection region is monotone, permitting integer binary search rather than a coarse numerical mean grid. Search endpoints are intersected with the deterministic completion bounds $[k,k+N-n]$. Empty sets defer and count as noncoverage; census review returns the observed total. These are computational and integer-support adaptations of the published construction, not a new confidence theorem or a fitted PPI power parameter. The same fixed sampling design supports finite-population coverage without a Gaussian approximation.

Verification and matched results

Checks compare integer searches with exhaustive candidate enumeration, compare 180 log-space classifications with direct products, and enumerate all 1,680 ordered samples in each of nine eight-record finite populations. All candidate checks agree; the small-population coverages are one. These checks supplement the published guarantee and do not establish general correctness solely by simulation. Saved-state verification reconstructs 126,000 policy decisions across the three weights from 42,000 interval pairs.

Total-count inclusion is 98.050%; one empty interval among 42,000 reviews gives .0024% invalid intervals. At $w=.10$, exact pooling increases correct rejection by 2.8357 percentage points (conditional paired Monte Carlo interval [2.6655,3.0059]), but also increases wrong acceptance by .0810 points [.0539,.1080]. Uncertainty here describes repeated review of the fixed policies; the policies share patients and are not independent clinical samples. The paired standard error is calculated from within-policy variances before averaging the 42 fixed policies.

Among the 20 acceptable policies at $w=.05$, betting PPI correctly accepts 55.60%, compared with 71.28% for exact pooling, 66.49% for Gaussian PPI and 55.28% for equal-allocation Gaussian inference. In the small removal policy with 20 disagreements and ten reviews, betting PPI correctly rejects 50.3% with no wrong acceptance, whereas the earlier Gaussian adapter wrongly accepted 45.3%. This resolves the earlier missing-baseline comparison without supporting a blanket claim against prediction-powered inference. The exact pooling and betting constructions trade decision frequency against realized error under the same valid fixed-frame target.

Reproduction and scope

The protocol, source, tests, aggregate intervals/states, per-policy outputs and paired comparison are in \nolinkurl{canonical_assets/icde_nonasymptotic_ppi_20261106}. The protocol was fixed before these outputs were inspected. A first invocation stopped at a relocated archive path before reading private predictions; the path was resolved from the frozen provenance manifest without changing the archived algorithm or samples. Source checks retain the original PPI repository and license. The notebook supplies a portable aggregate verification cell; regenerating review residuals requires authorized access to the unchanged frozen predictions. This extension supplies neither independent clinical confirmation, new utility preferences nor a comparison of every possible PPI variant.

The local release also includes recovered ICU extraction, landmark and model-preprocessing sources under \nolinkurl{review/revision_20261106/icu_source_recovery}. Their existing synthetic self-tests passed for eICU cohort logic, MIMIC landmark construction and model split/preprocessing rules. Source hashes and logs identify the recovered versions. Neither credentialed extraction nor training was rerun, and correspondence to every historical fitted checkpoint has not been established; these files therefore improve source availability without establishing end-to-end ICU reproduction.

Repeated timing of the declared workflow

We repeated the unchanged 234-query workflow five times, using a fresh process for each engine and a frozen randomized engine order within each repetition. Processes ran serially on the same shared host; the analysis adds no count laws or artificial revisits. Every engine completed all five repetitions. All 3,510 forecasts agreed with their frozen values within $3.45\times10^{-15}$.

Run totals ranged from 13.290 to 26.273 seconds, Index from 13.999 to 24.116 and Direct from 73.236 to 109.502. Run was slower than Index in four of five paired repetitions. These shared-host measurements confirm that the synthetic high-reuse gain does not establish a consistent gain in this two-law workflow; the broad time ranges also prevent treating the median ratio as a portable hardware constant. Preparation, law generation and integration are included, while startup, checking and file writes remain outside the timed sum. Raw phase times, source/input hashes, scheduling protocol and verification are under \nolinkurl{review/revision_20261106/workflow_repeats}. The original single-pass results remain in Table S94.
