Additional protocol and sensitivity detail retained from the main narrative¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Additional protocol and sensitivity detail retained from the main narrative

The following details accompany the condensed main results. They retain the original evaluations and are not additional experiments.

C1 validation includes 400 enumeration cases, 140 adversarial profiles and 24 original timing designs; Monte Carlo uses 78 configurations, five seeds and 1,000/100,000 draws. The inventory covers 39 FNR/FPR/selection families, 276 contrasts and three tolerances, yielding 117 feasibility configurations and 234 empirical-binomial (EB)/Jeffreys-predictive (JP) forecasts. Split-rule sensitivity covers all families at .10, separating the effects of the verdict rule from numerical integration accuracy.

Clinical traces retain principal race/ethnicity groups across five configurations varying FNR tolerance (.05/.10/.15), family error (.05/.10) or FPR denominators. EB, JP and ten smoothed-rate log-odds shifts from $-.5$ to $.5$, with two revisits, yield 62 queries, five preparations and 57 cache hits per cohort. Three fresh-process repetitions rotate engines on identical normalized full-support laws. Computation-only tests fix rules and native EB/JP masses for 30 cases, checking hashes across one warmup and 20 randomized paired repetitions. Phase timings separate preparation and integration.

The 640-record factorial varies disparity, reference rate, imbalance and pilot/confirmation fractions at matched costs and grids. Clinical controls are pilot-only, minimum-review and balancing. To isolate the decision rule, all 160 DP/balancing pairs also test an unrestricted-null exact gap rule; five-policy reoptimization uses the first five replicates in six $B=250$ strata. Historical corrections, including our adaptation of isotonic classifier calibration [15], remain diagnostic. Oversized projections use conservative envelopes, tested at increased limits for 15 complexity-selected pairs with unchanged targets to separate numerical limits from unsupported forecasts.

Across workloads, both indexes completed 40/42 workers versus 30/42 for direct integration; all 931 shared outputs agreed within $5.11\times10^{-15}$. Median completed ten-query cost ratios favored reuse by 1.37 against the preceding index and 9.50 against direct integration, but reuse lost four of 20 indexed comparisons, costing up to 1.21$\times$ more. At $G=40,n_0=10^4$, the preceding index won at support ratios .3 and 1; both indexes completed balanced $10^5$ counts but only one query at $10^6$ before timeout. Reference size alone does not ensure faster computation.

Reuse savings weakened in clinical workloads. Constructed traces had total-cost ratios (preceding index/run) of 1.40, 1.75 and .75 for Texas, eICU and MIMIC-III, with 13/45 losses. Paired integration calls on identical prepared inputs excluded preparation and law generation: ratios were 1.025, 1.204 and 1.046, with losses in 5/20, 3/20 and 7/20 repetitions; all 1,800 calls agreed within $2.67\times10^{-15}$. The actual analysis requires 234 queries across 39 families, three tolerances and two laws, with 117 preparations. The main computation table retains the original cold pass (468 matched outputs within $5.78\times10^{-15}$) and five further repetitions with randomized engine order. Run aggregation was slower than the preceding index in four of five repetitions, providing no consistent two-law workflow advantage.

Across 276 contrasts, the split pass/fail rule changed three failures to inconclusive and added no passes. EB conclusiveness increased/decreased/stayed unchanged in 13/19/seven families; JP counts were 12/20/seven. Texas EB rose from 59.37% to 60.88%, while eICU fell from .0602% to .0294%. Error allocation therefore changes the supported states without uniformly increasing resolution.

Reducing C--C's minimum support from 20 to one changed 185/54,000 cell states, with no Texas changes. Audits, other safeguards and seeds were retained. MIMIC size-$N$ resolution rose .075% to .450%; eICU half-budget resolution fell .083% to zero while family error rose zero to 1%. The calibration-family change therefore did not improve decisions uniformly.

In the VFR replay, 29/91 cells produced both binary outcomes; nine showed that minority frequency differs from recorded-verdict reversal probability.

The finest Texas grid completed 40 small-budget records; 40 larger budgets exceeded the pair cap. It attained the .10 target in 39/40 DP and 40/40 oracle cases versus 0/40 on coarser grids. Split pass/fail allocation had a smaller effect, raising Texas DP correctness from 17.67% to 18.59% (.79 points from the rule, .13 from replanning), reducing eICU from 31.65% to 31.51% and leaving MIMIC at 39.95%. Some nonresolution was grid-imposed, but attainment calculated from complete totals does not certify the pilot forecast.

Forecast accuracy depended on the pilot/confirmation split. Texas forecasts overestimated by 12.79 points at cost 2,223 and underestimated by 12.74 at 2,878. Exploratory fixed-cost replays diverted 25%/50% of confirmation spending to pilots, supporting more decisions but lowering Texas mean correct resolution from 34.92% to 27.22%. Coverage averages over original-plus-extension sampling; these correlated replays do not identify a universal pilot fraction.

Paired projection certified gains over minimum review in 42 records at 250 extra verifications, at most .03165 points, but none over balancing. Increased limits allowed exact projection for ten of 15 complexity-selected pairs; all spanned zero, while five retained conservative bounds. The safeguard still selected balancing.

Unrestricted-null exact gap tests improved Texas correct resolution but reduced eICU and some MIMIC outcomes at fixed allocations; maximum per-pilot family error was .224%. Reoptimizing 30 preselected $B=250$ pilots still showed no advantage over balancing.

We vary error allocation to assess how the rule limits resolution. The sensitivity uses rate-tail probabilities $\alpha/(2G)$ for pass and $\alpha/(4G)$ for fail. False passes and failures involve at most two and four tails, respectively, so a union bound controls family wrong assertions at $\alpha$ without independent contrasts. Nested bands prevent simultaneous pass and fail, but expanding the pass region contracts the fail region. Recorded states are therefore recomputed; conclusiveness need not increase.

Current workload and decision diagnostics¶

Scientific protocol, derivation and interpretation

Current workload and decision diagnostics

Code and the local verification package are available from the authors on request. Public code release is planned after acceptance; no public deposit is currently claimed. Credentialed source data remain subject to their access terms.

This section reconciles saved outputs for the same frozen workloads, policies, weights and budgets. It introduces no new clinical samples or independent validation. The executable checks and their source hashes are in icde_reuse_diagnostics_20261106 and icde_decision_diagnostics_20261106. A separate verifier reconstructed the numerical summaries below.

Why reference-run reuse did not accelerate the clinical workflow

For a query, let $M_0$ count reference positions with positive mass and $K_q$ count constant-boundary runs intersecting that mass. In 126 of 234 queries, $M_0=K_q$, so run aggregation removed no positive-mass reference positions. The median ratio $M_0/K_q$ was 1.0 and the maximum was 2.1198. Across queries, $\sum_qG_qM_{0q}=4{,}941{,}570$ and $\sum_qG_qK_q=4{,}369{,}733$, a reduction of 11.572%. These are nominal conditional-row counts, including constant unsupported groups, rather than a measured runtime model. Median preparation share was 83.338% across the five within-repeat run-engine fractions; it is not the ratio of phase medians.

The 117 preparations served two laws each. Median complete-workflow time was 15.2194 seconds for the run engine and 14.2553 for the uncompressed index; the run engine lost four of five repetitions. In the favorable million-reference synthetic design, the first query already cost 2.9419 versus 14.8539 seconds including preparation. Boundary geometry, as well as reuse count, therefore determines the computational benefit. The complete 21-design runtime/memory/status grid and 234-query structural inventory are retained as machine-readable tables. They do not establish speedups for an unobserved hospital workload.

Policy decisions by direction and declared truth

The same 42 policies comprise 20 addition-only and 22 removal-only changes. Each receives 1,000 repeated reviews at $\lceil D/2\rceil$ verified disagreements. Additions require a mean 992.20 reviews per decision (range 33--2,989); removals require 542.27 (10--1,665). One complete panel charges 31,774 verifications across 63,527 policy-specific disagreement records. Policies share patients, so neither total counts distinct patients. Frame construction, prediction linkage and staff time remain unpriced.

Table S98 reports all six methods, directions and three weights. Correct means acceptance of an acceptable policy or rejection of an unacceptable policy under the declared criterion; wrong means the opposite assertion. At $w=.1$, pooled correct rejection was 61.150% for additions versus 61.985% for Equal Gaussian inference, and 97.036% for removals versus 87.759%. The overall pooled advantage over Equal inference was consequently confined to removals. Saved pooled and betting-PPI removal states matched individually at all three weights, which is an observed equality rather than a universal equivalence claim.

At the primary weight, pooling produced 33,578 correct rejections, 40 wrong acceptances and 8,382 deferrals out of 42,000 state evaluations. Betting PPI produced 32,387, six and 9,607, respectively. Its comparison with pooling therefore trades 1,191 additional correct rejections against 34 additional wrong acceptances. Conditional paired 95% Monte Carlo intervals for these differences are [2.6655,3.0059] and [.0539,.1080] percentage points. The pooled-versus-Equal interval [4.16,4.76] uses separate acquisition streams at matched cost. These intervals measure repeated-review precision for fixed policies, not uncertainty about new hospitals or clinical benefit.

At $w=.05$, all 20 additions become acceptable and all removals remain unacceptable. There are no acceptable removals or acceptable policies at $w=.1$ or $.25$. Performance in those absent truth strata is unestimated, not zero. The released table explicitly records their zero denominators and undefined rates. A criterion-met decision can support further governance review; a not-met decision supports withholding that candidate; an unresolved decision supports neither assertion and defers adoption. These actions concern the declared research criterion, whose preferences have not been clinically validated.

Acceptance barrier for removal policies. The equal-tail exact pooled interval uses $\alpha=.05$. For an actually acceptable removal, $K=0$ and every reviewed outcome is negative. Candidate total $K=1$ nevertheless remains feasible whenever $\Pr(X=0\mid K=1)=(D-n)/D\geq.025$, preventing the required upper bound $U=0$. Excluding it requires strictly more than 97.5% review under the frozen boundary convention. An analytical check of the frozen functions covered all 42 original frame sizes ($D=20$--5,977), all 31,816 possible observed-positive counts at those half-frame budgets and weights .05/.10/.25. At $n=\lceil D/2\rceil$, zero observed positives always deferred a hypothetical acceptable removal, whereas any observed positive rejected it. The $D=1$ census exception correctly accepted zero positives. This is a structural power limitation of the criterion and review budget, not an additional clinical policy result or a coverage failure. The reproducible check is check_removal_barrier.py in the decision-diagnostics directory.

Separating grid, forecast target and comparative gain

The primary 160 pilot--budget records derive from 120 pilots: 40 Texas pilots each support two budgets, while each ICU cohort contributes 40 pilots. The target-forecast decisions remain nine met, five not met and 146 unresolved. Of the unresolved records, complete totals attain the target in 111 and do not in 35. Target attainment is mean conclusiveness, not a fairness pass or a gain over balancing.

The original paired safeguard has 71 identical allocation pairs with exact zero gain and 89 nonidentical pairs evaluated with conservative computational bounds. The 146 unresolved target forecasts consist of 62 identities and 84 nonidentical pairs; the nine met targets occur among identities and the five not-met targets among nonidentical pairs. Per-plan target projection separately uses 80 exact mortality calculations and 80 conservative Texas envelopes. These different denominators and computations must not be interchanged. The existing complexity-selected follow-up completed exact paired projection for ten of 15 distinct plans, none certifying a gain, while five remained capped. All 640 synthetic paired projections were exact and selected balancing.

Table S99 isolates grid effects on the identical 40 Texas $B=250$ records. Its oracle optimizes total conclusiveness and is unavailable to the auditor; it is not a ceiling on correct resolution. The finest grid attains the true .10 mean-conclusiveness target in 39/40 DP and 40/40 oracle cases, versus none on either coarser grid. These complete-total evaluations are not pilot certificates. Forty larger-budget Texas cases per rule were excluded by preflight estimates of 958,120--994,023 allocation pairs, exceeding the fixed 250,000 cap; they were not run and must not be counted as timeouts or zero gains.

The safeguard can retain a simpler allocation when a pilot cannot support switching, but its unchanged choice is not evidence that balancing is clinically optimal. Useful prospective collection recommendations still require a validated target, attainable costs and independent evaluation.

Decision-cost sensitivity at matched outcome-review budgets

The policy comparison can inform an auditor only after specifying the consequences of incorrect and unresolved decisions. For the same frozen policy and reviewed records, define loss $L=c_A\,1\{\text{wrong accept}\}+c_R\,1\{\text{wrong reject}\}+c_D\,1\{\text{defer}\}$, with nonnegative costs and zero loss for a correct assertion. For $c_D>0$, set $\lambda_A=c_A/c_D$ and $\lambda_R=c_R/c_D$. These ratios describe hypothetical audit preferences. They are distinct from the policy criterion's weight $w$, which defines acceptable policy truth. Neither set of weights has clinical endorsement. The matched outcome-verification budget cancels between methods; differential implementation, linkage and staff overheads remain unmeasured.

At $w=.10$, pooling produces 1,191 more correct rejections and 34 more wrong acceptances, reducing deferrals by 1,225. Its empirical mean-loss difference in deferral-cost units is $(34\lambda_A-1225)/42{,}000$, with crossover $\lambda_A=36.0294$. Below this ratio pooling has lower loss; above it betting PPI has lower loss. At zero deferral cost and positive wrong-acceptance cost, betting PPI is preferable on this panel. An approximate paired normal-Fieller 95% Monte Carlo interval for the crossover is [27.0704,53.7836], using within-policy covariance of paired outcome indicators, 1,000 independent repetitions per policy and equal weighting of the 42 fixed policies. It describes simulation uncertainty conditional on this panel, not uncertainty in clinical preferences or generalization to new policies.

The aggregate masks policy differences. At the primary weight, pooled counts are no worse in any loss component for ten policies and strictly better in at least one; betting counts have that property for one policy; three have trade-offs and 28 are identical. The three policy-specific crossovers are 2.7143, 1.35 and 29, so 36.03 must not be applied as a universal policy threshold. All differences arise from additions; all 22 removal policies have identical paired decisions. At $w=.05$, 18 policies favor pooling by the same empirical component comparison and 24 tie; at $w=.25$, three favor pooling and 39 tie. These are observed count comparisons, not stochastic dominance guarantees, and zero observed errors do not establish zero error probability.

All primary and $.25$ policies are unacceptable under the declared criterion. An unconditional reject-all action therefore has zero empirical decision loss in those panels, without supplying an inferential certificate. This analysis compares two inference procedures; it cannot establish the value of auditing over withholding every policy. At $.05$, the 20 additions are acceptable but no acceptable removals are observed. Rejecting and deferring may both withhold adoption, so assigning deferral a distinct positive cost requires an operational justification. The result supplies a checkable preference frontier for the saved audit decisions, not measured financial savings, staffing reductions or patient benefit. The executable check is analyze_decision_costs.py in the decision-cost directory; it reconciles 252,000 saved states and 1,260 category counts.

Retrospective reuse across saved model and threshold candidates

The practical replay includes the 12 displayed seed-11 model fits and all 54 frozen threshold outputs from the existing policy panel. The 42 direction-eligible policy contrasts are not treated as 42 distinct predictors. Two duplicated baseline outputs leave 64 distinct prediction/count inputs (two Texas, 31 eICU and 31 MIMIC) and 128 EB/JP queries. All 66 provenance entries retain their individual outputs. The protocol and aggregate inputs were frozen before timing; no new thresholds, model fitting or artificial probability shifts were introduced.

Each cohort shares one FNR race/ethnicity family at tolerance .10 and family error .05. The ordered groups, reference, denominators, eligibility and decision rule are fixed, whereas candidate error counts, repetition laws and recorded states vary. Zero-positive groups remain inconclusive. This differs from the earlier sensitivity workflow, whose 39 families at three tolerances required 117 preparations for 234 queries. The changed family subset and geometry mean that query count alone cannot explain timing differences.

Five fresh-process repetitions rotate engine and query order with one numerical thread, a 20-second query cap, a 180-second worker cap and a 1 GiB memory cap. Timings include endpoint/boundary/run preparation, recorded-state computation, full-support laws and integration. They exclude source-prediction extraction, training/inference, process startup, checking/writes and clinical acquisition. Full-worker times and aggregate input-read costs are retained separately in the verification archive.

All 45 workers and 1,920 calls completed, with maximum absolute output difference $2.22\times10^{-15}$. Independent reconstruction verified recorded CP states, cohort identities, outcomes, groups and every original candidate's counts across 16 private prediction files. The portable aggregate replay also completed all workers and checks in a separate validation run; those timings are excluded from Table S101. Private predictions and identifiers are not exported.

Run aggregation was slower than the uncompressed index in two Texas, two eICU and one MIMIC repetition; direct integration had the lower MIMIC median. The replay therefore establishes feasible reuse across existing candidates, not a consistent speed advantage or operational query demand. The five repetitions measure timing variation rather than create additional candidate demand. C1's probabilities remain conditional on supplied independent-count laws and do not provide candidate-selection or selective-inference guarantees. Outcome denominators are observed retrospectively; changed denominators require rebuilding.
